§ 33. As collateral security for a present advance.—Accommodation paper, in the hands of the party accommodated, without restrictions as to its use, may be negotiated as collateral security for a debt then created by the holder, or to become due, or in payment of antecedent debt, and the person making, indorsing or accepting the same as an accommodation party, has no defense as against the pledgee for value, before maturity, without notice of equities. The Supreme Court of Ohio, in a recent case, stated the rule as follows: "Where one, not induced by fraud, indorses a negotiable promissory note for the accommodation of another, without restriction as to its use, a third person who receives it before due as collateral security for a debt to become due from the person for whom the indorsement was made, and subsequently prosecutes an action against such indorser, will not be affected in respect to his right to recover, by the fact that such defendant is an accommodation indorser. The obligation of the indorser in such case is held to be the same whether the indorsement was for value received or for accommodation." A payee of an accommodation note, under an agreement with the maker, gave collateral security to the person discounting the note, who had no knowledge that it was accommodation paper. Afterward, the payee agreed that the collateral securities might be held to secure other obligations. The accommodation maker was held not entitled to require the application of the collateral securities to the accommodation note as against the party discounting it.

ACCOMMODATION PAPER. 59

§ 34. As collateral security for an antecedent debt.—  
The freedom of use and credit accorded to accommodation paper, when given to the accommodated person without restriction upon its use, has led it to be treated, when indorsed and delivered as collateral security for antecedent debt, with greater favor in connection with such use than the ordinary negotiable instrument issued for value. The undertaking of the accommodating party is liberally construed. Even in the states where the restricted rule prevails, under which the indorsee of ordinary commercial paper receiving the same as collateral security for an antecedent debt, without more, is not a holder for value, the pledgee of accommodation paper, receiving the same as collateral security under the like circumstances, before due, properly indorsed, and without notice, is a holder for value, in the usual course of business, and entitled to enforce the same free from antecedent equities. Nor is it necessary that the pledgee of accommodation paper under such circumstances should have parted with value, in order to be within the rule.

Pledge of memorandum.—Where a note was given as a memorandum, and not for negotiation, but the payee fraudulently pledged it as collateral for an antecedent debt, it was held that the holder, not being a purchaser for value, could not recover. Carpenter v. National Bank, 106 Pa. St. 170. Said the court in the latter case: “These exceptions rest on the proposition that fraud in the procurement or misappropriation of the note, as against one not a purchaser for value, is not a defense.”

b. Alabama.—In Alabama it was held, in a recent case, that when a creditor takes the note of his debtor, with accommodation indorsements, in payment of an antecedent debt, he is a purchaser for value, in due course of business, equally as if he had advanced money on the faith of it, although the rule is different when such note is taken as collateral security for an antecedent debt. Marks v. First National Bank, 79 Ala. 550.

c. Restricted use.—An accommodation note restricted by the maker, and by agreement between maker and payee to a particular purpose cannot be diverted from that purpose and held as collateral security for a pre-existing debt contrary to the purpose for which it was given. Germania Bank v. Schafer, 42 Hun, 630; 6 N. Y. W. Dig. 26; Ayers v. Doynig, 26 N. Y. W. Dig 13; see Partridge v. Bartholemew, 11 W. Dig. 34; Benjamin v. Rogers, 126 N. Y. 60; Continental Nat. Bank v. The precedent debt is a sufficient consideration for the transfer, and no new consideration need be shown. It is only where the note has been diverted from the purpose for which it was intended by the payee, or some other equity exists in favor of the maker, that it is necessary that the holder should have parted with value on the strength of the note, in order to enforce the same.

An accommodation note was received in good faith and without notice of equities, other notes being surrendered to the payee. This was a good consideration, the parties receiving the same being bona fide holders, and the fact that the note was executed for the accommodation of the payee, and fraudulently diverted from the use intended, forming no defense. The rule, as thus limited, is recognized in several cases in New York. A surety is liable on an accommodation note where used as collateral security for an antecedent debt. And, in another case, where promissory notes, made for accommodation, without restriction as to their use, were transferred to the plaintiff on the last day of grace, during banking hours, to be held as collateral security for indebtedness of the payee to the pledgee, and when collected the proceeds to be applied on such indebtedness, the pledgee was regarded as a holder for value. The notes were transferred before maturity, the maker having the whole of the last day of grace in which to pay them. A different view has been expressed in a Massachusetts case.

§ 36. The rule in Ohio and Pennsylvania.—The Supreme Court of Ohio considered the liability of an accommodating indorser, where the paper has been used as collateral security for an antecedent debt, for the first time in the case of Pitts.

Accommodation paper is a loan of the maker's credit when made without restriction as to the manner of its use. The fact that the pledgee holds other security more than sufficient to cover his debt is no defense for the accommodation maker. Where, however, such paper is misappropriated by an agent as collateral security for his own antecedent debt, the pledgee is not regarded as a holder for value in the usual course of business.

Beale, although the note in the case being non-negotiable in form was not enforced against the surety. In Watson v. Russell, in the Queen’s Bench, the rule was announced that a party who by means of a false pretense, or condition which he does not fulfill, procures another party to give him a note or acceptance in favor of a third person, to whom he pays it, and who receives it bona fide for value, the accommodation maker or acceptor remains liable to pay the same, because his acceptance or transfer of the same imparts value prima facie, and he can only relieve himself of his promise to pay the holder by showing that he is not a holder for value, or that he received the instrument in bad faith, or with notice of its infirmity.

§ 35. Misappropriation of accommodation paper as collateral security.—The pledgee of commercial paper given for accommodation, receiving the same from the holder thereof before maturity, in good faith, for value, and without notice of any equities or fraud, although the accommodation maker has imposed secret restrictions upon its use, and the act of pledge is a misappropriation by the accommodated party, is a holder for value, in the usual course of business, and entitled to enforce such paper to the whole amount of the face thereof, as against all parties thereto. This is an undoubted right of a pledgee for value, but where such paper is received from the accommodated party, and exceeds in its value the amount of the loan, and the pledgee is liable over to nobody for the surplus, if he should collect the whole, his recovery, as against the accommodating party, may be equitably restricted to the actual advance and proper charges. The inference in such cases is, that the pledgee of such accommodation bill or note gave value for it, that being the object for which such paper is given, although the act of pledge be a misappropriation.

A bona fide holder of accommodation paper, for value, before maturity, without notice of equities, receiving the same from a pledgee thereof, is entitled to recover the whole amount, although as between the maker and the payee and pledgee there is a complete defense. Where accommodation paper is given for the purpose of being used as collateral security, for a present loan, it is no defense thereto that it was received by a pledgee as collateral security for an antecedent debt, the purposes of the accommodation party having been obtained, and no fraud being charged; and where the power was to sell, and the note was pledged as collateral security for an antecedent debt, the maker remained liable; as also where the accommodation paper was pledged for a much larger amount than that authorized.

§ 39. Such pledges not sustained for antecedent debt, without more.—Pledges of accommodation paper, in cases of misappropriation, are not sustained in states where the more restricted rule as to the title of the holder of ordinary commercial paper as collateral security for an antecedent debt, without more, prevails. A pledgee, receiving accommodation paper by an act of misappropriation, merely as collateral security, without any further consideration, although without notice and in good faith, is not, in such states, a holder for value, in the usual course of business. The rule was applied in a case in New York, where restrictions had been placed upon the use of accommodation paper; the pledgee, although

The original taint of invalidity affects subsequent transactions, as, where a pre-existing debt for which collateral notes had been pledged, having been discharged, the notes were, by agreement of the parties, retained as collateral security for an overdrawn account. Under this class of decisions, the second transaction was vicious equally with the first. Nor will a pledgee become a holder for value, where, upon a tortious pledge of an accommodation note by an agent, to whom it had been intrusted to get discounted, for his own antecedent debt, the collateral note was afterward renewed, without consideration. But no recovery was allowed to the maker of an accommodation note wrongfully pledged by one intrusted therewith for a specific purpose, as collateral security for his own antecedent debt, who had paid the same, and then before the statute of limitations had barred any rights he might have had, but after the relations of the parties had been greatly complicated and changed, brought a suit to recover the money back. The lower court decided in favor of the accommodation maker, but was overruled by the court of appeals.

§ 40. Pledgee chargeable with notice of fraud or forgery, cannot recover.— Where accommodation paper is fraudulently misappropriated, and the pledgee receiving the same is chargeable with knowledge, actual or presumptive, of such misappropriation, or where the names of parties to such paper are shown to have been forged, no recovery is permitted as against the injured party. The fraudulent pledge of an accommodation note, purporting to be indorsed by a partnership, for an antecedent debt, where the pledgee was chargeable with notice of the facts, will not entitle the pledgee to recover as against the partner without whose consent the paper was so used. And where accommodation paper was fraudulently misappropriated by a member of a partnership, being received with knowledge of the fraud, and subsequently the maker of the accommodation note, having full knowledge of the fraud, gave a new note in renewal, which he subsequently paid, under the facts, the maker not being liable to pay the first note, his subsequent payment of the note given in renewal created no valid claim on the partnership to reimburse him the amount paid. The accommodation note of an individual partner, secured by a mortgage upon his wife’s separate property, the name of the wife being forged upon the note as joint maker, is utterly void as against the wife in the hands even of an innocent holder. The note and mortgage are one contract, and the former being void, the wife was discharged.

§ 41. Pledge of accommodation paper, after maturity.— It results from the character and purposes of accommodation paper, that the obliged party, permitted to retain such paper after its maturity, may transfer the same, either absolutely by sale or as collateral security, and the accommodation maker or indorser will have no defense, by reason of such negotiation after maturity as against a bona fide pledgee, advancing a valuable consideration, and taking the same without notice of equities. a. Mixed question of law and fact.—In Bacon v. Harris, 10 Atl. Rep. 647, the action was against the accommodation indorser of a promissory note payable on demand. And it was held, that the question as to what is a reasonable time within which a note due on demand may be negotiable before it shall be considered overdue, is a mixed question of law and fact, and, as a general rule should be submitted to the jury. The court said: “The rule in this country is that a note payable on demand is overdue for the purposes of negotiation unless it is negotiated within a reasonable time; and what constitutes such reasonable time cannot be determined by any fixed and exact rules, but must depend upon the circumstances of each case.” The same rule was laid down in Paine v. § 42. The amount of recovery by the pledgee.—Where an accommodation bill or note, upon which no restriction as to the mode or time of its use has been placed by the accommodation party, has been transferred as collateral security, in good faith, in the usual course of business, the pledgee holding for value is entitled to recover the full amount thereof, although he may have had knowledge that it was accommodation paper. But if he is chargeable with knowledge that the paper was intended to be pledged for a specified debt, and accepts it as collateral security for a larger sum, his recovery is confined to the sum actually intended to be secured. The presumption is, both where the note is taken as collateral security for a debt then created as well as where it is taken as collateral security for an antecedent debt, that the holder paid full consideration for the note. It is upon the defendant to prove, in order to overcome this presumption, that the holder did not give full consideration for it. The pledgee of such negotiable accommodation paper holding the same as collateral security for an antecedent debt simply, in good faith, although a holder for value, is, under an equitable rule, permitted only to recover as against the accommodating party the amount of his advances thereon, where less than the value of the collateral securities. Unless accountable to some third person for any surplus, no reason exists why the pledgee should recover the amount of his advances.

In Mechanics’ Bank v. Barnett, 27 Lou. Ann. 177, the pledgee was only given the amount of his advances.

Where an accommodation note was pledged as collateral security for letters of credit, the holder was not required to show that his actual advances had reached the amount of the letters of credit in order to enable him to recover the face of the note if the letters of credit were still unrevoked and his liability continued. a. Amount of recovery. — The children of H. executed to him their promissory note for $25.00, secured by a real estate mortgage, worth more than the face of the note, for his accommodation, but with no other consideration, to enable him to pledge the same as collateral security. H. executed his note to S. for $15,000, and pledged the aforesaid note and mortgage as collateral security therefor, with a power to sell the collateral at public or private sale, and to purchase the same. Subsequently the father and children assigned to W. $10,000 in the note secured by mortgage, to secure a claim of that amount due from H. to W. Neither the children nor W. knew of the power of sale contained in the pledge from H. to S. In consideration of such assignment W. extended the payment of his claim against S. for one year. S. indorsed upon the assignment from H. to W. an agreement to hold the note and mortgage, and deliver the same to W. upon payment of S.’s claim for $15,000. On default of his claim against W., S. sold the collateral note and mortgage at public sale, and bid in the same for $15,000. S., in proceedings to foreclose the mortgage, claimed $25,000, the amount of the note secured thereby, with interest. Held, that he could only recover $15,000, the amount of his claim, and that W. was entitled to $10,000. Handy v. Sibley, 46 Ohio, 9.

b. Withdrawal of indorsement. — An accommodation indorser may withdraw indorsement before note is discounted, unless other rights have intervened. But where such note is pledged as collateral security for advances, the pledgee can recover from the indorser the amount of such bona fide advances, but no more. In this case the maker of the note indorsed for his accommodation unable to get it discounted, pledged it to the bank for a loan by it of a much lesser sum. The indorser offered to pay the note loan, and withdraw the indorsement, but the bank refused, but assigned it to creditors of the maker, upon their payment of the loan. Berkeley v. Tinsley, 88 Va. 1001.

c. Judgment—Effect. — Where a creditor holds an accommodation note of a third person, which his debtor has indorsed to him as collateral security for the payment of the debt, the creditor may, after maturity

d. Limitations on use.—Under an agreement between the maker of a promissory note and an accommodation indorser, it was to be "used" only at a certain bank. McDowell, 95 N.C. 219.

e. Right of action.—Where a mere accommodation note given for the purpose of being used as collateral security for a loan, and made payable to the party for whose accommodation it is given, is transferred to one who advances money upon the faith of it, the holder may bring suit upon such note whenever, by its terms, it is due, whether the money loaned has become due and payable or not, and may recover the whole amount specified in the note, though it may exceed the amount loaned. Berenbroick v. Stephens, 8 Weekly Dig. (N.Y.) 163.

f. Unlawful diversion.—Where a bank receives an accommodation note, which has been diverted from the purpose for which it was intrusted to the payee, as collateral security for a past due check, the bank will not be protected as a bona fide holder for value of the note. State of N.Y. Bank v. Coykendall, 58 Hun, 205.

g. When purchaser put to Inquiry.—The purchaser, before maturity, of a promissory note drawn in the ordinary form and not referring to collaterals, is not bound to inquire whether there is collateral accompanying it or not. Islay v. Smedes, 26 St. R. 938.

§ 43. The pledgee of negotiable bonds and coupons a holder for value.—Bonds issued by a municipal or other corporation under statutory authority, and made payable to “bearer” or “holder,” are valid commercial instruments, and a pledgee receiving the same before maturity, for a valuable consideration, without notice of equities in the usual course of business, is vested with the legal title thereto, free of prior equities between antecedent parties, as in the case of negotiable promissory notes and bills of exchange. The title of such pledgee, so advancing a valuable consideration, upon the faith and credit of the representations of such negotiable collateral securities, in good faith, is good against the world. a. Payable to bearer.—Municipal bonds payable to bearer are subject to the same rules as other negotiable paper. Cromwell v. Sac, 96 U.S. 51; Pana v. Bowler, 107 U.S. 542.

b. Definition of municipal bond.—A municipal bond in the ordinary form is a "promissory note negotiable by the law merchant" within the meaning of that term in the act of March 3, 1875, (U.S. Rev. Stat. 18, Ch. 137, Sec. 1,) which allows a suit on instruments of that class to be brought in the courts of the United States by an assignee, notwithstanding a suit could have been prosecuted if no assignment had been made. Ackley School District v. Hall, 113 U.S. 135; New Providence v. Halsey, 117 U.S. 888.

c. Over-issue.—Municipal bonds are not invalid in the hands of a bona fide holder by reason of the bonds having been voted and issued in excess of the statutory limit, if the recitals import a valid issue. Dallas County v. McKenzie, 110 U.S. 686.

A municipal or other corporation which has paid interest for several years on its negotiable bonds, without objection, is estopped by its affirmative acts, amounting to a ratification thereof, to dispute the validity of them, in the hands of bona fide holders, advancing money thereon, without notice of equities.* Nor will mere irregularities in the organization of the municipal or other body issuing the same, defeat the title of holders of bonds for value where otherwise legally issued.3 Nor the failure by the officers of a municipal or other corporation to follow special directions in relation to particular bonds where a holder for value is not chargeable with notice.*

b. Corporate powers.—Substantially the same rule announced in the text applies to private corporations, which as a general rule, can have and exercise only such powers as are expressly conferred upon them by the act of incorporation, and such implied powers as are necessary to enable them to perform their prescribed duties. Fertilizing Co. v. Hyde Park, 97 U. S, 659; Solomons v. Laing, 12 Beav. (Eng.); Eastern Counties Railway v. Hawkes, 5 H. L. Cas. 331; Scoville v. Thayer, 105 U.S. 148. c. Irregularities.—Mere irregularities in the calling and holding of an election for the purpose of authorizing the issue of negotiable bonds by a county will not invalidate the bonds in the hands of bona fide holders, where no question as to such irregularities was raised until after the bonds were issued and had passed into the hands of such holders, although the election might have been declared invalid had the question been raised in time. State, Robb, v. Kiowa Co., 39 Kans. 657; 7 Am. St. Rep. 569; State v. Hordey (Kan.), 18 Pac. 942.

d. Rights of bona fide holders.—In County of Warren v. Marcy, 97 U.S. 96, 104, Bradley, J., in discussing the rights of a bona fide holder of municipal bonds, observed that "if a municipal body has lawful power to issue bonds or other negotiable securities, dependent only upon the adoption of certain preliminary proceedings, such as a popular election of the constituent body, the holder in good faith has a right to assume that such preliminary proceedings have taken place, if the fact be certified on the face of the bonds themselves, by the authorities whose primary duty it is to ascertain it." This rule is also sustained in Orleans v. Platt, 99 U. S. 676, 682; Commissioners of Johnson County v. January, 94 U. S. 202, 206; Commissioners of Douglass County v. Bolles, 94 U. f. Mortgage security bonds—What it Includes.—The rule announced by the United States Supreme Court in respect to bona fide holders of bonds secured by mortgage is, that rails and other articles which become affixed to and a part of a railroad covered by a prior mortgage, will be held by the lien of such mortgage in favor of bona fide creditors, as against any contract between the furnisher of the property and the railroad company, containing a stipulation that the title to the property shall not pass till the property is paid for, and reserving to the vendor the right to remove the property, and notice of such a contract to a purchaser of bonds covered by such mortgage will not affect his rights if he purchased from those who were bona fide holders of them, free from any such notice. Porter v. Pittsburg Steel Co., 122 U. S. 267; see Toledo, etc., Ry. Co. v. Hamilton, 134 U. S. 296, 300.

g. Payment of interest—Effect.—Payment of interest for several years on school bonds does not constitute an estoppel against denying their validity on the ground that the signature of one of the officers purporting to have signed the bonds was forged, where the fact was not known when the interest was paid. Ashwelot National Bank v. School Dist. No. 7, 41 Fed. Rep. 514. But see Brown v. Bon Homme County, S. D. 46.

h. Same—Questions of doubt.—In Moulton v. City of Evansville, 25 Fed. R. 882, 888, the court said: "While it is unquestionably true that the payment of interest will not validate a municipal bond issued without authority of law, yet in cases where the objection is not a want of power to issue, but of compliance with a condition, in respect to which there may be an estoppel by recital or other act of the city officials, such payments of interest ought to have, and have been held to have great weight.” In Portsmouth Savings Bank v. Springfield, 4 Fed. R. 276, Judge Drummond said: “All questions of doubt in relation to the validity of these bonds should be answered in favor of their legality, because the city has recognized their validity repeatedly, and has paid the interest on them for a series of years. Therefore, under such circumstances as these, it should appear beyond all doubt that the issue of the bonds was void.” See also County of Clay v. Soc. for Savings, 104 U. S. 579.

Pledge by broker.—Where a broker was permitted to retain bonds by permission of the owner, and he deposited similar bonds with a bank as collateral security for a loan to himself, the owner is not entitled to the bonds deposited by the broker, in the absence of proof of their identity; and even if identified he cannot recover them from the bank which received them without notice of any defect in the broker’s title, without paying the bank the amount loaned thereon. Nesbit v. Riverside Independent Dist., 144 U.S. 610.

Recitals—Effect of.—Recitals in municipal bonds issued in violation of the constitution, as distinguished from legislative provisions, can give no estoppel in favor of a bona fide purchaser. Hedges v. Dixon County, 150 U.S. 182; see Swan v. City of Arkansas, 61 Fed. Rep. 478; National Bank v. Town of Granada, 4 C.C.A. 692.

Notice on face.—The face of a municipal bond itself is notice to a holder that its validity depends upon the regularity of its issue. Mayor v. Ray, 19 Wall. 468; Wall v. County of Monroe, 103 U.S. 78; Claiborne County v. Brooks, 111 U.S. 400, 409.

Railway consolidation.—Bonds, voted in aid of one railway, which is subsequently consolidated with another company, may be delivered to the consolidated company. New Buffalo v. Iron Co., 100 U.S. 73; Town of Chickaning v. Carpenter, 106 U.S. 663.

Power to issue.—Express authority granted school boards, to issue bonds bearing interest, carries with it the power to issue interest coupons attached to bonds. Board of Education v. De Kay, 148 U.S. 59. And the grant of authority to issue long time, interest-bearing bonds, authorizes by implication the issue of bonds negotiable in form. Ashley v. Supervisor of Presque Island Co., 60 Fed. Rep. 55, 8 C.C.A. 455. So, under the Michigan statutes (How. Ann. St. Mich., Sec. 2717), it has been held that statutory power to issue bonds to meet loans lawfully made includes power to make the bonds negotiable. Brenham v. Bank, 144 U.S. 173.

Lack of recitals.—Municipal bonds which do not contain recitals asserting them to be issued in conformity with statute, cannot be collected even by a bona fide purchaser. Bergen County v. Merchants National Bank, 12 Fed. Rep. 743.

“But if the officers making the recitals are not such agents (of the municipal corporation) there is no room for the doctrine of estoppel. Their recitals, on no conceivable principle, can, in such cases, bind the corporation.” Court in Liebman v. San Francisco, 24 Fed. Rep. 707, 712.

Restrictions of contract.—If holders of bonds paid value for them, without actual notice of the restriction by a contract upon authority to issue them, they will be deemed bona fide holders for value unaffected by the agreement. McMurray v. Moran, 134 U.S. 150; 338 L. Ed. 814.

Pre-existing debt.—Bondholders may be deemed holders for value, although they took the bonds in payment of, or as security for pre-existing debts. McMurray v. Moran, 184 U.S. 150; 83 L. Ed. 814.

Security for margins.—A person who receives bonds payable to bearer, from a broker who obtained them as collaterals to secure margins, in the usual course of business, and for value, afterward advanced upon their faith and security, is entitled to hold them even against the real

aa. Bonds given for railway equipment.—Bonds given to raise necessary funds to complete a railroad, which are secured by a mortgage, are negotiable instruments, and in the hands of purchasers cannot be impeached for any neglect of the company issuing them to pay the demands of other creditors. Fogg v. Blair, 133 U.S. 535; 33 L. Ed. 721.

bb. Overdue bonds.—Holders of overdue railroad mortgage bonds who purchased them for forty per cent of their face value from the vice-president of the company, after the commencement of foreclosure proceedings and the appointment of a receiver, who was in possession of the property, are not bona fide purchasers so as to entitle them to share in the fund, where inquiry would have revealed the want of authority in the vice-president. American Loan & T. Co. v. St. Louis & C. R. Co., 42 Fed. Rep. 819; 8 Ry. & Corp. L. J. 282.

cc. Municipal corporation as stockholder.—A municipal corporation cannot lawfully become a stockholder in a railroad corporation without express authority from the legislature; and the grant of authority to subscribe for stock does not carry with it the power to issue negotiable bonds in payment of such subscription, unless such power is conferred expressly or by reasonable implication from the enabling statute. ff. Effect of statute.—Where the liability of a municipal corporation upon negotiable securities depends upon a local statute, the rights of the parties are to be determined according to the law as declared by the State courts at the time when such securities were issued. Green County v. Conness, 109 U. S. 105; Anderson v. Santa Anna, 116 U. S. 356, 361.

gg. Lis pendens.—The general rule adopted by the United States Supreme Court in regard to notice is, “that the pendency of a suit relating to the validity of negotiable paper not yet due, is not constructive notice to subsequent holders thereof before maturity. This general rule cannot be changed by State laws or decisions so as to affect the rights of persons not residing and not being within the State.” Enfield v. Jordan, 119 U. S. 680, 692. See, also, County of Warren v. Marcy, 97 U. S. 96; Scotland County v. Hill, 107 U. S. 114.

hh. Decision of court before issue of bonds.—In Illinois before certain municipal bonds were issued, the supreme court had decided that such bonds were issued without a compliance with the conditions of the statute, act of April 16, 1869, and were invalid, even in the hands of innocent holders without notice. Eagle v. Kohn, 84 Ill. 292. The Supreme Court of the United States recognized this decision of the Illinois court as “an authoritative construction of the statute, made before the bonds were issued,” and upon the authority of Douglass v. County of Pike, 101 U. S. 677; Burgess v. Seligman, 107 U. S. 20; Green County v. Conness, 109 U. S. 104; and Anderson v. Santa Anna, 116 U.S. 356, held, that the case of Eagle v. Kohn must be followed. German Bank v. Franklin County, 128 U. S. 526, 539. In Douglass v. County of Pike, 101 U. S. 677, 687, the court said: “After a statute has been settled by judicial construction, the construction becomes, so far as contract rights acquired under it are concerned, as much a part of the statute as the text itself.”

ii. Lis pendens—Effect of.—It was said by the court in Enfield v. Jordan, 119 U. S. 693, that “rights to real property and personal chattels within the jurisdiction of the court, and subject to its power, may be affected by lis pendens, but not those acquired by the transfer of negotiable securities.”

j. Execution—As to execution of municipal bonds, see Bates v. Ind. School Dist., 25 Fed. R. 193.

§ 45. The rule as to registered bonds.—A different rule is applied to “registered” bonds for the payment of money by municipal or other corporations, which are but quasi negotiable instruments, being made payable to a particular person, or “assigns,” and not to “bearer” or “holder.” Such bonds are like shares of stock, and usually books of registration and transfer are kept, and the transfer of such bonds is generally covered by statutory charter provisions, and are also by the terms thereof transferable only upon such books. A full legal title thereto, as against third parties, can only be acquired by a transfer thereon. Until such transfer is made, the assignee receives an equitable title only, and the bonds are subject to all the defenses to which they would have been subject in the hands of prior holders. Other bonds are sometimes issued by corporations, payable to bearer, which may, at the option of the holder, be registered on the books of the company, a certificate thereof being indorsed on the bond by the transfer agent of the company. After such registration, no transfer, except upon the books of the company, conveys the legal title thereto as against third parties; but such transfer may, usually at the election of the holder, be made to bearer, restoring negotiability to the bond. This power of registration, and the conditions thereof, generally appear on the face of the bond, and cover any number of successive transfers and registrations.

§ 46. The pledgee of negotiable bonds, when subject to equities.—Negotiable bonds and coupons, when received after due, as collateral security upon an advance or as collateral security for an antecedent debt, are subject in the hands of the pledgee to the like equities and defenses as other instruments of commerce, bills of exchange and promissory notes. The pledgee, receiving such collaterals after maturity, obtains no better title or greater interest therein than the pledgor, and is subject to the defenses available against the holders, although for value, of dishonored paper. The like rule is applied to bonds and treasury notes of the United States, payable to

§47. The negotiability of severed coupons.— The coupons or warrants for interest generally attached to corporation or municipal bonds are usually made payable to “bearer,” and are negotiable equally with the bond. When severed, they cease to be mere incidents of the bonds, and become independent claims, assimilating to negotiable promissory notes. Their validity, negotiability, or ability to support separate actions on the promises contained therein, is not lost or destroyed, although the bonds with which they were issued be, for any cause, canceled or paid before maturity. Suit may be maintained upon them in advance of the maturity of the principal debt, without any production of the bond, and interest collected upon them from the time of their maturity. The holder is not required to present them at maturity at any certain place which may be designated for payment before suing thereon, but it will be a matter of defense for the com-

The title of the pledgee of negotiable coupons, overdue.—The right of action upon coupons payable to bearer, and issued with negotiable bonds, whether they remain attached to the bond or have been severed therefrom, begins from maturity. a. Foreclosure.—A pledgee of bonds may also institute foreclosure proceedings the same as the original owner. He only differed from an absolute owner in this, that he was bound to account for any surplus received from the bonds and coupons, over and above what was necessary to the payment of his debt. Warner v. Rising Fawn Iron Co., 8 Woods, 514.

b. Past due coupons.—Past due coupons of municipal bonds bear interest at the rate fixed by the law of the place where payable. Pana v. Bowler, 107 U. S. 677; Huey v. Macon County, 35 Fed. Rep. 481; Nash v. El Dorado County, 24 Fed. Rep. 253; see N. E. Mtg. & Tr. Co. v. Vader, 28 Fed. Rep. 266.

c. Overdue coupons.—Overdue and unpaid coupons attached to municipal bonds are not sufficient to put a purchaser upon inquiry, so as to charge him with notice of defects of title. Ronede v. Mayor, 18 Fed. Rep. 719.

d. Interest on coupons.—It is the settled law of Illinois that coupons attached to municipal bonds draw interest after maturity. City of Cairo v. Lane, 149 U.S. 122; see N. E. Mtg. & Tr. Co. v. Vader, 28 Fed. Rep. 266.

e. Equities affect each coupon.—Each coupon is affected by the original invalidity of the bond. Bissell v. Spring Valley Township, 124 U. S. 225.

f. Interest in arrears.—That interest upon unmatured negotiable bonds is in arrears, is no notice to a purchaser of any irregularity or other matter rendering them invalid. Coler v. Santa Fe Co. (N. M.), 836 Am. & Eng. Corp. Cas. 460.

g. Pledge—Insolvency—Sale.—Where coupon bonds of a corporation, having a long time to run, and made payable to bearer, are pledged as security for the promissory notes of the corporation having a short time to run, the fact that the courts of the state in which the affairs of the corporation are being adjudicated in insolvency proceedings will not permit the creditor—a corporation of another state—to share in the assets while holding the bonds so pledged, is not a sufficient ground for restraining such creditor corporation from selling the bonds in case of non-payment of the notes at their maturity. Union Cattle Co. v. International Trust Co., 149 Mass. 492.

h. Who are not ‘bona fide holders.—Overdue coupons of corporate bonds, in the hands of one who was not a bona fide purchaser, but to whom the coupons were given by the owner, who cut them off, thinking the bonds would sell more readily without the coupons, and who, upon subsequent sale of the bonds, represented that all detached coupons had been paid and canceled, will be regarded as canceled and their collection restrained. Chicago, G. T. R. Co. v. Turner (Mich.), 7 R. R. & Corp. L. J. 189.

i. Payment—Set-off.—Where the coupons upon bonds issued by a township, accruing before a certain date, are invalid, and those after that date have been validated, payments made by the township upon the former cannot be set off as against the latter coupons, in the hands of a bona fide purchaser, although he purchased them, after maturity, from the person to whom such payments were made. Granniss v. Cherokee Township, 47 Fed. R. 427.

mercial paper by the law merchant. Where coupons, payable to bearer, are fraudulently transferred after maturity, the holder receives no better title than his transferror, and the latter having obtained them by fraud or theft, not being the owner, nor authorized to sell or pledge, no title passes by the transfer as against the real owner. Nor can the doctrine of estoppel be invoked to protect the holder as against the owner’s claims.

The bona fide holder of coupons payable to bearer, transferred for a valuable consideration, is not chargeable with notice of attached coupons past due and unpaid, do not thereby appear dishonored upon their face; but the presence of such unpaid coupons is a material circumstance bearing upon the question whether the purchaser acquired them in good faith, and without notice. Morton v. N. O., etc., Ry. Co., 79 Ala. 590.

k. Interest after maturity.—After the maturity of coupons attached to municipal bonds, they will bear interest at the legal rate established at the place where they are made payable. Thus, where bonds were payable in New York, and the bonds and coupons were silent as to the rate of interest after maturity, it was held that interest should be allowed upon the coupons at the rate established by the statutes of New York when the coupons matured. Scotland County v. Hill, 182 U. S. 107, 117. In Bank of Louisville v. Young, 37 Mo. 898, 407, it was said that “interest is to be paid on contracts according to the law of the place where they are to be performed; where interest is expressly or impliedly to be paid.” See, also, Andrews v. Pond, 18 Pet. 65, 73, 77, 78, 10 L. Ed. 65.

l. Suspicion of defects not equivalent to knowledge.—A purchaser of negotiable bonds or other commercial paper, in good faith, for valuable consideration, and before maturity, is entitled to protection, although he may have had suspicion of a defect of title, or knowledge of circumstances sufficient to excite such suspicion in the mind of a prudent man, and even although he may have been guilty of gross negligence; and this protection equally extends to a mortgage, or other security, given for such commercial paper or bond. Spence v. Mobile, etc., R. Co., 79 Ala. 576.

m. Sale to director—Fraud.—Certain bonds pledged to a bank as collateral were sold by the cashier to a director of the bank, who was also surety for the debt to secure which the bonds had been hypothecated, for a sum clearly less than their value. Held, that the sale was fraudulent and void. Dana v. Buckeye Coal & C. Co., 88 Ill. 871. As to bona fide holder of coupons, see Kneeland v. Lawrence, 140 U. S. 209.

§ 49. The title acquired by bona fide holders, pledgees, to “debentures.” — English “debentures” have many of the features of American bonds. They are instruments showing that the corporation issuing them owes money, and is bound to pay; and being negotiable in character, a bona fide pledgee advancing funds upon the credit of such representations, without notice, is not subject to any equities or defenses existing between the company and the original holder. p. Bill to cancel.—A bondholder cannot maintain a bill to cancel bonds issued to stockholders of the corporation upon the ground of lack of consideration, where the bonds have not matured and no default has occurred, where the plaintiff has no voice in the management of the company and no control over its property. Richardson v. Green, 183 U. S. 80.

r. Amount which may be proved upon insolvency.—In a leading case in Alabama it was held that when negotiable coupon bonds, or other commercial instruments, are transferred as collateral security, for the repayment of money advanced on the faith of them, the holder should be permitted, on foreclosure of the deed of trust given to secure them and other bonds issued at the same time, to prove for the entire amount of the collaterals so held by him; but he can only recover the amount of his original debt, with lawful interest thereon. Morton v. N. O. & Selma R. R. Co., 79 Ala. 590.

Sale—Notice.—Bonds pledged by a company as collateral security may be sold upon notice in case of default in the debt secured, in the same manner as stock; and this is so although the bonds are promises to pay and the sale has been enjoined in another state. Subsequently the president obtained the bill of his associates in the syndicate and attempted to secure an absolute title to the bonds by crediting a certain amount on the debt which the railroad company owed. Held, that such transaction was merely voidable at the election of the railroad company, its shareholders or creditors, and the other pledgees of the bonds could not impeach it. Hook v. Ayres, 63 Fed. Rep. 347; S. C., petition for rehearing overruled in 64 Fed. Rep. 660.

un. Security for contract—Enforcement.—Where a person holding a contract has assigned all his right thereto as collateral security for a debt, he cannot, before the maturity of the debt, require the assignee to sue for the enforcement of the contract. Reynolds v. Louisville, N. A. & C. Ry. Co., 148 Ind. 579.

y. Winding up corporation—Sale.—Where coupon bonds of a corporation having a long time to run and made payable to bearer are pledged as security for the promissory notes of a corporation having a short time to run, the fact that the courts of the state in which the affairs of the corporation are being adjudicated in insolvency proceedings will not permit the creditor—a corporation of another state—to share in the assets while holding the bonds so pledged, is not a sufficient ground for restraining such creditor corporation from selling the bonds in case of non-payment of the notes at their maturity. Union Cattle Co. v. International Trust Co., 149 Mass. 492.

w. Surrender—Garnishment.—Where bonds of a corporation, pledged to secure its own obligation, are surrendered to an officer thereof upon payment of the debt, they are not property of the corporation liable to garnishment in the hands of the officer. Galena & So. Wis. R. R. Co. v. Stahl, 108 Ill. 67.

Notes.

a. Past due coupons.—Where past due interest coupons of railroad mortgage bonds have been detached from the bonds, but are still in the hands of the owner thereof, and by the terms of the bonds the obligor has

<br>

### --- Page 0183 ---

94 NEGOTIABLE COLLATERAL SECURITIES.

the option to redeem them, a tender, in exercise of the option, of payment of the bonds and accrued interest, on condition that said bonds be surrendered, is valid, and will stop the running of interest after date thereof.

b. Past due coupons.—The presence of past due coupons upon negotiable bonds will not affect them in the hands of a bona fide holder for value. McLane v. Placerville, etc., Co., 66 Cal. 606.

c. Same.—The fact that negotiable bonds have interest coupons past due, does not destroy the negotiability of the bonds. Fairfax v. Bier, 37 La. Ann. 821.

d. Statute of limitations.—The statute of limitations cannot be interposed to defeat a recovery upon coupons which have not been detached from bonds; nothing can avail to defeat a recovery upon them except the presumption of payment which the law allows at the end of twenty years. Phila. Trust Co. v. Railroad, 160 Pa. St. 590.

e. Date of payment.—When no day is named in a bond or note given for the payment of a debt, it is due and payable on the day of its date, and bears interest from date, though no interest be reserved. McVeigh v. Howard, 87 Va. 599.

f. Coupons interpreted by terms of bonds.—In Goodwin v. City of Bath, 77 Me., it was held, that in case of a discrepancy in the amount of interest named in a bond, and coupon attached, the amount named in the bond controls. And the holder of such coupon, after its severance from the bond, cannot recover the sum named in the coupon, if larger than that named in the bond, as the interest, without showing that he or some prior holder of the severed coupon, acquired the same in good faith, before maturity, and without notice of the error. Respecting the character of interest coupons, as commercial securities, when detached from the bonds, Earl, J., in Bailey v. Buchanan, 115 N. Y. 297, said: “It is true that past-due coupons, payable to bearer, when detached from the bonds, are for many purposes independent, separate instruments. They may be negotiated and may be sued upon by the holder without the production of the bonds. *** But the coupons, nevertheless, always have some relation to the bonds. Their force and effect and character may be determined by reference to the bonds. They are secured by the same mortgage, and, although unsealed, are specialties like the bonds, and are governed by the same statute of limitations which is applicable to the bonds. Until negotiated or used in some way they serve no independent purpose; and while they are in the hands of the holder they remain mere incidents of the bonds, and have no greater or other force or effect than the stipulation for the payment of interest contained in the bonds.” See, also, McClelland v. Norfolk Southern Ry. Co., 110 N. Y. 469; Wood v. Consol. Electric Light Co., 36 Fed. Rep. 588.

g. Bona fide holder—Presumption.—Where negotiable county bonds, payable to bearer, have been floated for value, and the interest coupons, in a suit to recover interest due, have been received in evidence, a prima facie presumption arises that plaintiff became a holder of the coupons for value. Coler v. Commissioners, 27 Pac. Rep. 619.

h. Virginia.—In Virginia, it has been held that where a coupon purporting to have been cut from a state bond, is offered in evidence, the burden of proof is upon the offering party. And the party who attacks its

<br>

validity may demand the production of the bond as a condition precedent to his right to recover, and the question may be raised without a plea of non est factum. Code of 1837, Sec. 412; Commonwealth v. Hurt, 85 Va. 918; Commonwealth v. Adams, 85 Va. 921; Commonwealth v. Tunstall, 86 Va. 372.

i. Pennsylvania.—In Pennsylvania, the supreme court has held that the statute of limitations cannot be set up to prevent a recovery upon coupons which have not been detached from bonds; nothing can avail to defeat a recovery upon them but the presumption of payment which the law allows at the end of twenty years. Such a presumption, however, may be rebutted by evidence of non-payment. Phila. Trust Co. v. Phila. & Erie R. R., 160 Pa. St. 590.

j. Coupons—Interest.—Authority to execute coupons necessarily implies authority to fix the rate of interest they shall bear after maturity, at any sum not prohibited by law; and a coupon is a part of the debt covered by the mortgage which secures its bond. Benneson v. Savage, 130 Ill. 352; Gilbert v. W. C. V. M., etc. R. R. Co., 83 Gratt. 599.

k. Registered bonds—Pledge by executors.—That registered bonds offered as a pledge for an individual debt to a bank appear to have been transferred by executors is insufficient to put it upon inquiry as to the title of the person offering them, although he is one of such executors. Gottberg v. United States National Bank, 40 N. Y. St. Rep. 910; aff'd in 131 N. Y. 595, 42 N. Y. St. Rep. 883.

l. Pledge—Accounting.—In DeGraaf v. Wyckoff, 118 N. Y. 1, the action was brought to obtain an accounting for forty railroad bonds issued by the U. & P. V. R. R. Co., of $1,000 each, delivered to the defendant as security for the payment of five promissory notes made by S., and indorsed by plaintiff, amounting in the aggregate to $20,000. These notes were made and indorsed for the use of S., and the bonds were deposited in pursuance of an agreement between S. and plaintiff for the ultimate benefit of plaintiff as indorser. Afterward, plaintiff consented that forty first mortgage bonds of the W. & J. V. R. R. Co., with the value of which he was acquainted, be substituted in place of the like number of U. & P. V. R. R. Co. bonds held by defendant to secure the loan made to S. on the five notes. But in place of the bonds, which, by the authority of the plaintiff, the defendant was to receive the surrender of—the U. & P. V. R. R. bonds—he received what was in effect second mortgage bonds, issued on a consolidated road, formed in part of the W. & J. V. R. R., which bonds were worthless. These notes were renewed, and a second series of notes given, which, when they became due, at the request of the plaintiff, their indorser, the defendant took up from the bank which had discounted them for his, defendant's benefit. This was done on the promise of plaintiff to give defendant his notes for a like amount. But plaintiff discovering that defendant had received bonds from Scofield, different from those authorized by him to be taken upon surrendering the U. & P. V. R. R. Co., declined to make and deliver the notes as agreed. An action was brought by the defendant herein, as plaintiff, against the plaintiff herein, as defendant, for damages, in not making and delivering said notes as agreed, which resulted in a judgment in favor of the plaintiff (the defendant herein) for the amount of the notes, with interest. Held, that the defendant, being aware of the

<br>

fact that plaintiff was entitled to the benefit and advantage of the forty U. & P. V. R. R. bonds, and, having surrendered said bonds without complying with the authority under which that alone could be done, became liable for the loss plaintiff sustained through that surrender; that the recovery, however, should not exceed what was the then value of the forty W. & J. V. R. R. bonds, which plaintiff had authorized to be substituted for the forty U. & P. V. R. R. bonds, with interest. Affd in 83 N. Y. St. R. 1030.

m. Re-hypothecation—Bona fide holder.—M., a banker, borrowed of the defendants (except the defendant C.) $20,000, and at the time agreed to send them collaterals. Some days afterward he sent them fifteen one thousand dollar bonds of the P. M. Co. and three one thousand dollar bonds of the M. & St. P. R. R. Co. to hold as collateral security for the loan. These bonds were the property of the plaintiffs, and were, at the time of the loan, held by Meyer as collateral for the balance of a loan previously made by him to the plaintiffs. It appeared that the plaintiffs knew at the time of delivering them to M. that he expected to hypothecate the bonds for loans to himself if he found it necessary. Held, that the defendants were bona fide holders of the securities in question for value; that the mere lapse of time, under the circumstances, would not convert the loans into debts without security, so that the subsequent giving of the bonds would be giving of the securities for an antecedent debt; nor would it cut off the title of the pledges, there being no proof that the defendants knew that the securities did not belong to M. Greeff v. Dieckerhoff, 22 N. Y. St. R. 283.

n. Character of coupons.—Coupons partake of same character as bonds, and may be sued upon without producing the bond. McClelland v. Norfolk Southern R. R. Co., 110 N. Y. 469, 2 N. Y. State Reporter 250; 18 N. Y. State Reporter 344.

o. Same.—Coupons bear interest after maturity. Beatty v. Solon, 64 Hun, 179.

§ 50. The partner’s right to borrow money and give and receive collateral security.— Members of an ordinary commercial partnership have a general authority to borrow money upon the credit of the firm, in the usual course of business, and for partnership purposes. Such authority includes the drawing, acceptance and indorsement of bills of exchange, and the making and indorsement of promissory notes in the name of the firm, upon the sale or pledge of which money may be obtained or the payment of a partnership liability be secured. The exercise of this authority may

Such contracts are sustained as between the parties thereto and parties chargeable with notice thereof; but as against third parties who have advanced value, in good faith, upon such securities, in the usual course of business, without notice, they form no defense. The general authority of partners in commercial undertakings to bind the firm in regard to the sale or pledge of its paper cannot be secretly destroyed or restricted to the injury of an innocent indorsee thereof for value. The authority is given to partners in commercial or trading partnerships, and does not extend to farmers, doctors, attorneys, or others of the non-trading class.

Notes.

a. Pledge by survivor.—A sole surviving partner may pledge a chose in action, or other personal property belonging to the partnership, to secure a firm debt; and, if the transaction be made in good faith, the pledge will stand against not only the creditors of the firm but also against the representative of the deceased partner. Bohler v. Tappan, 1 Fed. Rep. 469.

b. Sale of collateral.—A note was discounted by a partnership which accepted certificates of stock as collateral security. A power of sale of the collateral on default of payment, without notice, was inserted in the note. After dissolution, default having occurred, the partners distributed the collateral among themselves and sold it separately at private sale, without notice. Held, that the sale was lawfully made. Appeal of Jeanes, 11 Atl. 862; Appeal of Elbert, 11 Atl. 866.

d. Louisiana.—In Louisiana a partner has no authority to pledge the property of the firm for his individual obligations without the consent of his partners. La. Civil Code, 1870, p. 374, Art. 351.

e. Pledgor as agent.—The pledgee of personal property acquires the legal title and possession, and the pledgor, retaining apparent possession, holds as his agent, Easton v. German-American Bank, 127 U. S. 532.

f. Pledge by executor.—The fact that executors have left to one of their number, who is a surviving partner of the testator, the entire management of the estate, and he retains in the firm (without authority) the capital of the testator, will not give him a right to pledge securities of the estate for a loan to the firm. In such case the pledgee may be subrogated to whatever rights the pledgor has as cestui que trust or legatee in the securities pledged. Allegheny Nat. Bank v. Farmers Deposit National Bank, 5 Cent. (Pa.) 505.

g. Pledge on winding up.—So, where a partner has power to wind up the partnership affairs, to dispose of its property and perform any and all acts which he may deem proper in the collection and disposal of the assets, he may pledge notes held by the partnership as security for a loan obtained to discharge an obligation of the firm, or a prior indebtedness of the firm to the same creditor. Smith v. Dennison, 101 Ill. 531.

h. Pledge for firm debt.—Where an officer of a bank received notes, payable to an individual member of a partnership, to secure the latter's private debts, knowing that the notes belonged to the company as proceeds of a sale of the firm business and stock, the notes were properly subjected to the payment of the firm debts in a creditors’ bill by the partnership creditors. Tolerton v. McLain, 35 Neb. 725.

erty of the partnership, or the indorsement of its commercial paper, as collateral security for the payment of an antecedent debt, is within this authority! Even after dissolution, a deposit of collateral securities or of the property of the firm, may be made to complete the contract obligations of the firm by the partner, to whom has been intrusted the settlement of its affairs.”

One of two or more partners may, in the conduct of partnership affairs, receive collateral securities for moneys loaned or debts due to the firm. Where the business carried on is that of banking, the acceptance of collateral securities upon a loan of money by one of the partners is such a transaction as would be a part of the ordinary banking business; and in cases of doubt the other partner may, by his acts or by his silence, waive his right to object to any results following the acceptance of such collateral securities with title. Where one of two partners in a banking firm received collateral security for an advance by his firm and taking the title thereto in the name of the firm the better to secure repayment of the money loaned, the other partner making no objection upon learning of the transaction, was equally bound by the liabilities which eventually followed the vesting of the title of the securities in the pledgees.”

§ 52. The pledgee, when a creditor of the firm.—The appropriation of the avails of a loan to partnership purposes, where such loan is made to a partner upon his individual credit, who gives his own note or other security for the payment thereof, is not of itself sufficient to create the relation of creditor and debtor between the lender and the partnership, nor to make the partnership liable upon the loan. And where money has been loaned to an individual partner, although the intention be to provide for his share of the partnership capital, and the money is so applied, no liability is created on the part of the firm, the loan not having been made to the firm, nor upon its credit. The decisive question as to the firm liability is, whether it, by one of its partners or otherwise, entered into the contract of loan so as to be chargeable thereunder, and not whether the firm obtained the benefit of the loan made by the partner. Where such money, however, has been obtained generally, by the individual partner, the fact that the funds thus obtained have been applied to partnership purposes, is prima facie evidence to charge the firm, or where the loan is not made upon the individual credit of the borrowing partner, and it is shown that the money was borrowed for and appropriated to the use of the firm, notwithstanding the false and fraudulent representations of the borrowing partner relating to the business of the firm by which the money was secured. Where one partner contracts a debt representing to the creditor that the money obtained is for the benefit of the firm, if the contract is within the scope of its business, the firm is liable, whether the representations were true or false. And where money was borrowed by a partner in his own name, his individual note being given, and the money is used for partnership purposes, a note of the partnership given in renewal of the individual note, is such a ratification that the firm is held.

Where there was a partnership liability for a debt, evidenced by a note with sureties, and a new note given in renewal signed by one partner alone, with the same sureties, who signed such note on the faith of representations that it was necessary in the business of the firm, and that the other partner would sign it, upon paying the note, the sureties may recover as against the partnership, although the other partner did not in fact sign the note.

§ 53. The use of trust funds and securities by partners. — Where one of two or more partners is a trustee, having the control and management of a trust estate, and fraudulently uses the trust money and securities in the business, but without the knowledge or privity of the other partner or partners that the money so furnished belongs to any trust fund, no joint debt or obligation is created as against the partnership by such use. The act of the partner is a breach and abuse of his trust, but this of itself is not sufficient to change the innocent partners into implied trustees, nor to render them liable as under contract, to the cestuis que trust. Where, however, such trust funds or securities are fraudulently loaned by one partner having the control thereof, and the other partners are chargeable with knowledge that such securities are not the individual property of the trustee, the firm, in the event of their loss in the course of its business, is liable to the trust estate for the value of the securities. Knowledge of the other members of a partnership of or privity to such misuse of trust funds or securities will charge the partnership; aditer, if there be no notice.

§ 54. Pledge by partner for his own debt, or debt of third party—Its subsequent ratification. A member of a partnership has no authority to use the name and credit of the firm to secure the payment of his own indebtedness, or the indebtedness of a third party. A creditor of a partner, receiving the securities of the firm, as collateral security

The proposed limited partnership was duly formed, but under another name, and including additional parties besides A. and C. B. loaned money to A., by whom it was contributed as part of the capital of the limited partnership. B. never demanded the assignment agreed upon, and none was ever made. A. died insolvent, but upon the subsequent winding up of the partnership a balance of profits remained, and A.’s share thereof was paid to his executor. Where a partner has wrongfully pledged the credit or effects of the partnership, or has misappropriated its securities for his own individual advantage, the other partner or partners may, by their subsequent affirmative acts, so far ratify and confirm the same as to render the partnership liable. As where a partner had given a promissory note in the name of the firm for his individual debt and the other partner obtained forbearance in its prosecution by a promise to pay it, a judgment against both was sustained. Or a ratification or recognition of the note so misappropriated, by the remaining partners, is sufficient. Where such note has been ratified by the other partners, and a note in renewal thereof has been given, no further ratification is necessary. The promise of such partners, implied from such ratification, needs no consideration for its support, as it does not come within the statute of frauds.

§ 55. The rule as to guaranties and accommodation paper.—One of the two partners has no authority, without the consent of his copartners, to pledge the credit of the firm by signing commercial paper so as to make the firm a surety, indorser, or guarantor of a third person, or to make accommodation acceptances or notes in the name of the firm. Persons receiving such paper with knowledge of or chargeable with notice that the act is a fraudulent pledge of the firm's credit, cannot recover as against the other copartners, without proving their authority or subsequent assent. Except in the hands of bona fide holders for value, before maturity, without notice of the want of authority, such indorsements, or guaranties, or accommodation acceptances, are without validity, and no rights can be acquired thereunder as against the partnership. § 56. The rights of the bona fide indorsee, under such pledge.—A bona fide indorsee for value, before maturity, of a negotiable bill or note given by a partner in the name of a partnership, and without notice of the equities arising from the fact that it had been fraudulently transferred for the partner’s personal debt, is always protected. If any one should suffer by reason of the fraudulent conduct of the partner in thus misappropriating the firm’s credit or property as against an innocent indorsee of such paper, without notice, it should be the person who has had sufficient confidence to enter into such close commercial relations with him as that of partnership. §57. Notice of misappropriation to charge the pledgee. — Notice of fraud, in order to charge the pledgee advancing value, in good faith, upon commercial paper, wrongfully misappropriated by a partner, with knowledge thereof, and thus defeat his claim as against the partnership, must be more than a mere suspicion of defects or knowledge of facts which might excite suspicion in the mind of a cautious man. Neglect, not amounting to fraud or bad faith, will not defeat the rights of a pledgee of such paper. There must be actual knowledge, suspicion or cause of suspicion of fraud upon the partnership in the making and negotiation of the note, to defeat his title. No such knowledge or suspicion of fraud arose where one of two partners delivered to a third person, a copartner with him, in another firm, a blank draft drawn by the partner, in the name of the first firm, and the blank being filled by such partner with his own name as drawee, with the name of the other firm as drawer, in the presence of the person loaning the money, the partner indorsing the bill, the money was obtained upon the credit of the bill. The possession of a negotiable promissory note by the maker, after indorsement has been made in the name of the firm, is sufficient to charge a third person advancing money thereon, with notice that the indorsement was intended for the accommodation of the partner, or the character of the transaction may amount to notice. In such cases, the burden of proving the assent of the other partners to the use of such accommodation paper, bearing the indorsement of the firm, when its character as accommodation paper has been established, is upon the holder of such paper; but the proof may be from circumstances, and not of an express and positive agreement.

§ 58. The recovery of the bona fide indorsee for value.—Where one member of a firm makes his own note payable to his own order and indorses thereon the name of his firm, receiving and appropriating the proceeds to his own use, the firm being duly notified is liable therefor to an indorsee, who, in good faith, before maturity, has given value for the note, in ignorance of any circumstances affecting its validity. The same rule applies where a partner has general authority to accept bills of exchange for the firm, and a bill is accepted for more than is due from the firm; there being no fraud, the bona fide holder for value of the bill is entitled to sue the partnership upon it at all events, to the extent to which there is authority, although the additional sum be in payment of a pre-existing individual debt of the partner. § 59. Effect of taking security from individual partner.—Generally, where the holder of negotiable paper issued in the name of a partner receives a new security from one or more of the partners liable on the same, the remaining members of the partnership are discharged. But in cases where the holder for value of such bills or notes, by an agreement made at the time, retains the principal note or other personal evidence of the debt, and reserves his right to proceed against the other partners, he may maintain an action against the latter on the debt, in the event that the new note given by the individual partner should prove insufficient. Where the bond of one partner was taken at the time of making a loan to a partnership, and, as the consideration for loaning the money, the other partners are not bound thereon. The acceptance of the bond having extinguished the simple contract debt, it could no longer be treated as a collateral security. A judgment recovered against two persons as partners, for money borrowed for the use of the firm, although remaining unsatisfied, constitutes a bar to an action by the same plaintiffs against a third person who is afterward discovered to have been really interested as a partner in the business, for the purposes for which the money was borrowed.

THE BANKER’S LIEN.

113

CHAPTER VII.

COLLATERAL SECURITIES IN RELATION TO BANKS.

§ 61. The banker’s general lien on securities.

62. His lien under contract, and as against third persons.

63. The banker’s liability holding securities.

64. The rights of national banks under mortgage securities.

§ 61.

The banker’s general lien on securities.—A banker’s lien is either general or special. His general lien, arising under the usual relations of banker and customer, is upon all funds and securities held by him, for the general balance of the customer.

Such a general lien arises upon the maturity of a note discounted for the customer, and then held by the banker, and will extend to other commercial paper, subsequently acquired by the banker, in the usual course of business with his customer, and to any commercial paper belonging to the customer indorsed by him to the banker for the purpose of collection.

§ 62. His lien under contract, and as against third persons.—Where funds or securities are deposited with a banker as collateral security to cover a special advance or discount, the lien of the banker thereon is limited and is discharged upon repayment of such special advance; and a claim of a banker of a general lien for balances or on account of other loans, upon such funds or securities, is not supported, where a contract for the special appropriation thereof is established. The rule applies equally to stock.

a. Release of security.—An agreement on the part of a bank which held stock as security, to release it for certain bonds, to take effect on mutual delivery, does not relinquish the title. Minneapolis Agric. & Mech. Asso. v. Canfield Bank, 30 U. S., L. Ed. 962.

b. Title of pledgee.—In a leading case in New York it was held that where a bank receives stock as collateral security, with the right to sell the same, either at public or private sale, and apply the proceeds in liquidation of the indebtedness, the bank acquires a good title to the collateral, which can be extinguished only by payment of the debt. Thompson v. St. Nicholas Bank, 113 N. Y. 325; 22 State Rep. 929; 5 R. R. & Corp. L. J. 590.

c. Pledge by executor.—And where an executor deposited bonds with a bank as security for his individual debt, and the bank had no notice that the bonds belonged to the estate or of anything to put it upon inquiry as to a title that could not be transferred, or of any intention on the part of the executor to embezzle the funds in his hands, it was held that the bank acquired a good title to the bonds as against the estate. Gottberg v. United States National Bank, 40 St. Rep. 910; aff'd in 131 N. Y. 595; see also Saloy v. Hibernia Nat. Bank, 39 La. Ann. 90.

d. Sale of stock.—Where a bank sells stock pledged to secure a note, and applies the proceeds in payment of other notes after applying sufficient to pay the note secured, after an assignee for the benefit of creditors of one to whom the maker assigned the stock has informed the bank that he claims it, the assignee has an adequate remedy at law against the bank, and he will not be allowed to redeem the stock thus sold. Roland v. Lancaster Nat. Bank, 185 Pa. St. 598.

NEGOTIABLE COLLATERAL SECURITIES.

brokers and others, who have received collateral securities for their advances under a special agreement to cover a particular transaction. They are not allowed after repayment and settlement of the special contract, to apply such securities upon a general balance or other claim.

The banker’s general lien attaches to all funds and securities deposited with him by his customer, as against not only his customer, but the secret equities of third parties. In the current business of a bank, the fact that an account is kept in the name of a person “as trustee” does not charge the bank with greater duties in the payment of checks thereon, which it is entitled to presume are signed in the ordinary course of business of the trust estate. The rule is otherwise, where, upon the insolvency of the trustee, the bank seeks to assert a general lien on such fund as against the beneficiaries under the trust, since the bank is chargeable with knowledge that the trustee is acting for a beneficiary. This inference arises where the words “as trustee” are used, even without naming the cestuis que trust, or as “general agent.” The rule is applied against the general lien of a banker in cases where no trust is disclosed if the fund or securities can be traced, whether the trustee has also money belonging to him deposited in the same bank.

§ 63. The banker’s liability, holding securities.— Bankers, and national banks, may hold collateral securities for the performance of contracts between third parties, and such corporations are estopped to insist that the act is ultra vires, as to do so would enable them to perpetrate a fraud upon innocent persons entering upon such contracts.

But a national bank has no power, upon the deposit of collateral securities to guarantee the undertaking or obligation of the pledgor, since it has no power to loan its credit in this manner. Notes.

a. Sale to director.—The cashier of a bank which held bonds as collateral security sold the same at private sale for a sum much less than their value, to a director of the bank who was also surety for the debt for which such collateral was pledged. But it was held that the sale was fraudulent and void. Dana v. Buckeye Coal & C. Co., 38 Ill. App. 371.

b. Refusal to re-assign collateral.—In another case where collateral was assigned to the president of a bank as security for a note, and the cashier refused to re-assign the collateral upon tender of payment of the amount due on the note, it was held that the cashier and the bank were not liable in trover in the absence of proof that by their joint action and control with the president was deprived of his property. McIntire v. Blakely (Pa.), 12 Atl. 325.

c. Duty of making demand.—Where a bank holds a note with others as collateral security for a loan made to another bank, the duty to present the note at maturity is not waived by a letter from the debtor bank directing that none of the collateral paper be presented for payment, which also stated that such collateral would be ordered back and new notes sent, where other notes are ordered back and replaced but not the note in question, in sufficient time before maturity to enable the bank to present the note for payment at maturity; but where the indorser is released by failure to present the note and the maker is insolvent, the bank is chargeable with liability for its payment. Chemical National Bank v. Armstrong (C. C. Ohio), 50 Fed. Rep. 798.

burden of showing negligence was on the pledgor. Nor will evidence merely that bonds were received by a bank for safekeeping, and were not returned to the depositor when called for because they had been stolen with other securities, be sufficient to authorize a recovery of their value from the bank.

§ 64. The rights of national banks under mortgage securities.—A national bank is permitted to enforce the collection of negotiable promissory notes by foreclosing the mortgage or deed of trust on real estate, given as security thereon where such note and mortgage are held as collateral security for the payment of a present loan, notwithstanding the provisions of sections 5136 and 5137 of the National Banking Act, authorizing loans on personal property only and restricting the acquisition of real estate. In National Bank v. Matthews, a promissory note and deed of trust were pledged as collateral security with a national bank, and the principal debt not being paid at maturity, and default having occurred in the collateral notes, the trustee was directed to sell the mortgage security. The maker of the notes filed a bill in equity, seeking to restrain the sale on the ground that the bank had violated the provisions of sections 5136 and 5137 referred to. The United States Supreme Court (Swayne, J.) in its decision, declared “the impending danger of a judgment of ouster was the check, and none other, contemplated by Congress. That has always been the punishment prescribed for the wanton violation of a charter, and it may be made to follow whenever the proper public authority shall see fit to invoke its application. A private person cannot, directly, or indirectly, usurp this function.
