Responsibility of pledgees of national bank stock for assessments. — A firm arranged with a corporation for a loan or banker's credit, to be secured by a deposit of collaterals. The account was opened and the first drafts paid upon a deposit of gas stocks. Subsequently one of the firm transferred 450 shares of stock in a national bank standing in his name on the books of the bank, and had a new certificate issued in the name of the President of the corporation. Soon thereafter the directors of the corporation deemed it inadvisable to have the stock stand in the name of the president, and the certificate was transferred by the corporation to an irresponsible employee thereof, with the avowed intention of avoiding liability as a shareholder of the bank, and the stock was duly transferred upon the books of the bank to the “dummy,” and a certificate issued in his name. This arrangement was made with the knowledge and consent of the officers of the bank, who had knowledge of the character of the transaction. The dummy never had possession of the certificate, and at the request of the corporation, executed in blank an irrevocable power of attorney to sell or transfer the stock. Upon his death the transaction was repeated with respect to another dummy, who retained the certificate until the insolvency of the bank, seven or eight years later. The pledgors collected the dividends upon the stock, and the pledgees never exercised any powers or rights as stockholders in the bank. The firm failed, largely indebted to the corporation, which retained the stock as security. The bank went into insolvency and the receiver brought this action against the corporation, as pledgee of

<br>

### --- Page 0209 ---

120 NEGOTIABLE COLLATERAL SECURITIES.

the stock, to recover assessments thereon to pay the debts of the bank. Held, that the corporation, having acted in good faith and with no fraudulent intent, was not liable as a shareholder of the bank. Anderson v. Philadelphia Warehouse Co., 111 U.S. 479. Waite, C. J., said: “The avowed purpose of both transfers was to give the company the control of the stock for the purposes of its security, without making it liable as a registered shareholder. To our minds there was neither fraud nor illegality in this. The company perfected its security as pledgee without making itself liable as an apparent owner.” P. 454.

Miller and Matthews, JJ., dissented.

Nor is a corporation, holding shares of stock in a national bank as collateral security, liable as a stockholder where it is carried on the registry of the bank as holding such stock “as pledgee.” Pauly v. State Loan & Trust Co., 58 Fed. Rep. (C. C. A.) 666.

b. Same.—One who holds shares of stock in a national bank, as collateral security for a debt, who does not appear to be the owner thereof, either by the books of the bank or otherwise, will not be held liable for an assessment upon the shares, under U. S. Rev. Stat., Sec. 5151, rendering shareholders liable for the debts of such institutions, to the extent of the par value of their shares, where the bank becomes insolvent. Nor is a person liable for such assessment who holds such shares as trustee, as security for a debt due a third person, where such person’s name appears upon the stock book of the bank as “trustee.” Such person is exempt from such liability, under the provisions of Sec. 5152 of U. S. Rev. Stat. Welles v. Larrabee, 36 Fed. Rep. 866.

c. Pledge by brokers.—The appellants delivered to their brokers certain railroad bonds secured by mortgage, to be exchanged for bonds to be issued under a new mortgage. The brokers pledged these bonds to the defendant bank, with many others, as collateral security for advances. Appellant’s bonds were commingled with others pledged to the bank by the brokers, and no separate or specific entry was made of them. On the failure of the brokers, defendants demanded the bonds of the bank, and upon refusal to deliver them, brought this action for the amount thereof on the ground that the bonds were pledged for an antecedent debt. The only evidence of the identity of the bonds was conversations between the brokers and one of the appellants in the absence of the bank officers to the effect that part of the bonds pledged belonged to the latter, and this was considered by the court as inadmissible—as not a part of the res gestae. Held, that the identity of the bonds was not proven, nor was it shown that they were pledged for an antecedent debt, and that the bank was entitled to protection as a bona fide pledgee of the bonds for value without notice.

Appeal of Klein, 14 Atl. 869 (Pa.), 21 W. N. C. 479.

d. Analogous case.—A case analogous to the latter was Saloy v. Hibernia National Bank, 1 So. (La.) 657. In this case plaintiff alleged that upon the execution of a title he had deposited with a notary certain bonds, as a guaranty of his agreement to procure the extinguishment of a general mortgage upon the property conveyed by him. The bonds were not found among the effects of the notary after his death, and it transpired that he had deposited them with the defendant as collateral security for an account overdrawn or which might be overdrawn. Defendant claimed that it be-

came the holder of the bonds in good faith, for a valuable consideration before maturity. Held, in the absence of proof that the bank’s acquisition was mala fides, that it was entitled to hold the securities.

e. Bonds pledged to railway contractor.—Certain bonds of a railway company secured by a deed of trust, were given to a contractor upon his agreement to build a portion of the road—or nine miles. Pursuant to the contract, the bonds were issued to the contractor, in advance of performance of the work, presumably, as the court intimates, to enable him, by negotiating them, to secure funds to carry on the work of construction. The bonds were sold or pledged to the complainants, who had knowledge of the terms of the contract under which the contractor received them. Upon a bill filed by complainants to foreclose the trust mortgage, the receiver of the railroad company filed a cross-bill alleging that the contractor had defaulted, in that he had only constructed four miles of the road—which allegations were not disputed—and praying that upon foreclosure the complainants be adjudged to be entitled to receive upon the bonds from the proceeds of the sale, only upon the proportion thereof that the value of the four miles of road constructed sustained to the value of the whole nine miles, and that the bonds be scaled down accordingly. Held, that the contractor was invested with title to the bonds, and had a right to pledge or sell them; that the averments that the purchaser or pledgee had knowledge of the terms of the contract in question, and of the contractor's default thereunder, were wholly immaterial, and that the cross-bill did not show any ground for relief and should be dismissed. Mercantile Trust Co. v. Zanesville, Mt. V. & M. Ry. Co. (C. C. Ohio), 52 Fed. Rep. 342.

f. National bank taking deed of trust:—A national bank may take an assignment of a note secured by a deed of trust on real estate and an assignment of the deed, in security for a loan. Union National Bank v. Matthews, 98 U. S. 621; see Barton v. Bank, 6 N. S. Wales, 82.

g. Issue of fraudulent certificate by bank.—H., as cashier of the M. bank, fraudulently issued a certificate of deposit to G. without consideration. The M. bank went into voluntary liquidation and was succeeded by another bank of the same name, which assumed the obligations of the original bank. G. pledged this certificate to the C. bank as collateral security for a loan, for which he gave his promissory notes. J. paid G.’s debt to the bank, and the notes held by it against G. were canceled and surrendered by the bank, not indorsed and transferred by the bank to J. For the amount of G.’s debt to the bank, J. took notes of G. running to himself, with the certificate as collateral. At the time of this payment the C. bank had failed; and the certificate had been protested for non-payment. Held, that J. took the certificate with notice of its dishonor and was not a bona fide holder thereof. It was held, further, that the certificate being fraudulent and without consideration to the knowledge of G., “a knowing and willing party to the fraud,” one taking the certificate from him after dishonor could not be accounted an innocent holder. Reed v. Stapp, 52 Fed. Rep. 641. (C. C. A.)

h. Loan by bank to cashier.—The cashier of a bank desired to procure a loan therefrom in order to purchase certain stock, but under a rule of the bank he could not, as an officer thereof, become its debtor. He there-

<br>

fore made? an agreement with the defendant, who had notice of this rule, by which the latter should purchase two hundred shares of railroad stock, and the cashier should advance to defendant, funds of the bank to pay therefor, and defendant should give his note to the bank for the money and deposit the stock as collateral security. This was done, and the cashier assumed ownership of the stock and agreed to pay the note. The bank had no knowledge of this arrangement except that of its cashier. Held, that this agreement, not being authorized or ratified by the bank, did not bind it, and it was entitled to hold the note and stock as collateral security, unaffected by any arrangement between the maker and the cashier. Savannah Bank & Trust Co. v. Hartridge, 73 Ga. 223; see Bank v. Farmers, etc., 52 Fed. R. 98. A case similar to above is Merchants National Bank v. Demere, 92 Ga. 735.

i. Loan to executor.—One of the executors of an estate applied to the defendant bank for a loan upon his individual note and offered as collateral security therefor certain registered bonds which belonged to the estate. The bank required, as a condition precedent to the loan, that the bonds should be registered in its name; that being the usual requirement in such cases. The applicant, by means of forged “stock powers” purporting to have been issued by plaintiff, his co-executor, procured the transfer and registry of the bonds, and when the same were received by the bank there appeared thereon, immediately preceding the registry in the name of the bank, a registry in the names of the plaintiff and the applicant for the loan, as executors. The bonds were not seen by any of the officers of the bank prior to the time they were registered in its name, and the officers had no knowledge that the applicant was executor of any estate. Upon default in the payment of the note the defendant bank sold the bonds to satisfy the debt. In this action by the other executor for conversion of the bonds, it was held, that the facts in connection with the registry of the bonds were not sufficient to put the bank upon inquiry as to the right of the executor to pledge these bonds, and it was not liable. Gottberg v. United States National Bank, 181 N. Y. 595. Barrett, J., in deciding this case at special term, said: “Where one purchases property from a trustee, knowing that the subject is trust property, he is put upon inquiry as to the trustee’s power to change or vary the securities. But one who purchases property from an executor is not, necessarily, put upon even this inquiry.”

“On the death of a testator, the personal estate vests wholly in the executor; and in order that he may execute his office the law permits him, with or without the concurrence of any co-executor, to sell or mortgage, by actual assignment or equitable deposit, with or without a power of sale, all, or any part of the personal assets, legal or equitable.” Perry on Trusts, Sec. 809.

j. Pledge by treasurer of bank.—Certain shares of stock of a savings bank were transferred by its treasurer to a national bank, and upon the pledge to the bank of the new certificates, a loan was made by the bank to such treasurer in the name of the savings bank. Upon default of payment of the loan, the national bank sold the shares of stock, under a power given in the name of the savings bank by its treasurer. These acts of the treasurer were fraudulent and were repudiated by the trustees and receivers of

k. Aid to failing bank.—The Penn bank was in failing circumstances. Thereupon the defendants, under an arrangement with certain other banks and bankers, became accommodation makers for said bank of negotiable paper to the amount of $239,000, and received $450,000 of the bills receivable of the bank as collateral security to indemnify them for so doing. This arrangement was made by defendants in good faith to enable the Penn bank to resume payments successfully. These accommodation notes were then discounted by the other banks and bankers, pursuant to the arrangement, and upon the faith that defendants had taken $150,000 worth of bills receivable as indemnity. Owing to the fraud of, and misconduct of its president and cashier, the bank was insolvent, but of this fact defendants had no notice before they received the collateral. In an action by the plaintiff, as assignee of the Penn bank to recover the paper so pledged as collateral, or the proceeds thereof, held, that the securities passed over by the bank to the defendants to indemnify them for raising this loan of $289,000 inured in law to the benefit of the other banks advancing the money. Appeal of Warner, 7 Atl. 216; see Kramer's Appeal, 37 Pa. St. 71; Rice's Appeal, 79 Pa. St. 168.

l. Title of pledgee.—In Giovanovich v. Citizens Bank, 26 La. Ann. 15, it was held that Ducross was indebted to the bank when the notes were placed in its possession as collateral security therefor, and that the bank had the right thus to receive them; that Ducross was lawfully in possession of them, and as to third persons, the owner of them, and could dispose of them at his pleasure. The responsibility was from Ducross to his principal, and not from the bank to plaintiff.

m. Application of payments.—A bank in 1881 agreed to allow to a firm, credit on a cash account to the extent of £10,000. By the cash credit bond which was executed by the firm, and by the individual partners, the bank was entitled at any time to place to the debit of the cash account any sum or debt owing by the firm to them.

On the death of one of the partners in 1884, it was agreed that the credit should be restricted to £5,000, and in security, A., one of the partners, deposited with the bank securities of the value of £6,000.

The firm was sequestrated on 31st August, 1891, at which date the balance due to the bank on the cash credit account was £4,884, and for bills discounted, £3,200.

A. was also sequestrated.

In an action raised by the trustee in A.’s sequestration against the bank for delivery of the securities deposited by A. on payment of the sum due the cash credit account alone, the bank maintained that they were entitled to retain the securities until the whole sum due to them by the firm was paid.

Held, that the bank’s right to retain the securities extended to the whole balance due on the cash account was not limited to £5,000; that in terms of the cash credit bonds, the bank was entitled to debit the cash account

<br>

124 NEGOTIABLE COLLATERAL SECURITIES,

with all sums due to it by the firm. Alston’s Trustee v. Royal Bank of Scotland, 20 Cases in Court of Sessions (Eng.) 1887.

n. Pledge by national bank, in view of insolvency:—A national bank was in failing circumstances; in fact, insolvent. Its officers made an effort in good faith, to save it from insolvency, and by mustering available assets and raising money, and by pledges of securities with depositors, they met the run on the bank. Defendant’s intestate had $8,850 on deposit, and to satisfy his demands for security the officers guaranteed his deposit personally, and pledged to him a promissory note of $3,031.35. There was no intent on the part of the officers to favor the pledgee of this note over the others, nor was the pledge made in contemplation of insolvency; their motive was to retain the money. The bank continued business about six weeks after this pledge, but finding the effort to save the bank hopeless, stopped business. Upon a bill by the receiver of the bank to set aside the pledge of the note, under U. S. Rev. Stat., Sec. 5242, held, that the bill should be dismissed. Roberts v. Hill, 23 Fed. Rep. (Vt.) 311. This case is instructive because of its bearing upon the question of what constitutes insolvency or what facts are necessary in order to charge the officers of a bank with knowledge of its insolvency so as to vitiate a transfer executed by them, as made in contemplation of insolvency. In speaking of their knowledge of the condition of the bank, and of their motives in making the pledge here in question, Wheeler, J., said: “Their apprehension of the condition of the bank and motive to prevent suitable distribution of its assets, ought to be made to appear clearly in order to justify going back so far as to the time of this pledge and opening all pledges and payments on past debts; and their purposes and acts are to be considered in view of what they could see looking forward, and not wholly by what is apparent now, looking backward. If they saw at the time of the pledge that the bank was approaching failure, and made the pledge to keep the note out of the assets to be distributed, the pledge would be clearly void; but if they made it to prevent failure and expecting to prevent it, it would appear to be good. The insolvency had come gradually, and not by any sudden loss which would arrest attention at once.”

Upon this question of notice to the officers of the insolvent condition of the bank, Nixon, J., in Balbach v. Frelinghuysen, 15 Fed. Rep. (N. J.) 675, 685, observed “that no knowledge by any of the officers of the bank of its insolvency is sufficient to avoid the transaction, unless the evidence clearly shows that the directors, who represent the corporation, also had such knowledge.” See Discount & Deposit Bank v. Oosterhoudt, 21 W. Dig. (N. Y.) 25.

o. Pledges in view of insolvency.—Where a deposit has been pledged to a correspondent bank by a national bank long prior to the commission of an act of insolvency as collateral to secure the payment of loans made to the correspondent bank, neither the subsequent insolvency of the bank nor the appointment of a receiver destroys the lien of the pledgee, nor its right to dispose of the pledge to satisfy the debt thus secured. Such an act is not within the inhibition of U.S. Rev. Stat., Sec. 5242, which declares all deposits, all transfers of deposits, and all payments of money made by a national bank after an act of insolvency, or in contemplation thereof, to be

<br>

null and void. Bell v. Hanover Nat. Bank, 57 Fed. Rep. 821 (C. C. N. Y.); Scott v. Armstrong, 146 U. S. 499.

U.S. Revised Statutes—Effect.—Sec. 5212 of the U. S. Rev. Stat. is directed to a preference—not to the giving of security when a debt is created. And where security is given in good faith to protect a loan, the security will stand, although the debtor was insolvent at the time, and the creditor had reason to believe him so. Armstrong v. Chemical Bank, 41 Fed. R. 234.

Validity of debentures.—The C. P. & M. Railway Company being authorized by 38 Vic. c. 47, to issue preferential debentures, the holders of which, it was enacted, might, on default in payment, obtain a foreclosure or sale of the railway by suit in chancery, the directors passed a by-law enacting that such debentures should be issued, under the seal of the company, and should “be negotiated from time to time as the proceeds thereof shall be required for the purposes of the company by the managing director.”

Debentures were accordingly issued in blank, and handed to the managing director who subsequently, the railway being indebted to the plaintiff, delivered certain of them to the latter, as security for such debt.

The debentures were in the following form:

DEBENTURE. No.

The C. P. & M. Railway Company owes the Bank of Toronto, or order, the sum of $1,000, payable in ten years, with interest at eight per cent per annum, payable half yearly, on presentation of the proper coupons hereto attached.

The name, Bank of Toronto, was not filled in until about the time of delivery to the plaintiffs, who now brought this action for an account of what was due under the debentures, and payment, or in default, a sale by the court of the property of the company.

Held, that the debentures were valid, and judgment must go as asked.

The strict rules of the common law relating to the deeds are not applicable to such debentures, but rather the rules of the law merchant relating to negotiable securities. But if this were not so, the fact that the name, Bank of Toronto, was not filled in until delivery to the plaintiffs, did not make the debentures void; it would come within that class of cases where deeds have been held good, notwithstanding an alteration or subsequent addition, because, at the time of the execution there was something which could not be ascertained and was therefore to be filled up afterward. Here, however, there was no execution, which imports delivery, prior to the time when the name was filled in.

Held, also, that though the debentures were under seal, this did not detract from their character, which was rather that of promissory notes than of mortgages, and though the act made them a charge on all the property of the company, with a right of foreclosure and sale, this was something superinduced upon the security by virtue of the statute.

Held, further, that the company having issued the debentures in blank, and handed them to the managing director, who was also secretary and treasurer, to be dealt with by him at his discretion, he was empowered to complete them by the insertion of the obligee’s name, and the company would be estopped from relying on such defenses as the above.

Held, that inasmuch as it appeared that these debentures were delivered,

<br>

### --- Page 0215 ---

126 NEGOTIABLE COLLATERAL SECURITIES.

With a view to facilitate the company’s operations in getting out and disposing of ore, the main branch of its business, this was a “negotiation” of them “for the purposes of carrying on the company’s business,” and so within the meaning of the aforesaid act and by-law.

Bank of Toronto v. Coburg, etc., R. W. Co., 10 Ont. Rep. 376.

r. Distinction between power to sell and power to pledge.—The Court of Appeals of Maryland have held that registered Virginia coupon consols, whether treated as bonds or as promissory notes, are not negotiable without indorsement.

The plaintiffs, two sisters, were the owners of certain of these securities, $17,200 in amount, which they assigned in blank to V., with a power of attorney to sell them. V. wrongfully pledged the securities to the defendant bank, which disposed of them at a private sale. Plaintiffs were advised that their securities had been hypothecated, but did not understand the meaning of such a transaction. Subsequently, under a representation that the bonds could be sold for a greater sum in Richmond than in Baltimore, and that such an act would be necessary in order to recover any part of the proceeds of the bonds, plaintiffs acknowledged the power of attorney before a notary, and thereupon the bank paid plaintiffs $2,094, being the increase of price obtained upon a sale of these securities at Richmond. Thereafter, the plaintiffs indorsed the securities.

In an action against the bank for conversion of the securities, the supreme court, reversing the judgment of the court below, held:

1. That the power of attorney disclosed on its face the fact that V. was not the owner of the bonds, and that he had power to sell the bonds, not to pledge them; that the power of attorney did not constitute an indorsement of the bonds, and that V. took no interest in them at all as assignee, and the bank, claiming through and from V., took, therefore, no better title than V. had.

2. That the subsequent indorsement of the bonds was not a ratification, because there was no power in the agent originally, and there could be no ratification of an act utterly void for want of authority.

3. That plaintiffs, being in ignorance of their rights, the receipt of a part of the proceeds of the bonds by them did not constitute a ratification, because:

a. There can be no ratification where there is no knowledge of the facts. To make a ratification effectual, it must be shown that there was previous knowledge, on the part of the principal, of all the material facts and circumstances attending the act to be ratified.

b. The mere payment to the rightful owner, by the wrong-doer, of part of the money realized by the latter from an unauthorized and tortious sale of the property of the former, can, upon no legal principle, be held a ratification or confirmation of the wrong, and a surrender of all claim to what may still be unjustly withheld.

4. That the plaintiffs were entitled to sue the bank for the full value of the securities.

Taliferro v. Baltimore First National Bank, 71 Md. 200. This case was followed in German Savings Bank v. Renshaw, 78 Md. 475.

THE BANKER’S LIEN. 127

ers v. Evans, 71 Wis. 188. The plaintiff, in October, 1882, deposited certain U. S. bonds with H., a banker, for safe keeping. In January, 1884, plaintiff directed H. to sell her bonds and remit the proceeds to her at once, in California. In August, 1883, H., in the course of his regular business as a banker, deposited the bonds with a bank as collateral security for the payment of his note, then made, of $7,000. The proceeds of this note, it was claimed, were put into his general banking business. In February, 1884, H. directed the bank to sell the bonds, and apply the proceeds on his note, which had been renewed, and was not then due. The bank sold the bonds, and applied the proceeds as directed. Subsequently, H. failed, and made an assignment for the benefit of his creditors. Held, upon authority of McLeod v. Evans, 66 Wis. 401, and Francis v. Evans, 69 Wis. 115, that plaintiff held a lien superior to that of the general creditors upon, and a paramount right to be first paid out of, the assets in the hands of the assignee. Taylor and Cassoday, JJ., dissented, citing Cavin v. Gleason, 105 N. Y. 256, and Appeal of Hopkins, 90 Pa. 69; see Hone v. Boyle, L. R. (Irel.) 27 Ch. D. 187.

t. Pledge for advances—Action.—A note was deposited by defendants with H., a commission merchant, as collateral security for advances to be used in the purchase of tobacco to be consigned to him for sale. Advances were made upon this agreement, and while the same was in force, a creditor’s bill was brought against defendants, and the commission merchant was made a party defendant and served with process, in order to reach the note as assets in his hands. Held, as to advances made by H. for the purchase of tobacco before he was served with process, he was entitled to hold the note as collateral for their repayment, whether they were actually used for that purpose or not; that the pendency of the suit amounted to an equitable attachment of the collateral in his hands and limited his claim to the terms of the agreement; and as to advances made after the service of process, he could hold the collateral only for such as were actually used for the purchase of tobacco. Brooks-Waterfield Co. v. Brookover, 55 Fed. Rep. 699.

u. Mortgage and stock as collateral.—W. was indebted to a bank $1,500, and held stock in the bank to the amount of $1,200, worth its face value. To satisfy the demands of the bank for additional security, W. gave it a second mortgage on live stock, and procured H. to sign a note with him to the bank for $1,500. Prior to signing, H. was informed by the bank that it held $1,200 of W.’s stock and this second chattel mortgage, and that in no event would H. be liable for more than the difference between the value of the bank stock ($1,200) and the amount of the note, with interest; and upon this assurance H. signed the note. The note was not paid at maturity. Afterward, W. borrowed $1,100 of P., the plaintiff. W. took his stock from the bank cashier and gave it to P., without indorsement, who handed it to the cashier. No record was made on the bank books, and there was no understanding with the bank that there was any transfer of the stock. Afterward, the $1,100 note not being paid, P. and W. endeavored to have the stock formally transferred on the bank books from W. to P., but the cashier refused, stating that it was held by the bank to secure H. and the bank on the $1,500 note. Packard then purchased the $1,500

<br>

### --- Page 0217 ---

128 NEGOTIABLE COLLATERAL SECURITIES.

note, and had the stock transferred to him. The cashier indorsed the note “Pay to P. without recourse.” This arrangement was effected after the maturity of the note, and at the time of the transfer P. had notice of the arrangement between the bank and H., and P. was told by the cashier that he must accept the note under such conditions and take his chances. Upon the action to recover the full amount of the note and interest, held that H. was entitled to have credit for the full value of the bank stock, and was only liable for the difference between the value of such stock and the amount of the note and interest. Packard v. Herrington, 41 Kan. 469.

y. Purchase by national bank of real estate—Where a national bank, at a judgment sale of real estate mortgaged to it, purchases the mortgaged property, and also other property not secured by the mortgage, this does not invalidate the title to the mortgaged property, which Sec. 5137 of the U.S. Rev. Stat. authorizes the bank to acquire. Reynolds v. Crawfordsville First National Bank, 112 U.S. 405; see Barton v. Bank, 6 N.S. Wales, 82.

w. Loans on real estate by national banks.—A national bank may make loans on mortgage security, if not objected to by the United States. Fortier v. New Orleans Bank, 112 U. S. 439.

x. Foreclosure of trust deed.—Where a party borrowed money of a bank under a general agreement that all collaterals should be held by the bank for any balance due from him, and gave the notes of a third party, secured by a deed of trust on real estate as collateral security, and the bank sold and assigned his note, and the purchaser foreclosed the trust deed, it was held that the surplus arising from the sale could be decreed to the bank, which was made a co-defendant, without filing a cross-bill, Walker v. Abb, 83 Ill. 226.

y. Security for doubtful check.—In State of N.Y. Bank v. Coykendall, 58 Hun, 205, S. C., 34 St. R. 432, the note in suit was indorsed by the defendant for the purpose of taking up other paper which he had indorsed for the accommodation of the maker, but it was given to the plaintiff out of the ordinary course of its issue, as collateral security for a doubtful check. But it was held that plaintiff was not a bona fide holder for value so as to charge the defendant upon the note. See Taft v. Chapman, 50 N.Y. 445.

z. Subsequent delivery of collateral.—Money was loaned to a banker upon the pledge of hypothecated securities (negotiable and passing by delivery) by parties who were ignorant that the securities did not belong to the banker. Held, that although the pledgees did not receive the securities until three or four days after the loan was made, they were still bona fide holders for value. Greef v. Dieckerhoff, 22 St. Rep. 282.

aa. Action against sureties of defaulting cashier.—In an action by a national bank against the sureties of its defaulting cashier, the following facts appeared: T., the owner of certain shares of plaintiff's stock and who was indebted to it, desired to have his notes discounted to apply upon such indebtedness. To avoid the statutes which prohibit a national bank from making loans upon the security of its own stock, T., for the purpose of securing the notes, assigned his stock to R., the cashier, individually, and the same was transferred to the latter on the books of the bank. R. then indorsed the notes, which were discounted by plaintiff, and the proceeds

<br>

### --- Page 0218 ---

THE BANKER’S LIEN, 129

applied in payment of T.’s indebtedness. The bank retained the certificates of stock and applied the dividends thereon to pay the interest on the notes. Thereafter R. misappropriated the shares and pledged the same to other banks as collateral security for loans made to him individually. And upon default of payment the shares were sold to pay R.’s indebtedness. But the notes given by T. to plaintiff were not paid. The defendants contended that the loan by plaintiff upon the security of its own stock was illegal, under U.S. Rev. Stat., Sec. 5201, but the court held that, assuming this to be true, the defendants could not take advantage of it because the act "imposes no penalty, either upon the bank or borrower, if a loan upon such security be made" (National Bank of Xenia v. Stewart, 107 U.S. 676); that R. took and held the stock in trust for the bank, and it was the equitable owner thereof, subject to the right of T. to redeem it; and that the transfer thereof by R. was a violation of his duty, and so a breach of the condition of his bond given to the bank for the faithful performance of his duties as cashier.

Previous to this suit the bank recovered a judgment on the notes against R., as indorser. Held, that this was not a waiver of the right to sue him in tort for the misappropriation, and so was not a waiver of the right to sue the sureties for the damages caused thereby; that the two remedies were concurrent and not inconsistent. Walden Nat. Bank v. Birch, 180 N.Y. 221.

bb. Estoppel.—A bank which held certain securities belonging to another bank to cover advances, stated in writing that they were held subject to the order of the other bank. Held, that this did not create an estoppel or preclude the bank from showing that it held the securities as an indemnity under a prior agreement for advances made—where it was not shown that the written statement was acted upon, or that the bank which owned the securities changed its position in reliance upon the letter. Jones v. Merchants Nat. Bank, 55 Hun (N.Y.), 290.

cc. Certificate of deposit is negotiable—Loans by bank on their stock.—A certificate of deposit in the usual form, issued by a bank and made payable to order or bearer, is negotiable, and a bona fide purchaser thereof for value before maturity, without notice of equities, is protected to the same extent as an innocent holder of other negotiable paper. Kirkwood v. First Nat. Bk., 40 Neb. 484; First Nat. Bk. v. Security Nat. Bk., 34 Neb. 71.

dd. Statute of frauds.—An agreement made by a bank which holds a mortgage as collateral security that in consideration of the payment of said mortgage to it before maturity it will release said mortgage and also procure the release of another mortgage on the same property held by a third person is not within the statute of frauds nor ultra vires. McCraith v. Nat. Mohawk Valley Bk., 104 N.Y. 414.

ee. Savings bank as pledgee.—Where a savings bank becomes the pledgee of bank shares which it has no right to own, and appearing as owner on the books of the bank, is not the owner of such shares within the meaning of the statute relating to liability of owners of stock. Exchange Bank of Canada v. City & Dist. Sav. Bank, Montreal L. Rep. 6 Q.B. 196.

The title of the pledgee under misappropriation of negotiable instruments.—The use of negotiable instruments, as bills of exchange or promissory notes, for the purposes of collateral security, indorsed where required, or indorsed in blank, or payable to bearer, is, under the general commercial law, so highly favored, that the pledgee thereof receiving such negotiable collateral securities before maturity, in good faith, and without notice of equity, is a holder for value, and protected, although the act of pledge by the person

Protection thus afforded the pledgee of negotiable collateral securities, receiving the same before maturity, for value, and without notice of equities, is extended to cases of pledge of such collateral securities where they have been received from one who has stolen or found the same. The pledgee, receiving such negotiable instruments in good faith and without notice is a holder for value; and only bad faith, which is never presumed, can defeat his title.

§ 66. Misappropriation of blank acceptances and accommodation paper.—A holder for value of bills of exchange, before maturity, without notice of equities, in the usual course of business, is protected, although the act of pledge be a fraud and misappropriation of such paper by a person who has been entrusted, with mistaken confidence, with a blank acceptance. The rule of estoppel in pais is applied in favor of the pledge, that where a man signs his name to a blank piece of paper, and delivers it to another to be negotiated, the latter has the right to fill it up, treating the signature as that of an acceptor.

A, owing a debt of £50 to B, writes to him enclosing a blank paper with a stamp sufficient to cover a bill for

latter his supply account was completed, and nothing was due from him on account of which the note could longer be held as security. The bank was informed of the consideration of the note, that it was only collateral paper, but was not informed that the defendant's indebtedness to its transferrer had been, at the time, completely paid. Held, that plaintiff was a bona fide holder for value and could recover on the note. The court said: ‘The consideration of the note was a lawful and valuable consideration. * * * As the consideration of the note was a valuable one, plaintiff could not have been affected prejudicially by the knowledge of it. If the consideration be lawful, the knowledge of that consideration can, of itself, have no bearing on the rights of the transferee. It is the knowledge of the failure of the consideration, or the knowledge of secret equities between the original parties thereto, that would prevent recovery thereon as between said parties.’

In Sadler v. White, 14 La. Ann. 173, the court said: ‘Plaintiff received the note before maturity, and before a failure of consideration. Even if it was known to him, taking it that the consideration was future and contingent, and that there might be off-sets against it, this would not make him liable to the equities between the defendant and payee. It cannot affect the negotiability of a note that its consideration is to be hereafter realized, or that from some contingency, it may never be enjoyed.’

The doctrine of National Bank v. Cason, 39 La. Ann. 865, is approved, under a similar state of facts, in Pavey v. Staulfer, 45 La. Ann. 358.

The title of a holder for value of an accommodation bill of exchange or promissory note, payable to bearer or indorsed in blank, receiving the same as collateral security for advances, is not affected by the fact that the party from whom it was received before maturity, committed an act of misappropriation thereby, having received the paper for other purposes. The presumption is, that the holder gave value for it, that being the object for which such accommodation paper is issued. In such cases of misappropriation the pledgee, who has advanced value thereon, in good faith, before maturity, without notice of equities, is entitled to recover the full face value thereof as against the accommodating maker, if less than the debt incurred, or to the amount of his advances where they are less than the value of the collateral securities. The like rule applies to the holder of accommodation paper for value before maturity, without notice, receiving the same from a pledgee thereof, although as between the maker of the note and the payee and pledgee there may be a complete defense.

The payee of a promissory note, upon obtaining an advance, indorsed the note to the pledgee by name, as collateral security. Upon repaying a part of the loan, the pledgor was allowed to take temporarily the collateral note, thinking he could make a beneficial sale of it, upon an agreement that it should be returned and indorsed by the pledgee upon payment of the balance of his advance. The pledgor immediately negotiated the note to a third person, to whom payment of the full face thereof, upon its surrender, was made by the makers. The pledgee sued the makers, setting up the restricted indorsement to himself, but the note was not produced. The makers and purchaser were held chargeable with knowledge of the rights of the pledgee to the note, although the purchaser could not read, while no estoppel arose, as against the pledgee, from the delivery for such a purpose, of a note specially indorsed. The failure to produce the note upon trial created of itself a presumption that the indorsement remained uncanceled at the time of payment by the makers.

§ 68. The pledge of forged collateral securities, and illegal pledges.—A claim founded on negotiable securities arising directly out of a forgery by one of the parties thereto, is not supported. Where, however, the action is to recover on collateral securities, which are independent of and not tainted with forgery, although the felonious act has entered into other parts of the transaction, the pledgee is entitled to recover. The pledgee was allowed to avail himself of the last securities, the agreement upon which they were received being a contract independent of the felony. Where a bill of exchange was accepted in blank for the purpose of being negotiated (the blank acceptance being given on account of a loan) and was afterward filled in with the name and signature of a person as drawer and indorser, the acceptor was not allowed, as against a bona fide indorsee for value, the bill having been deposited at a banker’s, who made an advance thereon equal to the full value of the bill, to introduce evidence to show that either the drawing or indorsement was a forgery, the forgery forming no part of the transaction by which the bank acquired the bill.

The rights of the innocent indorsee of negotiable instruments as collateral security for debts of the transferrer, receiving the same without notice of his want of authority to transfer, and in the usual course of business, is supported as against the rightful owner, even in states where the pledge or transfer, in any way, of collateral securities by the pledgee before the debt is due and payable, without the authority of the real owner, is made a statutory offense. Such assignment has been sustained in Massachusetts. Nor was the pledgee put upon inquiry as to their title, by the fact that the pledgors informed the pledgee that they would probably want to substitute other collaterals for the note before its maturity. A later case in the same state is to the like effect.

§ 69. Pledges of misappropriated, lost or stolen securities, after maturity.—The pledgee, receiving negotiable instruments as collateral security, after due, although for a valuable consideration, is subject to the antecedent equities and defenses in common with other holders of dishonored paper. The rule applies in cases where such negotiable paper

The pledgee in such cases acquires no title or right to such collaterals as against the defrauded owner. Nor will the doctrine of estoppel, founded upon the acknowledged equitable rule that where one of two innocent purchasers must suffer, the loss should fall upon the one who has enabled the third person to commit the fraud, be applied for the relief of the pledgee in cases where the possession given by the owner to the pledgor is for the legitimate purpose of making collection of the collaterals, and with no power to pledge, or in other like cases. A pledge made under such circumstances after the maturity of the paper vests in the pledgee no greater rights than those of the pledgor himself.

The rule that the pledgee of negotiable securities, receiving them after maturity, is subject to antecedent equities, is applied where such securities have been lost by the owner, or stolen from him. Where negotiable coupons were stolen from the owner before their maturity, and passed by several transfers into the hands of the defendant in good faith, for value, no presumption arising that the thief had negotiated the coupons before maturity, the defendant was therefore subject to all antecedent rights, and to all defenses of the promisor. The like rule was applied in a case where a negotiable coupon bond was pledged by a third person, who had obtained possession of the same by a felonious act, the bond at the time of the pledge being overdue five years, although continued payments of interest had been made thereon.

§ 70. Misappropriation of negotiable securities by agents.—The innocent indorsee of negotiable instruments as collateral security, for a valuable advance, before maturity and without notice, although the act of pledge be a misappropriation by an agent intrusted with possession and the apparent absolute ownership thereof, is protected, as a holder for value, in the usual course of business.* In a case where negotiable instruments were fraudulently misappropriated as collateral security by an agent, for a bona fide advance to himself, the United States Supreme Court say: “‘Although the pledgee took the note only as collateral security, he is entitled to the protection of a purchaser for value, without notice of anything to impeach his right. Conceding that the agent was not in fact the owner of the note when he transferred it, and that in transferring it, he perpetrated a fraud upon the true owner, it is still certain that he was clothed with power to make the transfer, and though its exercise was a fraud, if the pledgee advanced his money in good faith, relying upon the apparent ownership, the true owner thereby lost his title. He was bound by the act of his agent or attorney.”’ The pledgee, as a holder for value, is entitled to recover the full amount of such misappropriated securities.

The leading English case of Goodwin v. Roberts* fully supports the rights of the pledgee for value of negotiable securities, when taken in good faith, without notice of equities, although the act of pledge is a misappropriation thereof by an agent. The negotiable securities in that case were left with a stock broker, as agent of the owner, to be disposed of as the owner might direct, but the agent wrongfully pledged the same, with other negotiable instruments, as collateral security for an advance from a bank, and afterward became bankrupt. The bank sold the collaterals on the stock exchange, according to the usual custom, applying the proceeds to the payment of the debt, having no notice of the claims of the owner during the whole transaction.

The delivery of a government bond payable to bearer, by an agent, as collateral security for his own debt, notwithstanding he held the same simply to collect interest thereon, the pledgee receiving the same in good faith, without notice, was sustained as against an action of trover by the owner.‡

§71. Wrongful pledge by agent, for antecedent debt.—In states, including New York and Pennsylvania, where the rule prevails that the indorsee of negotiable instruments, receiving the same as collateral security for an antecedent debt, without further consideration, is not a holder for value, in the usual course of business, the pledgee, so receiving such securities from an agent, where the act is one of misappropriation, although without knowledge thereof, is not entitled to recover. The question of misappropriation by agents arose in the leading cases of Coddington v. Bay and Stalker v. McDon-

§ 72. The rule as applied to bankers.—Protection is also afforded the bona fide pledgee of negotiable securities in cases where the wrongful misappropriation thereof is the act of bankers or banking corporations, holding such negotiable instruments with full title. Where, by reason of misplaced confidence, a banker is intrusted with possession of such evidences of title as negotiable promissory notes, indorsed in blank, although the purpose simply be that he may collect accruing interest thereon, and the banker deposits the notes, with other securities, with his correspondents, as collateral security for present indebtedness and for future advances, the real owner is not allowed, in an action of replevin, brought after the country banker has become insolvent, to recover possession of the notes so pledged from the indorsee holding them in good faith, for value in the usual course of business, as collateral security. A banker, with whom negotiable bills have been deposited, making an indorsement thereof as collateral security for a loan to himself, the property in such bills, to the extent at least of the advances, passes to the bona fide indorsee as against the real owner. And a pledge of such negotiable paper, intrusted to a bank director as an individual, for the purpose of getting the same discounted for the benefit of the owner, to the bank of which he is a director, for his own past debt and a present advance, was supported as against the real owner, the bank not being chargeable with notice of the real transaction, as the director was not acting in his official capacity in obtaining the loan.

The pledge of negotiable instruments by a bank, holding them on deposit for safe keeping, for the purpose of securing the repayment of a loan to itself, vests in the pledgees a title thereto good as against all the world, to hold and dispose of them according to the terms of the contract of pledge. Such title cannot be divested by a “dishonest trick,” nor by the fact that the pledgor recovered possession by an act of gross fraud or violence. And where the managing cashier of a bank has been authorized by the directors thereof to transfer to another bank as collateral security for a loan, notes and bills discounted by the borrowing bank, and a loan was made in good faith, the right of the pledgee to recover was not affected by the fact that the cashier of the borrowing bank gave a note, signed by himself individually, and payable to himself as cashier, for the amount of the loan, if in fact the application was for a loan to his bank, and on its credit, and the loan was in good faith so made. The fact that the cashier misapplied the money to his own private purposes was held not to affect the validity of the contract, nor to prevent the pledgee from collecting the securities, and retaining enough to repay its advances.

§ 73. The rule as applied to executors and administrators.—Generally, an executor may dispose of the personal estate, including negotiable securities, of the testator by sale or pledge, in connection with the management of the estate, and even where the sale or pledge of such securities is made for other purposes, of which the person advancing money has no knowledge or notice, but receives the same, in good faith, for value, the transaction is sustained, for the pledgee is not bound to see to the disposition of the loan. The rule is otherwise where the pledgee is chargeable with knowledge that such disposition of the assets of the estate is a perversion, against the assignee in bankruptcy.

a. Pledge by executors.—In Smith v. Second National Bank, 70 Hun (N. Y.), 357, an ancillary administrator obtained, as such, a loan from a bank on the ground that he needed the same for the use of the estate, in anticipation of income. He gave to the bank for such loan a promissory note, with a municipal bond which stood in the name of and formed a part of the assets of the estate of his intestate as collateral security therefor. Upon default of payment the bank attempted to dispose of the collateral, but was enjoined from so doing in a suit by an ancillary administrator appointed as successor of the pledgor of the bond. Held, that an ancillary administrator has no right to pledge any portion of the assets of an estate which may come into his hands, and that the bank could not be deemed a bona fide holder of the bond, so as to be protected in its possession thereof. Gottberg v. U. S. Nat. Bank, 131 U. S. 595.

b. Same.—In a case decided by the Supreme Court of the Hawaiian Islands, it was held that a pledge by an executor of securities in his hands as collateral for a loan is unauthorized. But inasmuch as the pledgees are not put upon inquiry as to the executor’s misapplication of the funds, and the misapplication not being fraudulent, the court refused to compel the defendants to give up the note which was held by them as collateral security. c. Pledge as security.—In Rozers v. Squires, 98 N. Y. 49, an administrator transferred certain promissory notes belonging to the estate to the sureties upon his official bond as security against their liability thereon. In an action upon the notes it was held that the pledgees had such title to them as enabled them to recover thereon against the maker; that if there was a misappropriation of the notes, the debtor, defending solely in that character, could not raise the question. The notes were also pledged as security for any advances the pledgees might make in extinguishment of a judgment against the estate upon which the sureties were liable. The sureties made such advances, and it was held that whatever may have been their rights previously, upon making the payments their title to the notes as pledges became good.

§ 74. And to directors of corporations.—The pledge of bonds or other securities of a corporation by the officers thereof to themselves, or to some of their number, is required to be made in good faith, the tendency being to scrutinize such transactions closely and rigorously. Where a pledge of such bonds is made by the officers and directors of a railroad company to each other to secure an indebtedness of less than four per cent of the face of the bonds, the transaction on its face is nothing less than an actual fraud upon the corporation and its stockholders.? But there is no reason why a director, or officer of a corporation, may not receive the negotiable bonds or other securities thereof as collateral security, where a debt is honestly due him, or he has incurred a liability, or advanced money thereon. § 75. What notice of defects, etc., will defeat the title of the pledgee.—The knowledge or degree of negligence, on the part of one claiming to be a bona fide pledgee of negotiable paper, of defects in the same, or of the misappropriation thereof, or of the pledgor’s want of title thereto, sufficient to

a. Notice derivable from particular circumstances.—The later decisions both in this country and in England, fully sustain the rule that where one intrusted with the possession and apparent ownership of negotiable collateral securities pledges the same to persons who advance money thereon in good faith, before maturity, and without notice of equities, the pledgees will be protected, although the pledge was made without authority and in fraud of the rights of the true owner. But there are certain exceptions to this general rule arising from particular circumstances which have been held sufficient to charge the pledgees with notice of infirmity of the pledgor's title. In the case of Lord Sheffield v. London Joint Stock Bank, 13 App. Cas. 333, the facts were these: Lord Sheffield gave Easton authority to borrow £26,000, upon the security of stocks in the Grand Trunk Railway, and certain railway and canal bonds. To raise this sum, Lord Sheffield gave Easton the bonds and stock certificates, together with transfers executed by him, blanks being left for the names of the transferees. These stocks, transfers and bonds were deposited by Easton with Mozley, a money-lender, who lent Easton the £26,000 on their security. Some of these stocks, transfers and bonds were deposited by Mozley with the defendants, together with other securities belonging to Mozley's customers, as security for a large loan, accounts running between Mozley and the defendant bank. The transfers were filled in with the names or nominees of the banks, and registered with the Grand Trunk Company. Mozley went into liquidation, and in an action to recover the securities or the proceeds, less the amount advanced thereon to Easton, the trial court decided in favor of the defendants, and the judgment was sustained by the Court of Appeal, which held, on the authority of Goodwin v. Robarts, 1 App. Cas. 476, that these bonds were to be treated as negotiable securities between the parties. The House of Lords reversed the decision of the court of appeal on the ground that the banks either actually knew, or had reason to believe, that the securities did or might belong, not to Mozley, but to his customers, and held that the banks were bound to inquire into the extent of Mozley’s authority to pledge the securities. It appeared from the evidence that Mozley was accustomed to re-hypothecate securities belonging to his customers to the banks to cover loans to himself, and that it was the practice of the banks to release particular securities in pursuance of the demands of Moz-

This practice appeared to be for the mutual advantage of both Mozley and the banks, and Lord Chancellor Halsbury in speaking of the practice declared his belief that “Mozley’s business could not have lasted a month if the banks had not allowed this system to continue by exchanging securities.” The conclusion I draw from the facts proved,” continued the Lord Chancellor, “is that the banks knew very well the system of money-lending pursued by Mozley, and trusted to him that he would not over-pledge, so to speak, the securities of his customers. Otherwise the very first security refused to Mozley’s customer upon his tendering the amount advanced upon it would have brought the whole business to a very speedy end.”

The House of Lords placed their decision, as we have seen, on the ground that under the particular circumstances disclosed in this case, the banks were chargeable with notice of the facts affecting Mozley's title to the securities which should have put them on inquiry as to his power to pledge them. “The banks knew,” observed Lord Macnaghten, “that the person who dealt with them as owner was not acting by right of ownership. They took it for granted that he had authority, but for some reason or other they did not choose to inquire what that authority was. They relied either on some assured custom or general usage of bankers or on Mozley’s representations.”

This effort of the banks to prove a custom (which failed) Lord Chancellor Halsbury thought was “conclusive against them to show that they knew the nature of Mozley's business.” All the judges in the House of Lords filed concurring opinions.

Strenuous effort was made to bring the case within the ruling of Lord Sheffield’s case (13 App. Cas. 33). In the former case a firm of brokers held $15,000 Cedulas on account of respondent, for safe custody only. On the 12th of October, 1887, Delmar, without the knowledge of his partner, and in fraud of his customer, sold them. On the same day, Delmar, on account of his firm, contracted to buy Cedulas of the same amount and denomination to be delivered on the 28th, and the same were delivered and paid for. The defendant bank had for many years been in the habit of making advances to the firm of which Delmar was a member, receiving as collateral security stocks, shares and bonds, which were frequently changed. On the 28th of October, 1887, the said firm obtained from the bank a temporary advance, in addition to the then current loan, and in addition to securities which the bank then held for the moneys already advanced, and which by the terms of their security they were entitled to hold for any additional advances, the firm in question deposited with the bank the Cedula bonds which were purchased to take the place of those sold—the transaction being a mere cover for a fraudulent act. The bonds were obtained in exchange for a check on the appellants which was necessary to enable the firm to pay for the same. Delmar afterward absconded, and the action was brought to recover the bonds. The trial court decided in favor of the plaintiff, and its decision was affirmed by the court of appeal. The House of Lords reversed the decision of the court of appeal on the ground that the appellants received the bonds of brokers of hitherto unblemished reputation in the ordinary course of business to cover their current advance; that they took them in good faith, without notice of any defect in the pledgor's title. In deciding this case the House of Lords steadily adhered to the rule in Goodwin v. Robarts, 1 App. Cas. 476, holding that Lord Sheffield’s case did not purport to be a new departure or to lay down any principle of law differing from that already established, since that case depended on its own peculiar circumstances, and the settled law relating to negotiable securities was not there in question. Lord Chancellor Halsbury was of the opinion that there was nothing in the nature of the transaction in question or “nothing in the position of broker and customer respectively, which makes it a reasonable inference that the broker was exceeding his authority, or, indeed, that there was anything which could be reasonably supposed to raise a doubt on the subject.”

The facts were these: A stock broker in Dublin purchased for his principal fifty preferred shares of the Northern Pacific Railway Company. The certificates of these shares had indorsed on them an assignment in blank and a power of attorney; and by custom of the stock exchange they were treated by brokers and bankers as transferable from hand to hand by the mere delivery of the certificates. The broker bought and sold shares for his customer, and often retained possession of the same for a considerable period. Without the knowledge of his customer, the broker pledged these shares to the defendants as security for a loan of £550. The broker became insolvent, and the plaintiff, as administrator of the customer, brought this action to have the defendants, who had sold the securities to repay the loan, declared trustees for the plaintiff. owner of the shares, or that he had no authority to pledge them; that the customer was not the registered owner of the shares, and as his name did not appear anywhere in connection with the shares, the same were “in order” in the hands of the broker: and that consequently the defendants were bona fide purchasers for a valuable consideration, without notice of any defect in the title.

In Mulville v. Munster and Leinster Bank, L. R. (Irel.) 27 Ch. D. 879, the facts were similar to the preceding case. A broker in Dublin was directed by his customer to sell certain bonds, and to purchase others with the proceeds. The broker received the bonds so purchased and entered them by their numbers to the customer in his books, but did not deliver them to the customer. The broker, in fraud of his customer's rights, pledged the bonds with defendants, who were aware that he was a stock and share dealer, together with various other securities, to cover a balance due from him to the defendants on a loan account then opened, and also to secure an overdraft on his current account and future advances. The defendants were also aware that the broker, two years before the pledge of these bonds, made an arrangement with his creditors, and carried a composition of two shillings in the pound, and that the broker was in needy circumstances.

In an action to have the defendants declared trustees for the bonds of the plaintiff, held, that upon the purchase of the bonds, and the entry of them as the plaintiff's on the broker's books, they became the plaintiff’s property; and that the circumstances of the case were sufficient to put the defendants on inquiry, and that there were grounds for their suspecting that the securities pledged might not be the absolute property of the broker.

An effort was made to bring this case within the decision of Hone v. Boyle, but without success, the court holding, as in Lord Sheffield’s case, that the case was governed entirely by particular circumstances deemed sufficient to put the defendants upon inquiry as to the right or authority of the brokers to pledge securities belonging to customers.

In this country the rule announced by the House of Lords in Goodwin v. Robarts, 1 App. Cas. 476, and in London Joint Stock Bank v. Simmons, L. R. App. Cas. 1892, 201, have been recognized as authority by the highest courts. And in no cases in this country does it appear to have been held that knowledge that the pledgee was a stock broker, or of the fact that he deposited securities of his customers en bloc, were circumstances of themselves sufficient to put the pledgees on inquiry as to the pledgees’ title. In Thompson v. St. Nicholas Bank, 113 N. Y. 825, the Court of Ap-

§ 76. Notice by the terms of the collateral security.—Where the negotiable instrument offered as collateral security for an advance to the person presenting the same, shows upon its face the existence of a trust, or that the person offering it is not the absolute owner thereof, but holds it in some fiduciary character, or that it belongs to some other person, the pledgee is presumed to know the true owner, and is thus chargeable with knowledge, and can acquire no title as against the defrauded cestuis que trust or real owner. Holding under such circumstances, the pledgee is not a holder for value in good faith, in the usual course of business. What will be notice sufficient under this rule to charge the pledgee?

Railroad Co. v. Nat. Currency Bank, 102 U.S. 14, 41, by Mr. Justice Clifford.

Seybel v. Nat. Currency Bank, 54 Ib. 288, 295; Dutchess Ins. Co. v. Hachfield, 73 Ib. 226.

The appeals of New York sustained a pledge of stocks made to bona fide holders for value without notice, although made by brokers in fraud of the rights of the real owner, and the decision was sustained by the United States Supreme Court in 146 U.S. 240.

In Colonial Bank v. Williams, 15 App. Cas. 267, a man was registered owner of shares in a New York company. There was on the certificate a form of indorsement of transfer for value received, with a blank for names of transferor and transferee, with a power of attorney to carry out the transfer. The owner, having died without having signed the transfers, his executors, in order to have the shares registered in their own name, signed as executors the transfers, and sent the certificates to their broker, who fraudulently deposited them with the banks, which took them bona fide and without notice as securities for advances. It was held by the House of Lords that, as the transfers were not signed by the registered owner, but merely by his executors, whose position as such, and the genuineness of whose signatures were not duly vouched, the documents were not in conformity with stock exchange usage, or, as the term is, were not “in order,” and the banks were therefore not entitled to retain them against the executors. This decision is in conformity with the rule adopted by the New York Court of Appeals. See also Taliferro v. Bank, 71 Md. 209; German Savings Bank v. Renshaw, 78 Md. 475.

so as to defeat his title, is a question of construction, and is usually determined by the court as a matter of law. Every person is presumed to know the contents and meaning of written instruments, and the construction given to commercial paper at the time of its transfer, and of the order of the names upon it. Pledgees advancing upon negotiable instruments showing upon their face, or by indorsement, that they are already held as collateral security, as where an indorsement recited, “this note is held by me for note signed by X,” etc., are chargeable with notice as to the limited interest of the pledgor. Where bills are indorsed to an agent of the owner “for their account,” a pledgee thereof receiving them as collateral security for past and future advances to the agent, is chargeable with notice, and can take no title to the securities as against the real owner. The words “as trustees,” in the case of a pledge of securities for a greater sum than authorized is sufficient to put the pledgees upon inquiry as to the extent of the authority of the pledgor when asking an advance for his own benefit.

Security Bank v. McDonald, 127 Mass. 82; Nat. Bank v. Savery, Ib. 78. In Strong v. Jackson, 123 Mass, 60, 68, a case of wrongful misappropriation of negotiable instruments as collateral security, the court say: “Upon an examination of the cases, it will be found that it is very rarely decided that any one fact is or is not conclusive evidence of notice. Indeed, in the nature of things, it can scarcely happen that the question is to be decided upon an isolated fact. It may be that in a particular case some single fact in and of itself is sufficient, but generally it is not so. The question is ordinarily a broader one; it is this: Do all the facts, taken in connection with the subject-matter, with the situation and relation of the parties, their means of knowledge, the circumstances which should lead to inquiry, together show such a state of facts that it would be inequitable for subsequently acquired rights to supplant rights previously acquired? In this view, a fact, which under some circumstances and some situations and relations of the parties would be insignificant, in other relations of the parties and under other circumstances would be decisive; and thus many apparently conflicting decisions will be found harmonious.”

§ 77. Cases where notice was not presumed.—A negotiable promissory note, marked upon the margin, “this note secured by trust deed of even date herewith,” was received as collateral security. No notice of any claims of third parties was chargeable to the pledgee from such a notation. Promissory notes, worded “I promise to pay to A, as he is the trustee under the will of B, deceased, or order,” were pledged as collateral notes to secure the payment of a personal note of the trustee, discounted by a bank, the money being for his own use, the bank having previously refused to discount the notes afterward accepted as collateral security. No notice was charged as against the pledgee by reason of the wording of the notes that the trustee was acting in violation of his duty. And a mere indorsement of a note as “curator,” is not sufficient to charge a pledgee advancing money in good faith to the holder, although in fact the pledge be a misappropriation. A promissory note, containing the words “I promise to pay to the order of myself,” and executed by two persons, having been handed by one to the other, who misappropriated the same as collateral security for a precedent debt, the title of the pledgee was not affected by any notice or knowledge presumed from the fact that only one name was indorsed. If a negotiable instrument indorsed in blank is placed in the hands of an agent for safe-keeping, and the agent fraudulently appropriates and pledges the same before maturity, an innocent pledgee advancing money on such paper, without notice of equities, is a holder for value, and protected, as there is nothing in the fact of the pledge of such securities by persons having an absolute title, to put a pledgee upon inquiry.

§ 78. Recovery of the pledgee limited to advance.—The pledgee of negotiable instruments holding the same bona fide and for value, is entitled to recover from the parties the full face value of the same, holding any balance, where the collateral notes are greater in amount than the principal debt, for the defrauded he is allowed to recover only the amount of his loans. In such cases of misappropriation the pledgee is under no liability as to any possible surplus to the pledgor by whose fraud the

a. Accounting for securities.—Certain promissory notes were indorsed as collateral security by one bank to another, to cover a debt owing by the pledgor to pledgee. Among these notes was the one in suit belonging to H., which he alleged had been obtained from him by fraud, and the evidence tended to prove this. Held, that H. could not compel the pledgee of the note to first exhaust its other collateral; and that the fraud being proven, the pledgee was only entitled to recover the unpaid portion of the debt secured by the note. It appeared that the bank exchanged one of the collateral notes for other notes secured by a mortgage payable to its order. Held, that the pledgee was bound to account the same as though it had received payment of the original note in full. Haas v. Bank of Commerce, 41 Neb. 754.

b. Pledge by guardian.—Where a former guardian of plaintiff's ward pledged to the defendant to secure his own note, two negotiable bonds owned by the ward, on which bonds was an indorsement tending to show the ward’s ownership, and which was seen by the cashier at the time of the negotiation. Held, that the defendant was not entitled to the protection of an innocent purchaser; that it was put upon inquiry, and that it was not

sufficient to only inquire of the guardian; that the plaintiff could recover the bonds in an action of replevin; that the settlement of the guardian’s account in the probate court did not affect the title to the bonds. Langdon v. Baxter Nat. Bank, 57 Vt. 1.

ce. Diversion of authorized use.—Pursuant to a resolution of its directors a corporation issued certain bonds for the purpose of borrowing money in order to successfully conduct the business for which it was organized. But the bonds were not used for such purpose, but were used to purchase the stock of the company from a person who had sold it land, and received such stock therefor. It appeared from the evidence that plaintiff knew, when he took the bonds, the purposes for which they were issued and their diversion from such purpose, when he received them. Held. that plaintiff, not being an innocent holder of the bonds diverted, could not recover thereon. Kirkland v. Kille, 99 N. Y. 890.

d. Estoppel of owner of security.—The plaintiff was intrusted by the defendant with one of its bonds to use as collateral security in raising money for its use, on the note of a third person. He did, in fact, pledge the bond with one of his own notes, but accounted to the company for the proceeds, and was then, and for a time thereafter, its creditor for a large sum. He subsequently became a defaulter, owing to the company far more than the amount of the bond. In a suit upon it by the pledgee, it was held that he had substantially complied with his duty, and that the defendant, having received the money at the time, without objection as to the manner in which it was raised, must be considered to have ratified his action. Fleming v. Camden & Atlantic R. R. Co., 16 Phila. (Pa.) 60; S. C., 40 Leg. Tat. 36.

e. Pledge of notes—Estoppel.—B. purchased certain mining property of P. B. then associated with him J., and they arranged with G. and K. for financial aid, who turned over to B. certain stocks to raise money with. B. sold these shares to SS. who gave cash and negotiable notes payable to B. Subsequently J., who had possession of the notes, surrendered them to S., and received in lieu thereof five other notes payable to J., three of which were non-negotiable. The contract between B. and P. for purchase of the mining property was extended, and in default of certain stipulated payments being made thereon, B. placed in the hands of P. two notes of S., with

power to pledge them in default of redemption. G. was aware for some time of the pledge of the notes to P., but did not repudiate the transaction. When G. found that the enterprise was likely to prove a failure, he brought this action to recover the proceeds of the notes from P. Held, that he was estopped by his acts from repudiating the pledge made by B. to P. Held, further, that although P. was authorized to pledge the notes to raise money to apply on the contract for the sale of the mining property, his failure so to do did not destroy his lien thereon. Gregory v. Boston Safe Deposit Co., 36 Fed. Rep. 408.

f. Future advances.—Where a bond was transferred and delivered as a collateral security for future advances, and no advances were made until after the maturity of the bond, then the title of the holder would depend on the real ownership of the bond at the time the advances thus made, after its maturity, were received, and in such a case the rights of the wife as the
