notes as collateral security, he is liable for negligence in collecting the same before they are barred by the statute of limitations; and it is no defense that the maker of the collateral notes might not have availed himself of the bar of the statute of limitations. First National Bank v. O'Connell, 84 Ia. 377.

g. Negligence—Onus.—In the absence of a contract governing the disposition of a collateral security and the pledgor claims damages on account of the failure of the pledgee to collect the security, it devolves upon the pledgor to show that the negligence of the pledgee occasioned the loss. Murphy v. Bartsch, 23 Pac. (Idaho) 83; see Rice v. Benedict, 19 Mich. 132-135; Rozet v. McClellan, 48 Ill. 845; Robinson v. Hurley, 11 Iowa, 412; Goodall v. Richardson, 14 N. H. 567; Fletcher v. Harmon, 78 Me. 465.

h. Care defined.—In Wilkinson v. Culver, 83 Fed. Rep. 708, certain bonds and choses in action were assigned as collateral security, with the agreement that the proceeds from their sale should be applied to the reduction of the secured debt. The pledgee failed to sell the same, and loss resulted to the pledgor. The court said the obligation of the pledgee did not differ from that “usually and naturally resting upon holders of collateral security of the same character, viz., that a sale, in the absence of a request to sell, or the commencement of suits, was not compulsory, but was to be at the discretion of the pledgee.”

i. Degree of diligence.—In 3 White and Tudor’s Leading Cases in Equity, 556, 557, the editor in a note speaking of the diligence required of a creditor holding collateral security says: “He must use due diligence in the management and collection of securities binding the persons or estates of third persons at the risk of discharging the debt itself if guilty of negligence, and with it, of course, all liability on the part of principal or surety.”

j. Prosecuting both claims.—A creditor holding collateral security for his claim may prosecute both claims to judgment, and collect what is due him, though he could have but one satisfaction of his demand. Barnes v. Bradley, 56 Ark. 105.

k. Payment—Burden.—The burden of proving payment of the debt, whether by collection of the collateral security or otherwise, is cast upon the defendant. It is incumbent upon him both to allege and prove that defense, if he desires to make it. Barnes v. Bradley, 56 Ark. 105; Manufacturing Co. v. Falvey, 20 Wis. 211.

able with the face of such collateral securities as in payment and discharge of the principal debt. Where the opportunity of collecting collateral bills or notes is lost by the insolvency of the parties thereto, by reason of the supine negligence of the pledgee, when with ordinary care the same might have been enforced, the latter is liable to account for the full loss and damage of the pledgor. Such responsibility of the pledgee is limited to the actual loss. The liability of the pledgor as indorser upon such negotiable collateral notes of third parties is, in such cases of gross negligence, discharged.

§115. The pledgee, when not liable for mere delay in collection of collateral securities—The pledgee of negotiable collateral securities, however, is not held to strict responsibility in proceeding at once, upon default, in the enforcement thereof. Mere delay in so doing is not sufficient to create any liability upon his part to the pledgor. Where there is no suspicion that the maker is embarrassed, and no request on the part of the pledgor that collection should be promptly made, the pledgee is not answerable for a subsequent actual loss. And where the pledgee has information upon which he is certain that a suit upon the collateral note would be fruitless, he is not required to sue the same. § 116. The pledgee, when not liable for negligence of agent.—The pledgee of negotiable collateral securities who has employed an agent or attorney in connection with the collection or realization thereof, is not liable, where he has exercised reasonable care and judgment in his selection, by reason of the misconduct or gross negligence of the person or persons employed. If a pledgee of negotiable paper deposits the same in a bank or agency, for the purpose of having collections made, and such bank or agency fails or neglects to take the proper steps to charge the parties liable thereon, an action against the bank or agent may be brought in favor of any one beneficially interested in such collateral securities. a. Liability after tender.—The pledgee is liable to the pledgor for the depreciation in value of the property after a tender of the amount due and a refusal of the pledgee to deliver. Loughborough v. McNevin, 74 Cal. 250; 5 Am. St. Rep. 435. But see N. Y. Fire Ins. Co. v. Tooker, 4 N. J. L. J. 834.

Notes.

a. Effect of tender.—Where a pledgor makes a sufficient tender of payment of the debt to the pledgee, although made after maturity, and the same is discharged without good reason, the lien of the creditor upon the pledged property will be discharged, and the pledgee will not be permitted to retain the pledge against one who has, subsequent to the making of the pledge, acquired rights in the property. Norton v. Baxter, 41 Minn. 146.

b. Payment.—Where the transferee is the maker of the collateral note the payment of the collateral note extinguishes the original note. Gilliam v. Davis, 35 Pac. Rep. 69.

c. Collection—Expenses.—Where the holder of collateral security has the right to enforce its collection, and there are expenses attending such collection, the pledgee will be entitled to deduct from the proceeds the necessary, customary, and usual costs of such collection. Cressman v. Whitall, 16 Neb. 592; Furness v. Union National Bank, 147 Ill. 570.

d. Accepting a less amount.—One of two obligors, who were jointly liable as principals, pledged certain choses in action as security for the joint debt. Held, that the pledgee might, with the consent of the pledgor, accept less than the face value of such collaterals in settlement of the same, without incurring obligations to the other obligor for more than the sum actually received by him. Foltz v. Hardin, 139 Ill. 405.

e. Enforcement.—The holder of a promissory note indorsed it and deposited it in a bank as collateral security. Afterward a third party paid to the bank the amount due thereon and took the note, and after this the makers of the note paid to the third party several installments of interest thereon. Held, that from these facts a presumption arose that the transaction between the bank and the third party was a sale of the note to him, and not a payment of it by him for the makers. Rand v. Barrett, 66 Iowa, 731.

f. Enforcement—Pleading.—In Barnes v. Bradley, 19 S. W. Rep. (Ark.) 819, Cockrill, C. J., in speaking of the rights of parties in an action upon a debt secured by collaterals, said: "Under pleadings properly presenting the issue, the defendant might have cast upon the plaintiff the burden of accounting for, or of producing the collateral security unsatisfied, by proving a demand to that effect, accompanied by a tender of the amount due; and, upon his failure to properly account, the value of the security should have been deducted from his demand. A like state of proof would be cause for granting an injunction to stay proceedings after the case has gone to

judgment. Aldrich v. Cooper, 2 White & T. Lead. Cas. Eq. (Pt. 1.) 228, 312; Stuart v. Bigler’s Assignees, 98 Pa. St. 80.

g. Continuance of suit.—Notwithstanding the principal debt has been paid, pending suit on the collateral, such suit may properly continue to judgment, and, if the holder collect the same, he will hold it as trustee for the benefit of the debtor; that is, the owner of the collateral. Logan v. Cassell, 32 Am. Rep. 453; First National Bank v. Mann, 27 S. W. (Tenn.) 1015. But this is only when the maker will not be thereby deprived of some equitable defense he might have against the payee; or in other words, the holder can only recover subject to the equities of the maker against the payee. Logan v. Cassell, 82 Am. Rep. 453; First National Bank v. Mann, 27 S. W. (Tenn.) 1015.

h. Enforcement—Liability for loss.—Two persons, A and B, owed a bank $3,000 upon a note, and were at the same time liable to the bank upon a note of $3,500, made to C for his accommodation; also upon another note for $1,000. Upon all of the foregoing notes D was liable as guarantor. A and B owed the bank $2,420 on their own note, but D was not liable thereon. An extension of time of payment was desired by A, B, and C. To procure such time, C transferred to F, by deed, certain securities, to secure, first, D for carrying the $3,500 note, and guaranteeing the $3,000 and $1,000 notes; and second, to secure to the bank the payment of the $2,420, and the surplus to C, or his assigns. The securities were sold to D and the bank for $1,500. Subsequently, an offer of $11,000 was made to D and the bank for the securities, which was refused, as the bank asked $15,000 therefor. Soon thereafter, the securities became worthless, on account of a decision of the supreme court. Held, that the act of the bank, in refusing to sell the securities, did not release the liability of D as guarantor, since it acted in good faith in trying to get a better price for the securities. Kaufman v. Loomis, 110 Ill. 617; rev'g 13 App. Ct. 35.

i. Purchase—Surrender of collateral.—Where a note was given as collateral security for the payment of certain stock sold to the indorser, and afterward the holder of the collateral repurchased the stock for a less sum than was due thereon, such repurchase did not constitute a surrender of the collateral, and the rights of the pledgee to enforce the collateral cannot be defeated on the ground of failure of the consideration as between the maker and payee of the note. Hardie v. Wright, 83 Tex. 345.

j. Limit of recovery.—A person to whom a note is indorsed as collateral cannot recover from his indorser more than the amount of the debt to which the note is collateral security. Skillings v. Marcus, 34 N. E. Rep. 80.

k. Same.—An indorsee of negotiable paper before maturity, as collateral security for a debt then contracted, stands in the position of a bona fide purchaser, and may recover as such against the maker; yet, if the maker can show a good defense as to the pledgor, he is entitled to have the recovery limited to the amount of the principal debt for which the collateral security is held. St. Paul Nat. Bank v. Cannon, 46 Minn. 95.

l. Pledge stands until debt paid.—A sum of money collected by a creditor on a promissory note placed in his hands by his debtor as collateral security cannot be recovered from him while the debt secured remains unpaid. Jenkins v. Neal, 52 Ark. 418.

m. Pledge for precedent debt—Effect.—The acceptance by a creditor

of a note of a third person for a pre-existing debt, evidenced by note, is, in the absence of proof that it was in discharge of the debt, presumed to be as collateral security merely, and does not affect the liability of the parties to the old note, or any security for it. Caldwell v. Hall, 49 Ark. 508.

n. Surrender—Consideration for new notes.—The surrender of old notes, and their cancellation is a sufficient consideration for new notes given, and the holder, by such surrender and cancellation, puts it out of his power to sue on the indebtedness or enforce its collection until the maturity of the new notes. Price v. Dime Savings Bank, 124 Ill. 317.

§ 117. The pledgee of bills and notes has no right of sale.—The pledgee of negotiable instruments, such as bills of exchange and promissory notes, so as to become a party thereto, as collateral security for the payment of a principal note or obligation, is not entitled, upon demand of payment and default of the principal debt, and notice to the pledgor, to offer such negotiable collateral securities, at either public or private sale, in the absence of authority by special contract so to do. Negotiable collateral securities, such

Fletcher v. Dickinson, 7 Allen, 28; Nelson v. Edwards, 40 Barb. 279; Same v. Wellington, 5 Bosw. 178; Brookman v. Metcalf, 5 Ib. 429; Brown v. Ward, 8 Duer, 660; Lamberton v. In Joliet Iron Co. v. Scioto, etc., Co., 82 Ill. 648, the court (Dickey, J.) says:

“The pledge of commercial paper as collateral security for the payment of a debt does not, in the absence of a special power for that purpose, authorize the party to whom such paper is so pledged, to sell the securities so pledged upon default of payment, either at public or private sale. He is bound to hold and collect the same as it becomes due, and apply the net proceeds to the payment of the debt so secured. From the very nature of the case, prop-

as bills and notes, are held by the pledgee under a quasi trust in favor of the pledgor, and are of such a character that a public or private sale is generally made at a sacrifice. The solvency or circumstances of parties to the collateral paper may not be well known, and few persons will purchase, and those for speculation, and at low prices. The pledgor is not required to submit his negotiable collateral securities to an ordeal to which commercial paper is unusually subjected, and which must be destructive of its value except in rare cases.¹ The rule disapproving of sales of negotiable collateral securities, either at public or private sale, without express contract authorizing such sale, applies where such collateral bills or notes mature later than the original debt or obligation,² but does not apply to long time paper or negotiable bonds.³

§ 118. The right of sale under contract.—A power of sale of such negotiable instruments held as collateral security may be given by the contract of pledge. Such a power is not against public policy, nor is it open to any objections as to its validity.⁴

b. Sale—Conversion.—Where a pledge is sold in pursuance of an express power, the sale is not a conversion, and the pledgor cannot maintain trover. Cole v. Dalziel, 18 Ill. App. 28. And although the pledgor is insolvent, the pledgee may sell the property in pursuance of the contract. Jacquet v. His Creditors, 38 La. Ann. 863.

Betcher, 42 Minn. 210; Cooper v. Simpson (Minn.), 41 Minn. 46. But the parties may by contract make it the duty of the pledgee to sell the pledged property within a specified time. Cooper v. Such power of sale, upon default in payment, is not construed as excluding the right of the pledgee to sue upon such collateral notes. It is rather an additional power given him for the realization of his collateral securities. The pledge of a note to one creditor as collateral security with a power of sale does not affect the right of other creditors to levy upon the pledgee’s reversionary interest therein, and to sell the same, subject to the rights of the pledgee. It is questionable whether a valid sale can be made of a collateral note to the maker, at private sale, at any rate for less than its face value. Such a sale, without the consent of the pledgor previously obtained, would be “very suspicious.”

§ 119. The pledgee’s relief in equity to obtain sale of collateral paper.—Applications are rarely made to courts of equity for assistance in obtaining the realization by sale of negotiable collateral paper, such as bills of exchange and promissory notes. No ground exists, except in exceptional cases, for the aid of a court of equity, as the pledgee, receiving such collateral securities, indorsed where required so as to become a party thereto, and possessing the full legal title, has a complete remedy by an action at law against the parties bound thereon. Equitable relief was given in a case, where the maker of the collateral note resided in New York, the pledgor and pledgee in San Francisco. The maker had no property or estate in California subject to legal process, and upon presentment of the note to him for payment at maturity, it was protested. Upon a bill filed by the pledgee, a court of equity decreed that the note should be sold at a judicial sale, and that in

a. Purchase under attachment.—A pledgee of shares of corporate stock which are sold under attachment or garnishment proceedings, does not waive any right by purchasing at such sale. Harrell v. Mexico Cattle Co., Tex. 612.

b. Pursuit in equity.—Where property transferred to a person other than the creditor, was merely received as collateral security for the debt, the creditor may pursue it in equity, and at the same time maintain an action at law against the debtor; and the holder of a bill of exchange, to whom it had been transferred as collateral security by the payee, does not forfeit his right of action against other parties, by an unsuccessful suit against one. Williams v. Jones, 79 Ala. 119.

c. Waiver of notice.—Where a power to sell pledged property, either at public or private sale, contains no provisions for notice to the pledgor of the time and place of sale, such notice is waived. McDowell v. Chicago Steel Works, 22 Ill. App. 405; aff’d, 124 Ill. 491; see Carson v. Iowa City Gas Light Co., 80 Ia. 638. But a pledgee who has conditional authority to sell before maturity of the debt must, before sale, give notice to redeem. Illinois National Bank v. Baker, 128 Ill. 638.

§ 120. The pledgee’s right to sell negotiable bonds on default—The pledgee of long-time bonds issued by the government, municipal or other corporations, payable to bearer or holder, and negotiable by delivery, holding the same as collateral security for the payment of promissory notes or bills of exchange, maturing at early dates, has the right, even in the absence of contract, to sell such collateral securities upon default in payment of the original debt, under proper conditions as to notice of the time, place and manner of sale. The presumption is that a pledgee is entitled to sell such long-time bonds, and coupons thereto attached, as stocks, public securities, goods and chattels are sold, upon demand and default in payment of the principal debt, and after due notice of sale. Such collateral securities differ essentially from the ordinary negotiable notes and bills of exchange, or notes and bonds, secured by mortgage. The right to sell such long-time bonds is an incident of the pledge thereof, and part of the security, and passes with the collateral securities into the hands of any bona fide holder advancing money thereon, in the due course of business. The rule is otherwise where bonds issued by a railroad company are payable upon condition, so that no bidder at a public sale can, by mere inspection of the paper, form any just judgment as to the value thereof. In such a case, a sale by the pledgee is not approved.

If the pledgee of negotiable bonds and other securities having upon default in payment of the principal debt, and upon due notice, a right of sale of such collateral securities, fails to

Lewis, 12 N. J. Eq. 321; Duffield v. Miller, 92 Pa. St. 286; Alexander R. R. Co. v. Burke, 22 Gratt. 254; Newport Bridge Co. v. Douglass, 12 Bush, 6738; Union Cattle Co. v. The right of a pledgee of such negotiable bonds to sell is not defeated by the subsequent insolvency of the pledgor. A pledgee, holding such collateral securities in value largely in excess of the principal debt, will be restrained from selling the whole.

The holder of certain railroad bonds as collateral security sought by bill in chancery to foreclose the equity of redemption of the pledgor, alleging that if such bonds were sold, enough would not be realized to satisfy the debt, but that by holding the bonds until they were redeemed he would obtain payment of his debt. The court refused to decree a foreclosure, but ordered a sale of the bonds and allowed the pledgee himself to become the purchaser, he not conducting the sale. This decision was distinguished in a late case, as relating to the powers of a simple pledgee only, and where the collateral securities were transferred so as to pass the legal title thereto, the holder was given an order for foreclosure, with a short time for redemption.

§ 121. The requirements of a valid sale.—In the absence of special contract, the sale of negotiable bonds held as collateral security is governed by the following principles:

a. Purchase by pledgee.—When a pledgee purchases the pledge at a sale of which the pledgor has notice, the pledgor has a right of election to treat the sale as invalid, but loses that right by failing to exercise it within a reasonable time after knowledge of the fact. The right is lost by such unreasonable delay, as a rule of law, and not as an inference of fact as to ratification of the sale by the pledgor. Hill v. Finigan, 77 Cal. 267.

b. Retraction of election.—A sufficient election by the pledgor to treat a purchase of the pledge by the pledgee at his own sale as valid cannot afterward be retracted; nor can an election to disaffirm the sale be retracted or renewed at a later date for the purpose of increasing damages. Hill v. Finigan, 77 Cal. 267.

Collateral security should be made at auction, at a public place, after demand of payment of the principal obligation, and default, and reasonable notice of the time and place of sale. A sale of bonds, held as collateral security for a loan, payable on demand, made without demand or notice, is irregular, to be affirmed or not at the election of the pledgor. Where such bonds had been sub-pledged, a notice of the proposed sale to the pledgee thereof, upon default, is not sufficient, as it is the duty of the pledgee to give notice also to the pledgor. Nor will the error be cured by a notice of thirty days in which to redeem. A sale of bonds, held as security for the payment of advances, without authority and without notice, is a conversion, and renders the pledgee liable for any subsequent enhancement in value.

§ 122. Notice of sale of collateral paper when provided by contract.—The parties to a contract of pledge of negotiable bonds and coupons, payable to bearer or holder, may stipulate that the pledgee shall have the right to sell such collateral securities, upon default of payment of the principal debt, at public or private sale, without notice to the pledgor. Such bonds generally have a recognized value in the market, and the good or bad faith of the pledgee in the realization of such collateral securities is a matter of easy proof. A bona fide sale of such collateral paper, made after default, under a power of sale, vesting the title in a purchaser for value, in good faith, is not affected by a tender of the debt and charges made subsequently thereto. The usual requirements of demand and notice do not apply where, by the contract of pledge, a power

§ 123. “Notice of sale by pledgee, when sufficient.—Whether the notice by the pledgee of sale of negotiable collateral securities is sufficient to constitute such sale a valid transaction, is a question of fact depending upon the particular circumstances of each case. The pledgor has no cause for complaint where notices of the sale of municipal bonds held in pledge were published in a newspaper in a city where the bonds were issued and at the place of sale thirty days prior thereto, and that such bonds sold at the place of sale for more than in the city where issued, and the sale itself was bona fide. Actual notice to the pledgor, a reasonable time before the sale, is sufficient, and will excuse want of formal notice. But notice after the sale is not sufficient, for although the pledgor, having notice, might not have been able to raise funds to pay his debt and redeem his collateral securities, he has a right to be present at the sale to see that it is conducted in a proper manner, and to advance his interests by securing greater competition. Where negotiable railroad bonds were pledged as collateral security for the payment of certain notes, less in amount, with authority to sub-pledge the securities to a bank for other notes indorsed by the pledgor; and, upon default in payment of the notes held by the sub-pledgee, the bonds were sold in New York, at public auction, after advertisement, for much less than their value, with the knowledge and assent of the pledgee, but of

§ 124. Right of pledgee of negotiable bonds, upon default, to enforce mortgage security.—Pledgees of negotiable coupon bonds of railroad and other corporations, secured by mortgage or trust deed, are entitled to require foreclosure and sale of the property covered by such mortgage or trust deed, upon default.2. Upon such foreclosure proceedings, the bona fide holder of bonds as collateral security for a valuable consideration, is not limited to proof of the amount of his actual advances, but is entitled to prove the full face value of the bonds held by him as collateral security, and to share in the distribution accordingly, not receiving, however, more than the amount of the actual indebtedness secured.3 This rule is applied in cases where it is evident that the mortgaged property is insufficient to pay the debts with which it is incumbered. If allowed to prove only for the sums for which the bonds are held as collateral security, they would probably form an insufficient security; but if the sale should realize more than sufficient to pay all the debts, the distribution of the proceeds remain under the direction of the court. Should the pledgees receive an excess over the amount of the debt for which the bonds are pledged, such surplus will be held in trust for the parties entitled.4

§ 125. The title of bona fide purchasers for value, at sales of collateral securities—Upon a sale of negotiable collateral paper, whether coupon bonds, bills of exchange, or promissory notes, made in good faith, by the pledgee, in

THE PLEDGEE’S SALE, 223

In pursuance of a valid contract of pledge, a bona fide purchaser thereof for value is vested with an unimpeachable title to such collateral securities as against all parties. No relation of pledgor and pledgee exists between the pledgor who has permitted his collaterals to be sold upon default, and the purchaser, who has paid value therefor at such sale, nor is there any privity of contract between them, nor the assumption by the purchaser of any of the duties of a trustee in relation thereto. The bona fide purchaser for value acquires at such sale the title of the pledgor absolutely, and the negotiable collateral paper being under-due, takes the same free from antecedent equities. The fact that the negotiable collateral securities sold for less than the amount due thereon is immaterial, as affecting the title of the purchaser, if the sale be valid and the purchase made in good faith and for value. Upon a valid sale of negotiable bonds, held as collateral security, purchasers thereof, for value, in good faith, are bona fide holders for value for the full face of such collateral paper, although the amount of the principal debt for which the collateral security was given is less than the value of the bonds at the time of the sale. Where, however, the purchaser is chargeable with notice that the sale of such negotiable collateral securities is fraudulent and unauthorized, he can acquire no rights or title as against the defrauded pledgor, although the pledgee offered such collateral notes for sale, as the indorsee with full title.

§ 126. The pledgee as purchaser of negotiable collateral paper.—Where, upon a sale of negotiable collateral paper by a pledgee, without authority, the pledgee himself becomes the purchaser thereof, the relations of the parties to the contract of pledge are not affected. The pledgee is not permitted by such an act to change his relations with the pledgor from that of a pledgee, under obligations, upon payment, to re-deliver such collateral securities at once.

Rigdon, 93 Ill. 458; Stokes v. Frazier, 72 Ill. 428; Newport Bridge Co. v. Douglas, 12 Bush, 678; White Mountain R. R. Co. v. Bay State Iron Co., 202.

The pledgor, whether such sale would have been beneficial to him or not, is entitled to regard the possession of the pledgee, under such sale and purchase, as in continuance of the pledge relations of the parties. Notes.

a. Agreement to prosecute claims.—An agreement of a pledgee of securities that the proceeds arising from their sale, or recovered therefrom, are to be applied to pay off the notes of the pledgor, subject to the repayment of moneys expended by the pledgee in prosecuting claims or selling the securities, is not a contract on the part of the pledgee to prosecute or sell the securities mentioned in it, at his own risk and expense. Culver v. Wilkinson, 145 U. S. 205; 36 Law Ed. 676.

b. Sale after death of pledgee.—In the case of National Exchange Bank v. Benbrooke School Furnishing Co. (supra), it was urged that under the law of Texas, upon the death of the pledgor, the pledgee cannot proceed to sell the subject of the pledge, but must proceed through the probate court in the regular course of administration, and hence the pledgees of the school warrants in question could not proceed to sell the same in default of payment of the notes they were given to secure, after the dissolution of the pledgor corporation, but could only dispose of the collateral security in the regular course of the proceedings to wind up the corporation. The case of Robertson v. Paul, 16 Tex. 472, was cited in support of this contention. But the court thought that the statutes of Texas, in relation to corporations, were of such a character as to render the exercise of a power of sale of the school warrants, pursuant to the terms by which they were pledged, not inconsistent with the provisions of such statutes.

c. Pledge of school warrants—Possession of pledgee.—In National Exchange Bank v. Benbrooke School Furnishing Co., 278 S. W. Rep. (Tex)

297, certain unsecured creditors of a corporation begin a suit for the appointment of a receiver thereof, on the ground of insolvency. The plaintiff, an intervenor, showed that it held certain promissory notes against the corporation, which were secured by a pledge of school warrants, the property of the corporation, with power of sale in case of default in payment of the notes. The court below made an order appointing a permanent receiver for the property and assets of the corporation, including the school warrants held by the intervenor bank, and ordered and directed that the same be delivered up to the receiver. Upon appeal to the appellate court, held, that the court below had no authority to deprive appellant of its possession of the school warrants assigned and delivered in pledge by appellee as security for money loaned, and thus to take away appellant's right to sell such securities, which it possessed under contract with appellee. d. Pledgee by—Intrusted to sell—Question for jury.—The plaintiff was the owner of a certain railroad bond which she left with one K. for safe keeping. K. pledged the bond to the defendant as security for a note of one G. K., and indorsed by him. Upon payment of the note, he demanded back the bond, which the bank refused, claiming to hold it as collateral for other debts. Evidence was offered tending to show that when the bond was pledged, it was pledged for other debts of J. and G. B. K. Subsequently the bank did renew notes of G. indorsed by J. Upon those facts a verdict was directed for plaintiff. Held, that the case should have been submitted to the jury. Lombard v. Central National Bank, 22 St. Rep. 268.

e. Loss of pledge by theft—Liability of pledgee.—Certain United States bonds were pledged by the plaintiff to the defendant bank, as collateral security for a note which it discounted, under an agreement whereby the bonds were to be returned to the plaintiff upon payment of the note. The bonds were stolen by burglars. Upon payment of the note plaintiff demanded a return of the bonds, which was refused. In an action to recover the value of the bonds, where plaintiff did not allege any want of care on the part of the bank, it was held, that the transaction was simply a pledge, and inasmuch as the bank had taken due and reasonable care of the bonds, they were not liable for their loss. Jenkins v. Nat. Bank of Bowdoinham, 58 Me. 275; Field v. Brackett, 56 Me. 121.

f. Sale without contract.—A pledgee without an express agreement to that effect, has no right to sell commercial property pledged to him as collateral security. But a court may, under proper circumstances, order a sale of collateral. Cleghorn v. Minn. Title Ins. & Trust Co., 57 Minn. 841.

g. Colorable sale.—The rights of a pledgor to pledged property will not be defeated by a merely colorable or pretended sale thereof to a person not standing in the position of a bona fide purchaser. Norton v. Baxter, 41 Minn. 146.

h. Agreement for disposal of pledge.—The disposition to be made of a pledge in case of default or in any other contingency may be controlled by the agreement of the parties, providing such agreement be not fraudulent, not in contravention of statute, nor against public policy. Hunter v. Hamilton, 52 Kan. 195.

i. Purchase by pledgee—The right of a pledgee to purchase at a foreclosure sale without authorization seems to be recognized in Louisiana. Adams & Co. v. Coons, 36 La. Ann. 305.

j. Effect of purchase by pledgee—In White and Tudor's Leading Cases in Equity, 4th Am. Ed., p. 245, it is stated that “a creditor who sells the collaterals in his hands, although publicly, and purchases them himself, will hold them after the sale, as he did previously, as a mere security, and the debtor may redeem, or require the creditor to account for their market value as shown by the re-sale.” This rule was followed in Register v. Sellers, 19 Phila. (Pa.) 446; see Smith v. Traders National Bank, 82 Tex. 368.

k. Sale under power—Question of good faith.—Plaintiffs were commissioners appointed by the court to wind up the affairs of an insolvent state bank, at New Orleans. Prior to its failure the bank had deposited with the defendants, as agents of Baring Bros. & Co., a very considerable amount of public securities, bonds of the city of New Orleans, as collateral security for the indebtedness of the bank to said firm, with authority to the pledgees to sell the same at public or private sale. Upon default of payment of the loan secured, the defendants sold the securities, through brokers, and instructed another firm of brokers to see that the same were not sacrificed. The proceeds of the bonds did not liquidate the debt secured, and the defendants asserted a claim against the bank for the balance unpaid. In submitting to the payment of these dividends the defendants and complainants agreed to a judgment in the insolvency proceeds whereby the question of damages resulting from the sale of the bonds in pledge was “expressly reserved.” Thereupon complainants indorsed these bonds as payable to bearer, and delivered them in that condition to defendants with the knowledge that they had been or were to be sold again by the firm, and for the purpose of enabling them to transfer them with a good title, and it appeared that the bonds were sold from time to time to different persons who became innocent purchasers for value. It also appeared that the bonds were sold for their then market value, and no attempt was made to impeach the fairness of the sales. No tender was made by complainants for the purpose of redeeming the bonds, and no further protest was made against the sale of the bonds, or efforts made to reclaim them for two years. The right of the defendants to sell the securities, under the contract of pledge, was not denied, and it seemed, as the court intimated, that the sale was the wisest thing that could be done at that time for the creditors of the bank. After the securities had enhanced in value to par value, the complainants filed their bill in equity, alleging a fraudulent sale of the bonds and praying that the sale be adjudged void and complainants to be the owners thereof, and that complainants be ordered to return the bonds, or in default thereof that they be decreed to pay their full value of $336,400, subject to defendant’s claim against the bank for $120,000. Held, (1) that on the complainants' theory of the relief to which they were entitled, their remedy was at law and not in equity; (2) that the indorsement of the bonds

1. Execution sale.—An accommodation note was deposited by the payee with plaintiff, before maturity, as collateral security for his note to plaintiff, under a written agreement that the collateral note might, if the principal note was not paid at maturity, be sold at public or private sale, and the proceeds applied to the expenses of sale and payment of the principal note. The principal note was, after maturity, put in judgment, and the judgment provided for the sale of the collateral note on special execution. By mistake, a general execution issued in lieu of a special one, and the note was sold thereon, and bid in by the plaintiff. In an action to recover judgment on the note, held, that the plaintiff took the note as a pledge, before maturity, free from the equities which existed between the payee and the makers, and that its purchase of it, by mistake, under a general instead of a special execution, was not an attempt to acquire a title to it inconsistent with the lien which it had before, and thus a waiver of the lien, but only an attempt to enforce the first lien, under the contract by which it was created, and that plaintiff was entitled to recover regardless of the equities between the makers and the payee. Valley National Bank v. Jackaway, 80 Iowa, 512; Valley National Bank v. Johnson Directory Co., 80 Iowa, 772.

m. Sale—Purchase by pledge.—The sale and purchase by a bank of bonds pledged to it as collateral security, when authorized by the pledgor’s note and pledge of the collateral, is not void per se. And such a transaction is at most only voidable at the instance, and upon reasonable objection, on the part of the corporation or its stockholders. Third parties or strangers have no right to question or challenge the bank’s title to the bonds on the ground either of inadequacy of price paid for the same, or for the reason that it occupied such a quasi-trust relation to the pledgor as to disqualify it from purchasing at a sale made for its own benefit. Farmers Loan & Trust Co. v. Toledo & S. H. R. Co., 54 Fed. R. 759; C.C. A., rev’g in the main, 48 Fed. R. 223.

n. When time of payment accrues.—Where no time is stipulated for the payment of a debt secured by a pledge of property, the law will, in the absence of something from which a contrary presumption would arise, presume that the payment is to be made on demand. And the holder of property hypothecated for debt, having a legal right to sell on notice after demand, no time being fixed for payment, may sell it at public auction, and

0. Sale—Notice.—Defendant was the maker of an overdue note, for which stock in a corporation in which he was treasurer, and an endowment insurance policy, had been transferred as collateral security. § 127. The pledgor’s transfer or re-pledge of collateral securities.—The pledgor of negotiable instruments as collateral security, although he has indorsed the same to the pledgee so as to pass the legal title thereto, retains such a residuary interest therein that in cases where such collateral paper is of greater value than the debt he may make a further disposition of them by pledging the same for another loan, and the rights thus acquired are protected. Where the indorsement of such negotiable collateral notes has been made by the pledgor in blank, and they remain so indorsed in the hands of the pledgee, the pledgor is permitted to make a further transfer by special indorsement to a third party, who is entitled to maintain an action thereon in his own name as indorsee, upon his discharge of the debt for which the notes were held as collateral security before obtaining judgment. A re-pledge of the collateral securities by the pledgor binds the pledgee, upon notice, as to any surplus after the repayment of his

a. Sale of equity.—A pledgor may sell his equity of redemption subject to the lien of the pledgee; but if there is anything from which a different intention ought to be inferred, the transaction will not be allowed to have the effect of a transfer. Jordan v. Harrison, 46 Mo. App. 172,

own advances. Where collateral notes were transferred for a loan for less than half their value, and the pledgor made a re-pledge of the same for another loan, and the maker died and the pledgor became insolvent, the first pledgee, having foreclosed the title of the second pledgee, and the pledgor’s trustees having disclaimed, was allowed to prove for the full face of the collaterals against the maker’s estate, the actual recovery to be limited to the amount due on the principal debt, interest and costs.

§ 128. The pledgor entitled to surplus proceeds from collateral securities.—Where the collateral securities deposited by the pledgor for his principal note are greater in amount than the note, and the pledgee has collected the same by suit or in some other manner has realized the value thereof, the pledgor is entitled to the surplus remaining after the payment of the debt and proper charges in and about the collection of the securities. This residuary interest of the pledgor in the collateral notes is sufficient, where the act of the pledgee is a valid realization of them, to sustain an action for the surplus as for money had and received to his use. Where the act of sale is a tort, the action may be for conversion of the collateral notes, and the damages recovered will be subject to the set-off of the amount of the debt; or the tort may be waived, and the other action brought. Demand should be made for the surplus, as interest thereon will otherwise only run from the time of the service of the summons in the action for money had and received. The rule does not apply in the case of a wrongful sale of such collateral securities by the pledgee. The pledgee having already received the proceeds of such securities, to require a tender of the principal debt before action on the tort would be useless, as the amount of the debt is usually deducted from the damages. Where a creditor accepts collateral security from an administrator without knowledge of the insolvency of the estate, he is not required to re-assign, and accept a dividend, upon the estate proving insolvent.

§ 130. The re-delivery of collateral securities to the pledgor.—A pledgee may, upon agreement or at his pleasure, re-deliver collateral securities to the pledgor without affecting his right to proceed upon the original demand, even although there are other creditors to whom nominally the pledgee occupies the relation of trustee, if there be no violation of his duty in that character. Upon a relinquishment of securities, it is not champerty, where a debtor gives to the creditor a lien on other securities in the hands of a third person, with authority to sue the latter, and agreeing to use his best endeavors to assist in adjusting his accounts with the holder and in recovering his securities. The transaction is simply an assignment of an equity of redemption in such securities in exchange for the prior securities surrendered. Where bonds were pledged as collateral security, and upon maturity, the pledgee received other collateral securities for a valuable consideration, upon an agreement no surrender the bonds, and no demand was made therefor, and no opportunity given for re-delivery, the pledgee was not answerable for a subsequent depreciation in the value thereof, while in his possession.

§ 131. The pledgor’s remedy upon conversion of collaterals by pledgee.—After a wrongful sale by the holder.

§ 132. Relief of pledgor in equity. Equitable aid and relief is usually extended to the pledgor of negotiable instruments, where he seeks, upon proper terms, to redeem collateral securities, and the transactions between the parties to the contract of pledge, and third persons interested, are complicated, or it is sought to avoid a multiplicity of suits, or upon any other recognized head of equity jurisprudence. A court of equity will take jurisdiction of such matters upon the ground that such collateral securities constitute a trust fund, and that it has jurisdiction to order an account thereof, to convert the securities into cash, and distribute the proceeds arising.

CHAPTER XIV.
USURY, AS APPLIED TO COLLATERAL SECURITIES.

§ 134. Usury, as applied to negotiable collateral paper. — The rights and remedies of the holder of negotiable securities, given upon a loan tainted with usury, are generally the subject of statutory regulation. The effect of such usury in the transaction of loan is, under some statutes, to render the entire contract, and the negotiable notes given in connection therewith, absolutely void, and therefore incapable of enforcement in the hands of any holder, even for value. More generally, where an actual loan of money has been made, of which the maker of negotiable promissory notes tainted with usury had and retains the benefit, he is required to pay the valid portion of his debt, the penalty, upon proof of usury, being a forfeiture either of all interest, or of double the amount of the usurious interest, or such other penalty as is consistent with the theory that usury renders a contract of loan not void, but voidable. The like rules prevail as to the rights and remedies of the lender as to negotiable collateral paper, made by third parties, given to secure the payment of usurious loans. Where the principal note is void because of usury, the pledgee can acquire no greater or better title to the collateral securities, given for its payment, the indorsement

<br>

### --- Page 0328 ---

USURIOUS LOANS. 239

thereof being as void as the making of the principal notes. Where the more equitable rule prevails, the pledgee is allowed to enforce the payment of the collateral notes, where received before maturity, for an advance, without notice, given upon a usurious loan, as any other holder for value, in the usual course of business. A loan must be in contem-

NOTES.

a. What constitutes usury.—In order to constitute usury, there must be: (1) “a loan, express or implied; (2) an understanding between the parties that the money lent shall or may be returned; (3) that for such loan a greater rate of interest than is allowed by law shall be paid or agreed to be paid, as the case may be; and (4) a corrupt intent to take more than the legal rate for the use of the sum loaned. Unless these four things concur in every transaction, it is safe to affirm that no case of usury can be declared, and this may be regarded as a rule universally recognized in all of the states.” Tyler on Usury, 110, quoted and applied in Balfour v. Davis, 14 Oreg. 47.

b. Taking interest in advance.—One who loans money may retain interest in advance and deduct it from the principal sum loaned without rendering the transaction usurious. Maxwell v. Willett, 49 Ill. App. 564.

c. Accommodation paper—New York.—In New York the rule seems to be well settled by the court of appeals, that the discount of accommodation paper is merely a loan of money, the purchaser being the lender and the seller the borrower; and that if, in making such discount, the rate of interest reserved is in excess of the rate allowed by the laws of the state it avoids the contract. Claflin v. Boorum, 122 N. Y. 385; Eastman v. Shaw, 65 N. Y. 522; Dickinson v. Edwards, 77 N. Y. 573; Jewell v. Wright, 30 N. Y. 259; see, also, Bank v. De Shon, 41 Ark. 831; Tilden v. Blair, 21 Wall. 241.

d. Broker's option.—An agreement to buy stock and pay the price and “one per cent added,” is not, as a matter of law, a contract void for usury in its inception, and will not be so held in the absence of evidence that the transaction constituted a loan of money, or the scheme for the sale and resale of the stock was intended to accomplish that purpose. Phillips v. Mason, 66 Hun (N. Y.), 580; see Brown v. Mortgage Co., 110 Ill. 235; Hoyt v. Pawtucket Inst., 110 Ill. 890; Ammondson v. Ryan, 111 Ill. 506.

e. Usury ab initio.—To avoid a bond on the ground of usury, it must be shown to have been illegal ab initio; for if good in its creation, it cannot be avoided by any subsequent usurious agreement. Cobb v. Morgan, 83 N. C. 211; Wharton v. Eborn, 88 N. C. 344.

f. Compound interest.—If the original contract does not provide for a higher rate of interest than the law authorizes, an agreement to pay interest on overdue interest will not render the contract usurious. The compound interest would be somewhat in the nature of a penalty for not paying the interest when due, but it is not usury. Hager v. Blake, 16 Neb. 12; Timberlake v. First Nat. Bank, 43 Fed. Rep. (Miss.) 231; Hoskins v. Cole, 84 Ill. App. 541.

plation of the parties, and the contract between them must be to pay a greater interest than the law allows, to constitute usury. Where such is the contract, it is immaterial that the illegal interest is secured by an independent instrument, or is included in the amount of the principal note.

§ 135. The rule as to collateral securities.—As between parties to a contract of loan tainted with usury, the illegal consideration affects the title of the lender as well to the negotiable collateral securities received as to the principal note given for the loan. The title of the pledgee to the collateral incident is not more favored than to the principal evidence of the debt. § 136. The pledgee, not entitled to collect collateral accommodation paper on usurious loan.—Accommodation paper, made by a third person for the purpose of being used as collateral security for a void usurious loan, is also equally void with the principal evidences of indebtedness, and no recovery can be had by the pledgee as against the accommodation maker, or other parties thereto. It is a good defense to an action by an indorsee against an accommodation indorser of a negotiable promissory note that the same was received by the indorsee as collateral security for the payment of a usurious loan between himself and the maker. The rule is applied to sub-pledges of accommodation paper as collateral security for an antecedent debt, without more, where the pledgee held the paper as collateral security for a loan void by statute on account of usury. The sub-pledgee, receiving no better title (the transaction occurring in New York) than the pledgee, and the collateral note being void in the hands of the latter, no recovery can be had by the sub-pledgee.

§ 138. Estoppel of borrower on usury by his affirmative acts.—Where a person borrows money upon a bond and mortgage, he may deprive himself of the right to interpose the defense of usury by his own affirmative acts, as where he has given a certificate that the bond and mortgage executed by him are good and valid, and that he has no defenses, equities, or set-offs, at law or in equity. Where this has been done, if the bond and mortgage are in the hands of an innocent person who has advanced a valuable consideration thereon, without notice of equities, on the faith and credit of the representations contained in such certificate, the mortgagor is estopped to set up any defense of usury in the original transaction. This rule is applied in favor of the second assignee of a bond and mortgage, receiving the same for value, even with notice, if the first assignee holds the same free from equities. His title is supported by the title of his assignor.

Notes.

a. Who may invoke remedy.—The right of action against a national bank to recover usurious interest paid, under U.S. Rev. St., Sec. 5198, is in the person by whom the money is paid, and a joint maker of a note on which illegal interest is charged cannot recover the penalty from the bank, where the illegal interest is paid by the other maker. Timberlake v. National Bank, 43 Fed. Rep. 231; National Bank v. Rowley, 52 Kan. 394.

b. Effect of forfeiture.—The receipt of the usurious rate of interest will work a forfeiture of the entire interest which the note carries with it, including that which accrues after the maturity thereof. A judgment rendered upon such a debt will bear interest from the time of its rendition at the rate of six percent. Shafer v. First National Bank, 53 Kan. 614.

c. Interest paid.—Usurious interest actually paid to a national bank on discounting and renewing a series of notes cannot, in an action by the bank on the last of them, be applied in satisfaction of the principal debt. Bank v. Boylen, 26 W. Va. 554.

d. National banks.—A national bank, which makes a loan upon a note that embraces usury, and is renewed from time to time, forfeits the entire interest stipulated to be paid, and no portion of the usurious interest included in the renewal note can be recovered. First National Bank v. Grimes, 49 Kan. 219; Shafer v. First National Bank, 53 Kan. 614.

e. Same.—Where commercial paper is transferred to, and discounted by, a bank at a greater rate of interest than six percent, and the net proceeds, after deducting the interest charged, are credited to the transferrer, this is a payment of the interest, within the meaning of the statute. National Bank v. Carpenter, 52 N.J.L. 165.

f. National banks.—Limitations of action.—The two years limitation prescribed by statute within which an action may be commenced against a national bank to recover usurious interest, begins to run "from the time the usurious transaction occurred," which was at the date of the note, and not at the time of payment. Henderson National Bank v. Alves, 91 Ky. 142. Suit must be brought within two years after the date of actual receipt of usury by the bank. Bobo v. People’s National Bank, 92 Tenn. 444; National Bank v. Carpenter, 52 N.J.L. 165. "The usurious transaction occurred," within the meaning of the Federal statute, at the time

g. Penalty—How recovered.—This penalty must be enforced in the manner provided in the act of congress, and resort cannot be had to any other mode or form of procedure. National Bank v. Grimes, 49 Kan. 219; Bank v. Boylen, 26 W. Va. 554. Thus, where one has recovered against the bank a judgment for twice the amount of the interest thus paid, he cannot, in an action for penalty against the bank for not satisfying a chattel mortgage given to secure the note, demand that the usurious interest paid by him shall be applied in satisfaction of the principal of the note. Parkhurst v. First National Bank, 53 Kan. 136; see Hill v. Barre, 56 Vt. 582.

h. Practice in actions against national bank.—As to the requirements of an affidavit of defense in Pennsylvania, in an action for penalty against a national bank, see Osborn v. First National Bank, 154 Pa. St. 134.

i. National banks.—What is discounting and taking usury by. Danforth v. National State Bank, 48 Fed Rep. (C.C.A.N.J.) 271. Pleading in action to recover usurious interest. Henderson National Bank v. Alves, 91 Ky. 142.

j. Amount of penalty.—In an action against a national bank, under Sec. 5198, Rev. St. U.S., the amount of the penalty which can be recovered is twice the amount of interest paid, and not merely twice the amount paid in excess of the legal rate. Hill v. National Bank, 15 Fed. Rep. (Vt.) 432.

k. Effect of statutory forfeiture.—The forfeiture prescribed by the Federal statute is not merely a forfeiture of the interest which has been agreed to be paid, but a forfeiture “of the entire interest which the note, bill or other evidence of debt carries with it.” In other words, the reservation or acceptance of usury destroys the further interest-bearing capacity of the paper. Peterborough National Bank v. Childs, 133 Mass. 248; National State Bank v. Brainard, 61 Hun (N.Y.), 339; Guthrie v. Reid, 107 Pa. St. 251.

l. Renewal note.—Where usurious interest on a note to a national bank is included in a renewal note, without an agreement that the renewal note shall be a payment of the old one, and the renewal note is subsequently merged in a judgment which is afterward paid in full, the penalty provided by the act of congress for charging and receiving usurious interest on loans cannot be enforced. Kearney v. First National Bank, 129 Pa. St. 577.

m. Forfeiture of interest—National currency act.—In Alves v. Henderson National Bank, 89 Ky. 126, it was held, in respect to the act of congress of June 3, 1864, Sec. 80, that an agreement in a mortgage to pay usurious interest, although made after the maturity of the note, was sufficient to

q. Usurious interest included in note.—Where a national bank loans money at a usurious rate, which is included in the note, in an action to enforce the contract, the interest is forfeited. McGhee v. National Bank, 40 Neb. 92.

The rule is applied in the case of makers of valid negotiable promissory notes, pledged as collateral security on a usurious loan. The defense of usury in the original loan is not allowed to be interposed upon an action by the pledgee on the collateral note. Such makers not being either parties or privies to the loan tainted with usury, cannot litigate the validity of the indorsement under which the collateral notes are held. But where such collaterals, taken on a usurious contract, are rendered void by statute, no action can be brought on the collateral notes by the pledgee, against the parties thereto, as the indorsement to him is also void. Notes.

a. Bona fide purchaser without notice.—A bona fide purchaser of a note for value, without notice of any defenses to the same, takes the note free from the defense of usury. Evans v. De Roe, 15 Neb. 638; Wortendyke v. Meehan, 9 Neb. 221; Sedgwick v. Dixon, 18 Neb. 545; Cheney v. Janssen, 20 Neb. 128.

b. Onus—When shifted.—Where usury in the original transaction is proved, the burden is on one who claims to be a bona fide holder before maturity and without notice. Darst v. Backus, 18 Neb. 231; see Koehler v. Dodge, 31 Neb. 828.

c. To whom defense available.—A party not injuriously affected by a usurious transaction, is not allowed to complain or take advantage of the usury. So if a party sells land subject to a mortgage thereon, which is given to secure a debt, with usury reserved, and the purchaser assumes the payment of the debt as a part of the purchase money, such purchaser, or those claiming under him, cannot interpose the defense of usury to a bill to foreclose the mortgage. Stiger v. Bent, 111 Ill. 328.

d. Same.—The defense of usury is available, in an action of foreclosure, to the maker against an assignee of a usurious note and mortgage which had been transferred to him by a written assignment on the mortgage only, for value before maturity, and without notice of any defect. Doll v. Hollenbeck, 19 Neb. 689.

is a personal one, intended for the benefit of the borrower, a surety or accommodation indorser may take advantage of it. Nor will the usury paid to one lender affect the claims of another lender to the enforcement of negotiable collateral paper given as security for the payment of the money loaned, where the money was obtained as one loan by a note broker for a customer, with whom the collateral notes were deposited.

The defense of usury is not available to the mortgagor as against an assignee of a bond and mortgage which had been transferred under a general assignment for the benefit of creditors or as collateral security for payment of a note given by a partnership. In a suit by the assignee of a bond and mortgage against the mortgagor to foreclose the security, the mortgagor is not permitted to set up usury in the transfer between the mortgagee and the assignee. The rule, however, is otherwise as between the original parties.

Nor will equity grant relief to a mortgagor, alleging usurious consideration in a transaction where a mortgage was given to secure the payment of a loan, against a threatened sale of the property or other enforcement thereof, except upon the equitable condition that the mortgagor shall pay to the bona fide holder of the debt, for value, the principal sum, with legal interest. His position, under such circumstances, is different from that of one defending against a usurious contract. Nor can a purchaser of a mere equity of redemption in premises covered by a usurious mortgage, who purchased subject to the lien of the mortgage, set up usury as a defense thereto. And where the statute upon which the defense of usury rests has been repealed, it will no longer be available to any party.

§ 141. Usury not affected by taking new securities.—
The taint of usury attaching to the original evidences of indebtedness is not eliminated or defeated by the mere substitution of new securities in lieu of the old, or by renewals of the same, in which the original usurious consideration enters. As between the parties, the original taint of usury attaches itself as well where a further security is given or a guaranty is subsequently made, as in the case of renewal of the original note or the substitution of a new security. Where parties have calculated interest upon the old securities at a higher rate than that authorized by law, and made a settlement on such basis and the debtor gives such new notes, secured by a mortgage, for the whole sum including the illegal interest, such new notes, and the mortgage given to secure their payment, are voidable, and cannot be enforced as to the excess above the legal interest. But, though a past usurious contract be the basis on which the parties deal, yet if that contract be not

a. Rate lawful where contract made.—A note secured by a mortgage at a rate lawful in the state where made, though not in the state where it is made payable, is not void for usury. New England Co. v. McLaughlin, 87 Ga. 1.

b. Original taint affects new securities.—Where a loan is originally usurious, every subsequent security given therefor is subject to the defense of usury; and usury being proved, the court will apply all payments of interest as payments pro tanto of the principal. Simpson v. Evans, 44 Minn. 419; McDonald v. Aufdengarten, 41 Neb. 40; McDonald v. Beer, 42 Neb. 487; Estate of Riegel, 16 Phila. (Pa.) 388; see Schutt v. Evans, 1 Atl. Rep. 250 NEGOTIABLE COLLATERAL SECURITIES.

Absolutely void, a subsequent agreement which frees the transactions from all usurious taint will be valid. A contract tainted with usury in one state may be a valid basis for a new contract in another state. And where a usurious contract has been mutually abandoned, and the notes given therefor surrendered, if the parties agree upon the payment of the original loan, to the extent that it was a valid transaction, and the debtor gives new notes therefor, an action thereon by the payee is supported, as being founded upon a valuable consideration, free from the taint of usury.

§ 142. Revival of original valid debt where new securities are usurious.—If a security founded upon a prior one be tainted with the vice of usury, and the prior one free from it, but has been given up and canceled, and the new security is thereafter adjudged void, the valid note may be revived and enforced as if the one tainted with usury had never been given. Such cancellation and surrender of the prior securities under such circumstances are without consideration. If the latter securities are adjudged invalid, the creditor or pledgee has lost his debt without fault on his part, and contrary to the intent of both parties to the contract under which the change of securities took place. Upon such failure of consideration, and fraud and mistake, a court of equity will annul the cancellation and revive the securities.

Notes.

a. Delay in payment—No presumption of usury.—The fact that notes and mortgages, dated January 1, 1880, bore interest at ten per cent, but the money was not received until about the first of March following, there being no evidence as to the cause of the delay, will not warrant a presumption of a corrupt agreement for usury. Waterman v. Baldwin, 68 Ia. 255; see Cottrell v. Southwick, 71 Ia. 50.

b. Interest on overdue interest.—Where the original contract does not provide for a higher rate of interest than the law authorizes, an agreement to pay interest on overdue interest will not render the original contract usurious. So, a provision in a note to pay interest on interest overdue, does not render the note usurious. Hager v. Blake, 16 Neb. 12; see McGhee v. First Nat. Bank, 40 Neb. 92.

ce. Usury by parol agreement.—Notes were given at the legal rate, and by a parol agreement usurious interest was agreed to be paid, and such interest was paid pursuant to the agreement therefor. Subsequently the notes were renewed by taking the notes in suit, but no credit was given for the interest that had been paid in excess of the legal rate. Held, that the renewal notes were subject to the plea of usury. Koehler v. Dodge, 31 Neb. 828; Exeter Nat. Bank v. Orchard, 39 Neb. 485; Doyle v. Holland, 39 Neb. 89.

d. Dealings through agent.—Where an agent takes from the borrower a bonus for a loan, without the knowledge or participation of the lender, it will not constitute a usurious loan. Washington Life Ins. Co. v. Lane, 19 Atl. Rep. (N. J.) 617; see Jordan v. Humphrey, 31 Minn. 495; Bailey v. Hill, 77 Va. 492. Where usurious interest is paid to a third person for the benefit of, and with the knowledge of the lender, the taint of usury condemns the transaction. Borcherling v. Trefz, 40 N. J. Eq. 502.

e. Bill of sale—Minnesota.—Under the Minnesota statute (Laws of 1879, C. 66, Sec. 3), where a contract for a usurious loan of money is evidenced by a note secured by a bill of sale, the contract as well as the bill of sale are void, and there is no valid indebtedness for the money loaned. Ormund v. Hobart, 836 Minn. 806. As to a note given for services in procuring a loan, not held usurious. See Thomas v. Miller, 39 Minn. 339; Pass v. N. E. Mortgage Security Co., 66 Miss. 365.

f. Law of another state.—A contract valid in another state, but invalid in this state for usury, will not be declared invalid, where the defense of usury was not pleaded. Reiff v. Baklen, 86 Minn. 333; see First National Bank v. Mann, 94 Tenn. 17.

g. Statutory provision.—In Minnesota under the statute (Laws 1879, C. 66, Sec. 8) it was held that a plaintiff seeking the cancellation and avoidance of securities for usury, need not, as a condition of obtaining relief, offer to pay what he has received, with legal interest. Scott v. Austin, 36 Minn. 460; see Anderson v. Scandia Bank, 53 Minn. 191. As to knowledge and intent, innocent purchaser, see Jackson v. Travis, 42 Minn. 488; Holmes v. State Bank, 53 Minn. 385.

h. Equitable relief.—In an action to foreclose a mortgage securing notes, if the defense of usury be established, the plaintiff forfeits the entire interest. But the rule is otherwise when the debtor asks for equitable relief; he must then do equity by paying legal interest. Gore v. Lewis, 109 N. C. 539; Carver v. Brady, 104 N.C. 219; Cook v. Patterson, 103 N. C. 127.

i. Mortgage not affected by note.—Where a mortgage is executed to secure a usurious note, the vice of usury only affects the interest, but does not impair the validity of the mortgage itself. Spivey v. Grant, 96 N. C. 214.

j. Estoppel.—Where notes were secured by a deed of trust which recited that the notes were not tainted with usury, an estoppel is not created, in case the holders of the notes, before purchasing them, had notice of the usury. Central Trust Co. v. Burton, 74 Wis. 829.

k. Legal rate of interest in Nebraska.—As to the construction of the Nebraska statutes relating to interest (Comp. St. 1887, C. 44, Sec. 1), see Mathews v. Toogood, 23 Neb. 536.

l. Performance of contract in another state.—In North Carolina

o. Iowa—Statutory provisions.—As to construction of the provisions of Iowa Code in respect to legal interest, see Brom v. Cass Co. Bank, 86 Ia. 527.

p. Usurious mortgage not void.—Illinois.—In Illinois the statute does not declare a mortgage, securing a debt which is tainted with usury, void, but declares the interest charged or agreed to be paid, void. q. Wisconsin.—In Wisconsin, where the note is void for usury, the deed of trust securing it is also invalid. Central Trust Co. v. Burton, 74 Wis. 829.

t. Who may plead usury.—While the defense of usury may be set up by the debtor or those in privity with him, a junior incumbrancer by virtue of a judgment lien is not in privity with the mortgagor, so as to be able to set up the defense in his own behalf. Union National Bank v. International Bank, 123 Ill. 510; Mason v. Pierce, 142 Ill. 331.

u. Foreclosure of mortgage.—Where notes secured by mortgage given at a grossly usurious rate of interest were transferred to a bona fide holder for one-half their face value, it was held, in an action to foreclose the mortgage, that the same rule would be applied as where the original consideration was wholly fraudulent, and the recovery would be restricted to the amount paid by the purchaser with legal interest thereon. Cheney v. Campbell, 28 Neb. 378.

v. Defense against surety.—In a suit by a surety to foreclose a mortgage given by the principal to indemnify him against the note, the principal cannot plead usury on the note as a defense to the mortgage where the surety was not privy to the usurious agreement. Turman v. Looper, 42 Ark. 500.

w. Rule in equity.—Where a borrower goes into a court of equity to seek relief from a usurious contract, he must tender the amount of principal and lawful interest; and it is the duty of the court in granting relief to render a decree for the actual amount of the loan, with seven percent interest thereon. Eiseman v. Gallagher, 24 Neb. 79.

x. Two notes secured by same mortgage.—Notes executed about the same time, evidencing two loans, were secured by the same mortgage. Held, that though one of the notes was usurious, the other was not on account of such facts. Where loans are in fact separate and independent, they will be so treated in considering the question of usury. Jackson v. May, 28 Ill. App. 305.

y. Attorney’s fee.—An agreement to pay attorney’s fees in a foreclosure suit, in addition to legal interest, does not render the transaction usurious. Shelton v. Aultman & Taylor Co., 82 Ala. 315; Farmers & Merchants Nat. Bank v. Barton, 21 Ill. App. 403; aff'd, 122 Ill. 352; see Balfour v. Davis, 14 Oreg. 47.

z. Measure of recovery.—As to measure of recovery in actions grounded on usurious transactions, see Leonard v. Patton, 106 Ill. 99.

aa. Taking interest in advance.—In Illinois the taking of interest in advance is not usurious. Brown v. Mortgage Co., 110 Ill. 285; Hoyt v. Pawtucket Inst., 110 Ill. 390.

bb. Commissions.—A payment of $50 for commissions, to the lender's agent, above the legal rate of interest, was held usurious. Ammondson v. Ryan, 111 Ill. 506. See this case for rule for computing interest where the contract is usurious.

cc. Payment—Remedy lost.—Where a debtor voluntarily pays a debt tainted with usury, his remedy to recover back usurious interest, or to obtain any other relief on account thereof, is lost. So where he permits such payment to be made by a sale of his land under a power in a deed of trust, his remedy against any relief for usury is gone. Lake v. Brown, 116 Ill. 83; but see Harris v. Bressler, 119 Ill. 467.

<br>

### --- Page 0343 ---

254 NEGOTIABLE COLLATERAL SECURITIES.

dd. Usury as defense.—Sheriff holding writ of attachment against property of mortgagor. Stein v. Swensen, 44 Minn. 218. When failure to render judgment of forfeiture against defendant in favor of the state, for use of the school fund, is not cause for reversal, Seekell v. Norman, 78 Pa. 254.

ee. Evidence.—Character of evidence required to sustain charge of usury. White v. Benjamin, 138 N. Y. 623; Leonard v. Patton, 106 Ill. 99.

ff. Mortgage instead of conveyance.—As to an instrument held to be a mortgage and not an absolute conveyance, and not void for usury. See Hodge v. Brown, 81 Ga. 276; Holiday v. Lowry Banking Co., 92 Ga. 675.

gg. Usury—Missouri rule.—In Missouri a contract is not void for usury, yet while the creditor forfeits the whole interest, the legal rate is collectible from the debtor and goes into the school fund. Ferguson v. Soden, 111 Mo. 208; see Peters v. Lowenstein, 44 Mo. App. 406.

hh. Missouri—Who may take advantage of the statute.—The defense of usury is a personal privilege of the debtor, his representatives, vendee, execution creditor, or his attachment creditor who may defend against his debtor's mortgage on the ground that it secures usurious interest, as provided by laws of 1891, p. 171, Sec. 2, American Rubber Co. v. Wilson, 55 Mo. App. 656.

ii. Pleading.—As to when the defense of usury must be pleaded, see Moses v. Home B. & L. Ass'n, 100 Ala. 465; Timberlake v. First National Bank, 43 Fed. Rep. (Miss.) 231; Balfour v. Davis, 14 Oreg. 47; Owen v. Gibson, 74 Ga. 465.

jj. Parties.—Who may recover penalty of national bank for taking usurious interest. See Timberlake v. First National Bank, 43 Fed. Rep. (Miss.) 231. Or defend in such action. Danforth v. National State Bank, 48 Fed. Rep. (C. C. A. N.J.) 271; Hall v. First National Bank, 30 Neb. 99; Mason v. Pierce, 142 Ill. 831; see Black v. Reno, 59 Fed. Rep. (Mo.) 917.

kk. Burden of proof.—Where usury is shown, the burden is upon one claiming to be a bona fide purchaser of a note. Colby v. Parker, 34 Neb. 510; Darst v. Backus, 18 Neb. 231; Knox v. Williams, 24 Neb. 630; McDonald v. Aufdengarten, 41 Neb. 40. Where usury is set up as a defense, the burden of proof is upon the defendant, and he must clearly establish the facts necessary to sustain the defense by the decided preponderance of evidence. A usurious bargain must be proved, and not left to conjecture. Usury will not be inferred when an opposite conclusion can be reasonably and fairly arrived at. Berdan v. Trustees, 47 N. J. Eq. 8.

ll. Question for jury.—As to when usury is a question for the jury, see Hollis v. Swift, 74 Ga. 594.

§ 143. The negotiable note and the mortgage security.—  
A convenient form of security for money loaned is found in the negotiable promissory note, secured by a mortgage of real estate. The note itself, being a negotiable instrument, has all the advantages of commercial paper in hands of a holder.

<br>

### --- Page 0345 ---

256 NEGOTIABLE NOTES AND MORTGAGES.

for value in good faith, and represents the personal liability of the borrower, which can be enforced at maturity and upon default, as in the case of ordinary negotiable paper. Nor does it lose its negotiable character where secured by mortgage, by an indorsement and delivery thereof apart from the mortgage.

NOTES,

a. Meaning of rule.—Discussing this rule, the Supreme Court of Louisiana, in Schepp v. Smith, 35 La. Ann. 1, observes: “The conclusion thus reached is supported by law, justice and equity, and tends to give security in transactions of the kind considered in this case. Holding differently, would authorize debtors, ostensibly such, by their own acts or culpable omissions, to take advantage of their own laches in order to prejudice and entrap innocent parties becoming bona fide creditors, and to desecrate the sanctity of justice by closing the fatal door upon them, Carpenter v. Allen, 16 La. Ann. 435: Bank v. Flathers, 45 La. Ann. 75.

b. Pre-existing debt.—A mortgage to secure a pre-existing debt and a present loan, will constitute the taker a holder for value. Branch v. Griffin, 99 N. C. 173; Brem v. Lockhart, 93 N.C. 191; Bank v. Bridgers, 98 3 N. C. 67.

c. Contra rule.—The contra rule is held in Pepper v. George, 51 Ala. 190; Bridges v. Blake, 106 Ind. 332.

d. Interpretation of note.—Since mortgages securing debts are but an incident to and a mere security for the payment of the obligations evidenced by the notes, the terms of the notes must control in ascertaining the amount due thereon, and not the mortgage. Hutchinson v. Benedict, 49 Kans. 549.

e. Character of mortgage security.—“A mortgage possesses none of the distinctive qualities of negotiable paper. Its possession by any other person than the mortgagee, or his assignee, furnishes no evidence of title. * * * The title to a mortgage can only be transferred by assignment, or by operation of law.” Van Fleet, V. C., in Halsted v. Colvin, 51 N. J. Eq. 387.

f. Construed together—Note and mortgage.—A note and mortgage will be read and construed together. Brickell v. Batchelder, 62 Cal. 624; Leonard v. Tyler, 60 Cal. 299; Beal v. Stevens, 72 Cal. 454; Maddox v. Wyman, 92 Cal. 674. So as to interest. Winchell v. Coney, 54 Conn. 24.

g. Trust.—P., a creditor of a firm, received from B., a member thereof, as collateral security, two acceptances which were secured by a deed of trust. It was agreed that in case of foreclosure of the trust deed, and it was sold to P. he would reconvey the same to B. on payment of the latter’s debt. This transaction was held to constitute a trust in favor of B. for the two acceptances; and that such trust would attach to the property on foreclosure, if purchased by B. Peeler v. Lathrop, 1 C. C. A. 93; 48 Fed. Rep. 780.

h. Cancellation.—The cancellation of an old mortgage and the substitution of a new one are cotemporaneous acts, and such a transaction does not create a new incumbrance but simply changes the form of the old. Ponder v. Ritzinger, 102 Ind. 571; see Walters v. Walters, 73 Ind. 425; Burns v. Thayer, 101 Mass. 426.

i. New note.—Swift v. Kraemer, 13 Cal. 526. In Packard v. Kingman,
