a. Compound interest.—A note was given with a stipulation that, on default in payment of interest, compound interest should be paid. The payment of the note was secured by a mortgage, payment to be made “at maturity” with interest, pursuant to the terms of the note. Held, that the mortgage could not be foreclosed for default in the interest before the note matured. Van Loo v. Van Aken, 104 Cal. 269, Sept. 94.

b. Extinguishment.—The payment of the amount of a note and mortgage operates as an extinguishment of the debt. California Loan & S. Co. v. Hammell, 101 Cal. 250.

c. Failure to pay interest.—Upon failure to pay interest on coupon notes secured by mortgage, the whole debt may be declared due, pursuant to provisions to that effect contained in the instrument, and foreclosure obtained. Lantry v. French, 33 Neb. 524.

d. Installments.—Principle of right to declare debt due on failure to pay any installment is recognized in Morling v. Bronson, 37 Neb. 608.

e. Amount of recovery.—The holder of a promissory note, acquired for a valuable consideration, before maturity, can recover of the maker the full amount of the same and the enforcement of the mortgage securing its payment, when the only defense urged against it is a deficiency in the quality of the land sold, and the seller has been discharged from all responsibility thereon by defendants. People’s Bank of New Orleans v. Trudeau, 88 La. Ann. 898.

the face value thereof. But, in resorting to the collection of his debt from the mortgage security, if the assignment is made without the consent of the mortgagor, such indorsee stands only in the place of the original creditor, and is subject in all respects to the like equities and settlement of accounts as the mortgagee would be, the mortgagor not being bound by the amount appearing on the face of the mortgage.

In Vermont, a suit to foreclose a mortgage was brought by an indorsee for value, before maturity, of the negotiable notes secured thereby, without notice of equities. A defense was introduced that a part of the consideration of the notes was illegal. The indorsee, by his purchase of the notes and mortgage, having acquired all the rights, legal and equitable, of the mortgagee was allowed to maintain an action to foreclose the security for so much of the debt as was legally and fairly contracted. The rights of pledgees of notes properly indorsed and secured by mortgages have been sustained. The New York rule, that a mortgage is subject to equities, is followed in New Jersey, in Michigan, in Texas, and Nebraska.

§ 174. The restricted rule not applied to coupon accommodation paper.—Important exceptions are made in Illinois to the rule declared in Olds v. Cummings. Such rule was not applied in a case involving the right of persons holding long time coupon bonds issued by a railroad company, and payable to “holder;” the payment of which was secured by a deed of trust in like terms. Such bonds, intended to be thrown upon the market to be circulated as commercial paper, and used also as securities for permanent investment, are not within the reason of the rule. But what application can this doctrine have to an assignee or holder of accommodation paper? It would be most unreasonable to affirm the grantor in a mortgage to secure accommodation paper, has any equities superior to those of the assignee of the note, who thereby becomes the equitable assignee of the mortgage. Any application of the doctrine of Olds v. Cummings to the maker of a mortgage to secure accommodation paper, would be to make a most equitable and reasonable doctrine the means of enabling a party to perpetrate a great wrong on another. A court of equity will not lend its aid for any such purpose.”

NOTES.

a. Pennsylvania.—In Pennsylvania the assignee of a mortgage takes it subject to all defenses that might have been made against it in the hands of his assignor. Stephens v. Weldon, 151 Pa. St. 520.

b. Fraudulent transfer.—Where a promissory note secured by mortgage is transferred by a fraudulent assignment it will confer no right upon a subsequent assignee as against the payee, though he be a bona fide holder for value. Citizens State Bank v. Adams, 91 Ind. 280.

c. Assignment of judgment.—The right to maintain an action against the indorser of a note, whose payment has been secured by a mortgage given by the maker, after judgment has been recovered against the maker in a suit to foreclose, was established in Vandewater v. McRae, 27 Cal. 596; Allin v. Williams, 97 Cal. 403. And in such a case, after sale of the property under foreclosure and a deficiency judgment entered up against the mortgagor, an indorser of the note cannot obtain an assignment of such judgment until he pays the balance due on the note. Allin v. Williams, supra.

d. Judgment lien.—The lien of a mortgage is in no manner affected if a judgment is procured on the note secured by the mortgage; and the rule is that the mortgage may be afterward foreclosed and the lien thereby effectuated and enforced. Matthews v. Davis, 61 Iowa, 225; Sigworth v. Meriam, 66 Iowa, 477.

314 NEGOTIABLE NOTES AND MORTGAGES.

e. Deficiency judgment.—A judgment for a deficiency may be rendered against one who purchased the mortgaged property after the mortgage was made, and in his purchase assumed and agreed to pay the mortgage debt. Grand Island S. & L. Ass. v. Moore, 40 Neb. 686; Cooper v. Foss, 15 Neb. 515.

f. Judgment bar.—Recovery of judgment on notes secured by mortgage will constitute no bar to the creditor's action on other notes held by him as collateral security, so long as the judgment remains unpaid. Black v. Reno, 59 Fed. R. 917.

g. Conditional mortgage.—Where a mortgage and note secured thereby was to become void, either by the payment of the note, or “if the said mortgagee should die before the note is paid, then this deed and note are null and void,” it was held that the mortgage became void upon the death of the mortgagee, and before payment of the note. Hollis v. Hollis, 64 Me. 96.

h. Substituted note.—The parties to a mortgage may substitute a new note for the original by way of renewal without affecting the validity of the security. Buck v. Wood, 85 Me. 204.

i. Surety—Subrogation.—An agreement on the part of a grantee to pay and discharge a mortgage debt upon the granted premises for which his grantor is liable renders the grantee liable therefor to the mortgagee, and in an action for the foreclosure of the mortgage, if the mortgaged premises are insufficient to satisfy the mortgage debt, judgment may be rendered against him as well as against the mortgagor for the amount of such deficiency. This liability results from the familiar doctrine in equity that a creditor is entitled to the benefit of all securities or collateral obligations that his principal debtor may have given to the surety for the payment of the debt. By the conveyance of the mortgaged premises and the assumption of the mortgage debt by the grantee, the latter, as between him and his grantor, becomes primarily liable to the mortgagee and his vendor becomes his surety. Williams v. Naftzger, 103 Col. 438, where the rule thus enunciated was applied.

j. Purchase of property by creditor.—A creditor whose debt is secured by a deed of trust of real estate to a third party, as trustee, may purchase the property at a sale by the trustee under the terms of the trust; and if he credits the debtor on the mortgage debt with the amount of the purchase money it is, in fact and in law, a money payment to the use and benefit of the debtor. Easton v. German-American Bank, 127 U.S. 532.

k. Settlement of criminal prosecution.—In Georgia it has been held that a mortgage given partly upon an agreement to settle a criminal prosecution, whether that agreement was express or implied, and given partly to settle the debt of a son, it was illegal and could not be enforced by the mortgagee against the father. Code Sec. 2745. Small v. Williams, 87 Ga. 681.

l. Subject to inquiry.—A note and mortgage are open to inquiry when no money passed, and the object of the same remains in doubt. McAteer v. McAteer, 9 S.E. (S.C.) 966.

m. Burden of proof.—When the consideration of a trust deed is admitted, or properly established by proof, then the burden of proving that

the deed is fraudulent in fact is upon the creditor who assails the deed.

n. Production of note.—Where, upon trial of an action of foreclosure, and under the issues joined it was necessary to introduce the note secured, failure to produce the note was held sufficient ground for a non-suit.  
Weems v. Coker, 70 Ga. 746.

o. Mistake in note.—Where a mortgage describes a promissory note secured thereby sufficiently to identify it, a mistake in the date of the note is immaterial, and the mortgage may be foreclosed without being reformed.  
Snow v. Holmes, 71 Cal. 142.

p. Assignment by corporation.—As to sufficiency of assignment of mortgage from a corporation to enable the assignee to foreclose, see Burnett v. Lyford, 98 Cal. 114.

q. Land contracts as collateral.—Where contracts for land are absolutely and formally assigned as security for a debt, it is competent to show by parol that they were intended as security in the nature of a mortgage for money loaned. And the payment of the debt will discharge the lien.  
Lipp v. Syndicate, 24 Neb. 692; Scharman v. Scharman, 88 Neb. 39.

r. Consolidation of mortgages.—In case different mortgages upon one piece of property are executed in favor of one person, and are consolidated into one subsequent mortgage, the date of the latter instrument will prevail.  
Ker v. Ker, 42 La. Ann. 870.

s. Mortgage not invalidated by alteration of note.—Where a note was secured by a mortgage, and the note was rendered void by the alteration of a material part, it was held that the mortgage was not avoided, but was a valid security and could be enforced.  
Smith v. Smith, 27 S. C. 166; Plyler v. Elliott, 19 S. C. 264, approved and followed; Heath v. Blake, 28 S.C. 406.

t. Usury—Not void.—In Georgia it has been held that a mortgage made to secure a debt infected with usury is not void, since such an instrument passes no title, and is no attempt to pass a title, and hence is not embraced within the provisions of the Code, Sec. 2057(f) which enacts that “all titles made as part of a usurious contract, or to evade the laws against usury, are void.”  
Hodges v. Brown, 81 Ga. 276.

u. Executor’s mortgages superior to liens of creditors.—Where an executor of an estate, acting under a provision of the will of his testator, executes a mortgage to raise money in settling the estate, such mortgage security will be held superior to the lien of creditors whose claims have been established against the estate.  
Iowa Loan & Trust Co. v. Holderbaum, Iowa.

§ 175. The title of the pledgee of notes and mortgages.—The use by the holder of negotiable promissory notes of a third person, properly indorsed, together with an assignment of the mortgage given to secure the payment of the same, as collateral security for his own principal obligation, vests in the pledgee the legal title to the collateral securities, and enables him, upon default, to render the same available for the purpose of securing payment of his own advances. By such transactions the pledgee gains an additional security as compared with the indorsement and delivery of ordinary negotiable promissory notes as collateral security. The note secured by mortgage has all the characteristics and privileges of commercial paper; and the pledgee thereof receives the further collateral security of the property covered by the mortgage given to secure its payment. a. Execution of power.—Where a mortgage, containing a power of sale, was given to secure a promissory note, and the note has been assigned, the power can only be executed by the assignee of the note. Sanford v. Kane, 24 Ill. App. 50f. Reversed on other grounds. 127 Ill. 591.

d. Inhibition against speculation—A bank organized under the National Banking law may acquire title to real estate, even though encumbered, if honestly done for the purpose of securing a debt due it, and it may do this by taking a conveyance directly, or by sale under process of law. If the purpose is to speculate in real estate under the form or pretense of obtaining satisfaction of a previous debt, it is forbidden by law. Mapes v. Scott, 88 Ill. 852; S. C., 94 Ill. 879; see, also, Worcester National Bank v. Cheney, 87 Ill. 602; Libby v. Union National Bank, 99 Ill. 630.

e. Principal and surety.—The conveyance of premises subject to the encumbrance created by a deed of trust to secure a note will not subject the grantee to liability to pay the note, in the absence of words to that effect. To raise such a liability there must be words in the deed of conveyance from which, by fair import, an agreement to pay the debt can be inferred. Shepherd v. May, 115 U.S. 505; Elliott v. Notes,

a. Usurious mortgage.—Where an assignee of a usurious note and mortgage received the same by a written assignment on the mortgage only, for value, before maturity, and without notice of any equities, it was held, in an action for foreclosure that the defense of usury was available to the maker of the note against the assignee. Doll v. Hollenback, 19 Neb. 689; see Crosby v. Roub, 16 Wis. 645.

b. Assignment after maturity.—An assignee of a note and mortgage after maturity will not be held a bona fide purchaser. British & Am. Mtg. Co. v. Smith, 22 S. & E. (S. C.) 747.

c. Maturity.—The time of maturity of a note is not controlled by provisions of a mortgage as against its own terms, since the two instruments are separate. Owings v. Mackenzie, 23 S. W. (Mo.) 802.

d. Indemnity to guarantor.—Where a mortgage is given to secure a note given as payment of the guaranty of a mortgagor's note to a third person, it may be enforced. Fidelity Loan Guarantee Co. v. Baker, 54 Mo. App. 79.

e. Defenses.—Any defense available to the maker of a promissory note secured by mortgage, against the payee, is equally available against the assignee of the securities. Barry v. Guild, 126 Ill. 489.

Where the holder, however, although advancing value, is chargeable with notice of the invalid character of the consideration for such securities, no right or title thereto can be acquired.

Newman, 75 Ill. 215.

f. Trustee as agent.—The trustee in a deed of trust to secure the payment of a note, is the agent of the owner of the property as well as of the owner of the debt. Cassady v. Wallace, 102 Mo. 575.

g. Recovery—Kind of.—The general rule is that the pledgee of a note and mortgage is, on default, permitted to recover the full value of the security, holding the surplus for those having equities therein. Black v. Reno, 59 Fed. Rep. 917.

h. Quit-claim.—A quit-claim of a legal title by a mortgagee does not carry with it the mortgage interest. It passes only a bare legal title. The bare legal title will not stand against a clear equitable claim. Farrell v. Lewis, 56 Conn. 280.

i. What constitutes assignee an indorser.—A mortgage was given to secure the payment of a promissory note, and the payee indorsed upon the mortgage: "For value received I assign and transfer the within note and mortgage unto ____, and authorize him to collect and receive the proceeds thereof, the same as I could do," and delivered the note and mortgage to the person named in such writing. Held, that he was not liable as indorser of such note. May v. Dyer, 57 Ark. 441.

j. Antecedent debt.—A person was intrusted by the mortgagee with a note and mortgage only for the purpose of raising money upon them for his own use; but he pledged them for an antecedent debt. Held, that such pledge was good as against the mortgagee. Tomblin v. Callen, 69 Iowa, 239.

k. Same.—So where one intrusts the payee of a note with the apparent title of it, and a trust deed securing it, an indorsee of the note and deed will take them unaffected by any private agreement between the payee and the maker. Travelers’ Ins. Co. v. Redfield, 6 Col. Ct. App. 190.

l. Pre-existing debt.—A mortgage given to secure a pre-existing debt, without any extension of time of payment, although it has priority in point of record, will not be held superior to another mortgage given for a present advance. First Nat. Bank v. Conn. Mut. Life Ins. Co., 129 Ind. 241.

§ 177. The rights of the pledgee, in cases of misappropriation.—Where the owner of negotiable promissory notes, secured by mortgage or deed of trust, has placed the same in possession of another, so that the latter has, by indorsement where required and assignment, the legal title and apparent absolute ownership of such securities, an innocent pledgee, receiving such notes before maturity, and an assignment of the mortgage, express or implied, upon a valuable advance, made on the faith and credit of such apparent title and ownership, without notice of equities, is protected, although such use of the securities be a misappropriation thereof and a fraud upon the real owner. The like rule is applied for the benefit of an innocent pledgee, who has advanced value, in the usual course of business, upon a negotiable note, secured by mortgage, where the act of misappropriation is made by an agent, who has been entrusted with such a note indorsed in blank, and enabled to appear as the apparent owner thereof. Such pledgee is entitled to enforce the mortgage given to secure such note to the full amount, notwithstanding the fraud of the agent. An indorsement “without recourse,” before maturity, by a pledgor of a note made by a third person, and secured by mortgage, although such note was obtained from the maker by artifice, vests the title to the note and mortgage security in a pledgee.

'Morris v. Beacon, 123 Mass. 58.
A made a note to the order of B, and secured by mortgage, duly recorded. B indorsed the note to C as collateral security for a loan to a larger amount, stating that the note carried the mortgage with it. Subsequently B fraudulently substituted another note for the one secured by the mortgage, and indorsed it and the mortgage to D, for value. Both pledgees acted in good faith. No right of the first pledgee was lost by the fraudulent substitution. Even by agreement the mortgage could not be made a security for a note which it was not intended to secure. The utmost risk the pledgee took was that B might discharge the mortgage, but the note would still remain a valid security; or B might pass the legal title to another, who in law would become the trustee of the pledgee of the note.

*Swift v. Smith, 102 U.S. 442.
The rights of the holder of negotiable promissory notes, secured by trust deed, indorsed in blank by the owner, and handed to an agent for a certain purpose, were sustained, although the agent misappropriated the same by pledging them as collateral security for his own note, given for a loan of money. Default occurring upon the personal note of the pledgor, the pledgee, as a purchaser for value, without notice, was allowed to enforce the trust deed.

The lien of a pledgee, holding the legal title to the note and mortgage, is not defeated as against third persons chargeable with notice, by the fraud or mistake of the mortgagee in entering satisfaction of the mortgage upon the record.

§ 178. The pledgee, when chargeable with notice.—The pledgee of negotiable paper, secured by a mortgage or deed of trust, is chargeable with notice of misappropriation, or want of authority, under the same presumptions governing in other cases of pledge of ordinary commercial instruments. Where such securities show upon their face the existence of a trust, pledgees are bound to take notice thereof, and to make inquiry at their peril. A, as trustee, held a note made to himself personally, and a mortgage securing the payment of the same, the mortgage stating that the consideration was paid by A “as trustee for” B, and referred to A as “trustee as aforesaid.” After recording the mortgage, A struck out the words “as trustee,” and then borrowed money for his own use of C, transferring the note and mortgage as collateral security. The advance was made in good faith, but the pledgee failed to read the mortgage, and made no examination of the record. C being chargeable with notice of the contents thereof, the pledgee was not regarded as a bona fide holder for the value of the securities, and was ordered to return them to the successor in trust. The truth appears to be that the defendant (the pledgee) accepted the mortgage without taking pains to read it. If he had read it he would have discovered all that was necessary for his protection. § 179. The pledgor’s re-transfer of notes and mortgages.—The pledgor of negotiable notes, secured by mortgage, may, with the consent of the pledgee, re-transfer such collateral securities to another pledgee, or for a new loan, and the title thereto thus obtained will be enforced. Certain notes of a third person, payable at different times, and secured by a mortgage, were held as collateral security for indebtedness. The pledgor may, with the consent of the pledgee, transfer to another of his creditors a portion of the notes to hold as collateral security, and may agree that the mortgage securing the payment of the notes shall stand as a prior security for the notes so re-assigned, at the same time giving to the first pledgee new securities of equal value. A contest arose as between the two pledgees upon the question of priority in the distribution of the proceeds upon foreclosure and sale under the mortgage; the pledgor’s agreement in favor of the second creditor was supported, he having remained the general owner of the securities, and having furnished other collateral securities to the first pledgee. A bank loaned money on negotiable notes, secured by deed of trust. The loan was paid, but the bank retaining the securities, a further specific pledge thereof was made as collateral security for another loan. The rights of the pledgee under the second loan were supported as against

§ 180. The pledge of notes and mortgages to national banks.—A national bank, holding a negotiable promissory note secured by mortgage or deed of trust, as collateral security for the payment of loans is entitled, upon default, to the enforcement of the mortgage security, although it be insisted as a defense, that the taking of such real estate security by a national bank is an act under sections 5136 and 5137 of the United States Revised Statutes ultra vires the bank.’ In the leading case upon this subject,’ a negotiable promissory note, secured by a deed of trust, with the usual powers of sale upon default, was indorsed, with the mortgage security, to a national bank as collateral security for a loan. Upon default, the bank requested the trustee to sell the property. A bill in equity was filed in a circuit court in the State of Missouri to enjoin the sale, and an injunction was granted and sustained against such sale. Courts of equity have always refused, under like circumstances, to use the discretionary powers vested in their chancellors to relieve borrowers from national and other banks or corporations from the repayment of bona fide loans, upon a defense of ultra vires as against the lender. The equity of the lender of money in good faith is preferred to that of persons and corporations who have had the benefit thereof and still retain the same, or the property acquired therewith, and yet seek to avoid repayment upon a legal technicality, which was never intended to shelter fraud. The rule is applied, in the absence of restrictive statutory enactments, in favor of banking and loaning corporations, advancing money bona fide in states and countries.

NOTES,

a. Who may invoke the rule.—Only the United States government can invoke the rule against the taking of mortgage security by national banks. Merchants Nat. Bank v. Hanson, 83 Minn. 40; Baker v. Northwestern Guaranty Co., 86 Minn. 185; Bank v. Flathers, 45 La. Ann. 75.

b. The same.—Conveyances of real estate to national banks are valid for all purposes until called in question by a direct proceeding instituted for that purpose by the government. § 181. The recovery by pledgees and sub-pledgees of notes and mortgages.—The pledgee for value advanced in good faith, without notice, holding negotiable promissory notes, secured by mortgage, before maturity, as collateral security, is entitled to enforce the mortgage security in a court of equity, and to recover the full face of the notes secured, holding any surplus above the amount of the loan or debt for the benefit of those beneficially entitled thereto. The like rule is enforced in favor of a sub-pledgee of notes and mortgages, receiving the same, with the evidence of the principal debt for which they were pledged, upon an advance in good faith to the pledgee thereof, and with notice of equities. As against a subsequent purchaser for value of the property chargeable with notice, the sub-pledgee is allowed to collect the full amount of the note secured by the mortgage. In states where the restricted rule prevails, subjecting indorsees of negotiable paper, seeking to enforce payment by foreclosure and sale of the property in equity, to defenses not available against the note, a sub-pledgee who advances money to take up securities held in pledge for a loan is restricted in his recovery, as against the mortgagor and maker, his representatives, and bona fide purchasers for value, to the amount of the actual advance by the pledgee upon receiving such note and mortgage as collateral.

fore maturity by a pledgee, with full title, for a greater sum than the amount of the original loan to the pledgor, a sub-pledgee advancing a valuable consideration thereon, in good faith, and without notice of equities, is a purchaser for value of such note and mortgage, to the extent of his advances, and may enforce the same for the face thereof, holding any surplus for the persons entitled thereto. The pledgor—having, by reason of his misplaced confidence in intrusting the legal title and apparent absolute ownership of such negotiable securities and mortgage to a third person, enabled him to deceive an innocent sub-pledgee advancing money on the credit of such title and ownership—is estopped to set up any defenses existing between himself and the pledgee as against such sub-pledgee, and is only entitled to recover his securities upon payment of the full amount advanced.

Upon sub-pledges of mortgage securities made for less than the amount of the original advances, where the whole interest of the pledgee is assigned for the greater security of the sub-pledgee, and the persons bound upon the securities become insolvent, the sub-pledgees are allowed to prove for the whole amount secured by the first pledge, although not receiving more than what is due them for the principal, interest, and costs. The rule as to recovery of the sub-pledgee applies where the amount advanced by the sub-pledgee is less than the sum loaned the pledgor thereon by the pledgee. The actual recovery is limited to the amount of the advances where the owner of the securities seeks to redeem the same.

Such negotiable instruments, although secured by mortgage, come within the general rules governing the realization of negotiable collateral securities. The pledgee thereof is not permitted to sell them at either public or private sale, except with the consent of the pledgor, either given by contract of pledge, or agreed to subsequently. Conveyance to pledgee.—In a California case, where a debtor to secure a loan upon his promissory note, gave a mortgage to secure the same, and, as additional security, pledged with his creditor the note of a third party and accompanying mortgage, and the creditor, after foreclosing the mortgage given by the debtor and securing a deficiency judgment against the debtor, accepted a conveyance of the premises covered by the collateral mortgage from the mortgagor, it was held that the creditor must account to the debtor for the value of the property received by him, under the rule that the holder of a mortgage, as collateral security, cannot sell it, but may collect it when due (Civil Code, Sec. 8006), although he may foreclose the lien and himself become the purchaser. Webb, 44 Cal. 127, where the note in suit contained a provision to that effect, it was held that a failure to pay the interest when it became due made the whole amount of the note due absolutely at the option of the holder, without any notice from the holder to the payer. The court said: “The plaintiff had no duty to perform to the defendant, and the latter no excuse to delay the payments which he had stipulated to make.” And this case was followed in Hewitt v. Where a pledgee of notes and mortgages has returned the same to the pledgor for the purpose of making collection thereof for account of the pledgee, the latter may bring trover (or a statutory substitute therefor) against the pledgor, upon his failure, after demand, to return or account for the collaterals. The measure of damages in such a case, is the interest of the pledgee in the collaterals, being the amount of the debt where they are of greater value, or their full value, where less.

§ 183. The pledgee’s foreclosure and sale of the mortgaged land.—The holder of a negotiable promissory note, secured by mortgage, as collateral security for a debt, is entitled, upon default, to proceed with the foreclosure of the property included in the mortgage security, and to entry, and possession thereof, under appropriate proceedings. Such proceedings, however, do not change the relations of the parties to the contract of pledge, the land being simply substituted as collateral security in place of the notes and mortgage, and remaining subject to redemption. Nor, as between the pledgor and pledgee, is such foreclosure, entry and possession a payment of the debt for which the notes and mortgages are held as collateral security.

former notes for the amount and in settlement of such judgments, the same were held to be without consideration. Price v. Rea, 92 Iowa, 12.

1. Obligation of bank.—Where the cashier of a bank procured plaintiff to execute his note to the bank to be used as collateral for the bank’s accommodation, and at the same time promised to protect plaintiff against loss on account thereof, it was held that the execution of the note was a good consideration for the cashier's promise, and a good consideration also for a mortgage afterward made by him to plaintiff to secure him against his contingent liability on the note. Duncan v. Miller, 64 Iowa, 223.

After such foreclosure, entry, and possession, the pledgee is under no obligation to take the land as in payment of his debt. He should proceed with convenient speed to reduce such property to cash, by a fair and proper public sale. In this, he acts as trustee for the pledgor, and is required to pay over to him any balance remaining after the payment of the debt for which the notes and mortgage were held as security; or, if the debt and other proper charges be paid, to release and quit-claim the land to the pledgor. As against the mortgagor, the pledgee will have an absolute title, but not as against the pledgor; although where possession of the land for over twenty years has been held by the pledgee or his successive assignees, a claim to redeem by the pledgor is not favored in equity. It is only from the time of the realization in money, after foreclosure of the mortgage securities held in pledge, that the statute of limitations begins to run against the pledgor, where, the debt being paid, a surplus remains in the hands of the pledgee.

a. Foreclosure.—A note given for a specific sum was secured by a mortgage, but was intended to secure the mortgagee for any advances he might make on account for the mortgagor. Held, upon foreclosure of the mortgage that the amount for which judgment was rendered was properly the amount the mortgagee had paid under the liability for which he was secured, with interest from the day of payment. Vogan v. Caminetti, 65 Cal. 483; see Morris v. Cain, 39 La. Ann. 712.

b. ce. Foreclosure—Maturity of other notes.—A mortgage secured two notes, one payable in five, the other in ten years, with interest payable annually. The maker was to pay “the notes and all interest that may be due thereon, according to the tenor and effect of said notes.” Such notes were pledged as collateral security for a loan, and default was made in payment thereof at maturity. The holder brought a foreclosure suit, the first note being due and unpaid, and no interest paid on either note. Held, that a decree of foreclosure was proper, without waiting for the second note to mature. Black v. Reno, 59 Fed. R. (Mo.) 917.

d. Foreclosure—Effect of.—Where the mortgage of a third party has been assigned by the mortgagee as collateral security for his own debt, the foreclosure of that mortgage by the assignee and his purchase at the sale, as against the assignor, work no other result than to substitute the land for the mortgage in the hands of the assignee, and to leave it subject to the assignor’s right by payment of the debt to reclaim and hold his own property discharged of the assignee’s lien upon it. Matter of Gilbert, 104 N. Y. 200; Slee v. Manhattan Co., 1 Paige (N. Y.), 48; Hoyt v. Martense, 16 N. Y. 231.

e. Foreclosure—Rights of lienors.—In an action to foreclose a mortgage given by L. to W., the plaintiff claimed to have acquired title to the bond accompanying the mortgage by an assignment from W., May 17, 1884, and recorded June 21, 1884. W. had previously and on October 1, 1883, assigned this mortgage to B. which was recorded June 11, 1884. The assignment to B. did not in express terms assign the bond, but it stated that the mortgage was made to secure the payment of $1,700, “according to the conditions of a bond accompanying the same.” B. delivered the mortgage to W. to sell the same and pay B. the amount due on the note secured by the assignment, but W. did not effect a sale. Subsequently W. secured the bond and mortgage from B. to get some dates, or for some purpose other than to sell them. W. then in fraud of B.'s rights sold the instruments to plaintiff for $1,715.86, and of this sum $921.41 was applied upon antecedent debts due it from W. of which debts $887.89 matured after the assignment to B. had been recorded. Held, that to the extent to which the pre-existing debt to the plaintiff was paid by the assignment, the plaintiff was not a bona fide purchaser for value as against B. That the registry of the assignment to B. was notice sufficient to put the plaintiff upon inquiry, that as the bond was in fact transferred with the mortgage, the assignment to B. was valid; that instead of its authorizing the presumption that the bond had not been transferred, it was notice that everything essential to constitute an assignment of the mortgage had been done, nothing appearing in the assignment to the contrary. The court said: “Here the bond was, in fact, transferred with the mortgage, although not mentioned.

The assignment of the mortgage was therefore not a nullity * * * but valid." Citing Foster v. Van Reed, 70 N. Y. 19, Yates Co. National Bank v. Baldwin, 43 Hun, 186, aff'd, 124 N. Y. 633.

f. Foreclosure—Rights of parties.—W. borrowed of M. $5,300 and gave his note therefor, secured by a mortgage containing a power of sale. Upon his becoming insolvent, W. conveyed the premises covered by the mortgage to M. in payment of the debt, but the latter did not surrender the note or cancel the mortgage. Subsequently, and twelve years after the maturity of this note, M., to secure an indebtedness of $5,100 to a bank, executed to its president a note for $6,000, and to secure the same executed to W. a deed of trust upon the premises before mentioned; but M., instead of canceling the mortgage given him by W., assigned the same to the bank president, covenanting in the assignment that there was due under the original mortgage not less than $5,300, and that he had a good right to assign the same. There was no consideration for the assignment of the original mortgage, it being assigned to the bank president as further collateral security for his, the debt of M., to the bank. G. bought the $6,000 note of the bank, and received the collaterals securing the same, and foreclosed the deed of trust. The brother of G. purchased the property for the amount due on the $6,000 note and costs. M., the complainant herein, redeemed the premises upon payment of $7,874.89. Subsequently G. foreclosed the original mortgage and sold the premises to his brother, who purchased with knowledge of the facts. M. filed a bill against G. to cancel the sale made pursuant to the original mortgage. Held, that G. was not a bona fide purchaser as against M.; that the sale under the original mortgage was fraudulent and void, and that the conveyance made upon the second sale should be canceled as a cloud upon the title of M. Gage v. McDermid, 150 Ill. 598.

g. Foreclosure—Adjustment of rights.—D. executed and delivered to the grantors of land to him, a mortgage of the premises, to secure the payment of six promissory notes described therein. W. and others gave D. a warranty deed of the lands in question. D. gave to the defendant a deed in 1872, in which were these words: "and an undivided half of the tract I purchased of"—(D.'s mortgagee). When the deed was recorded these words were omitted until a second record was made in 1879, while this suit was on trial, in which these words were included. The notes and mortgages were reassigned by D. in 1876, to his assignors, the original mortgagees, who on the same day assigned them to the orator. Pursuant to agreement the notes and mortgage were, when executed, deposited with a third party to be held by him until the incumbrances were removed from the land, and if it fell short the notes were to be reduced to an amount agreed upon—$4 per acre. The orator, after the assignment to him, through some misunderstanding, obtained possession of the notes and mortgage, procured a foreclosure, and the decree against D. became absolute. The orator had no actual notice of the deed to the defendant. In the action to foreclose the mortgage: Held, 1. That the orator is entitled to a decree against defendant; that there was no constructive notice; that the filing of the deed is only the incipient record; and that when a deed has been recorded and taken from the town clerk's office, it is no part of the files, and the record is...

decisive of equities, 2. That the decree concludes all equities of D., and of all claiming under him. Potter v. Dooley, 55 Vt. 512.

h. Possession of note—Effect of.—The possession of a negotiable promissory note secured by mortgage is prima facie evidence of ownership. O'Keefe v. First Nat. Bk., 49 Kan. 347.

i. Purchases not a discharge.—M. executed to defendant certain notes secured by mortgages of lands owned by him. Thereafter M. conveyed the lands to W., subject to the mortgages mentioned. The defendant then "sold and assigned" the notes and mortgages to M., who assigned a portion of the notes to P. P. reassigned the same to W., and thereafter M. "sold and reassigned" all the notes and mortgages to defendant. Held, that the mortgages were not discharged or extinguished by their purchase by and assignment to M. but still remained in force, though in his hands, so that, as against W. and the plaintiff, who is his privy, claiming only under him, it was competent for M. to transfer them unimpaired to the defendant. Baker v. Northwestern Guarantee Loan Co., 36 Minn. 185; see also Smith v. Swan, 69 Iowa, 412.

j. Foreclosure—Payment to non-holder.—E. executed a mortgage to C. to secure two negotiable promissory notes. The notes were sold and assigned by C. to the plaintiff before maturity, but no assignment of the mortgage was made of record or otherwise. E. made a payment on the notes to C. relying upon the statement of C. that he owned the notes. Held, in an action to foreclose the mortgage by a purchaser of the notes for value and before maturity, that credit for the amount paid to C. should not be allowed to the mortgagor, nor to a purchaser of the land from him. Brayley v. Ellis, 71 Iowa, 155. The same principle was applied in a case in Michigan. A mortgagor, ignorant of the fact that the mortgage and negotiable note secured thereby had been assigned by the mortgagee, paid the mortgage debt to the administrators of the mortgagee, who did not have or produce the note or mortgage. And it was held, that such payment constituted no defense to an action of foreclosure brought by the assignee of the note and mortgage. Williams v. Keyes, 90 Mich. 290. Where a series of notes are secured by a mortgage, and the mortgagee indorses certain of the notes to a party with an agreement to hold the mortgage in trust to secure the notes so indorsed, the mortgage was not extinguished by the payment of the remaining notes to one to whom they and the other notes were assigned and that a writ of entry could be brought. Norton v. Palmer, 142 Mass. 433.

k. Foreclosure—Smaller debt.—Where a mortgage is assigned as collateral security for a much smaller debt, it may be foreclosed, when due, by the holder, at least against the defendant who is merely a junior lienholder, for the whole amount thereof, and before the last secured debt is due. Colby v. McOmber, 71 Iowa, 469.

l. Judgment or foreclosure.—If a written instrument constituted both a promissory note and a mortgage, the holder, at his option, may recover a money judgment upon it, as a promissory note, or proceed to foreclose. Frank v. Pickle, 2 Wash. Ter. Rep. 55.

m. Foreclosure—Attorney’s bonus.—Defendant bank received from A. as security for his indebtedness a note secured by a mortgage. A foreclosure suit was brought by the holder of a senior mortgage in which A.

appeared by his own attorney, and filed a cross-bill. The land was sold under a decree directing the foreclosure of both mortgages. The land was subsequently purchased by the bank and the attorney for A. in the foreclosure suit negotiated the purchase and received a bonus. Subsequently the bank resold the land at a profit. Held, that A. could not recover from the bank the amount of the note from such profits realized by the bank. Raben v. First National Bank, 37 Neb. 364.

n. Foreclosure—Assignment necessary.—A promissory note and mortgage upon personal property were combined together in one instrument, the promise being to pay the money to a named payee or bearer, and the mortgage portion of the instrument was in haec verba: “To further secure the payment of this note I hereby mortgage the following described property,” etc. Held, that one who is not the payee named in the instrument cannot foreclose the mortgage in his own name as holder and owner thereof without having a written assignment. Code, Sec. 1996; Nicholson v. Whaley, 90 Ga. 257; Planter's Bank v. Prater, 64 Ga. 609.

o. Foreclosure—Coupon interest notes.—The holder of overdue coupon interest notes, secured by mortgage, may maintain an action to foreclose the mortgage, although the principal debt is not yet mature, and is held by another person, who is made a party to the suit. Minn. Gen. Sts. 1878; c. 81, secs. 8,4; Fowler v. Johnson, 26 Minn. 388; Cleveland v. Booth, 43 Minn. 16. As to rate of interest upon coupon notes after maturity, see Holbrook v. Sims, 39 Minn. 122.

p. Same—Judgment.—The holder of coupon interest notes will not be entitled to judgment upon coupon notes not due, although the note provides that upon default in payment of interest when due, the holder shall have the option to declare the principal note payable. Cloud v. Rayrd, 6 Wash. 555.

q. Foreclosure—Right to redeem.—A executed a mortgage of land to B, to secure a promissory note for a specified amount. In fact the note was intended to secure advances to be made by B. After B had made advances to an amount less than the face of the note, he executed an assignment of his “interest” in the mortgage and note to C, and indorsed the note in blank, without recourse. B then sold the note and mortgage to D for certain property, and delivered to him the note, on which an installment of interest was then overdue, the assignment to C and what purported to be an assignment from C to D. There was no such person as C in existence, but D acted in good faith and without notice that the note was given for future advances. After D had notice of all the facts he took a new assignment from B. When D took the note he believed it to be of no value, and relied only on the land as security. Held, on a bill in equity by A against D, that A was entitled to redeem only on paying the full amount of the note. Bassett v. Daniels, 136 Mass. 547.

r. Foreclosure—Retention of funds.—Where a note secured by mortgage is pledged as collateral security, and an administrator of an estate is a party to the foreclosure, judgment may require the holder of the collateral to retain in trust the proceeds of the note and mortgage subject to, after extinguishing his claim. Williams v. Lumpkin, 74 Tex. 601.

s. Foreclosure—Application to secured note.—Where a savings bank holds two notes, one secured by mortgage, the other not, it will not

Tallman v. New Bedford Sav. Bk., 188 Mass. 330. To same effect is Bean v. New Bedford Inst., 187 Mass. 262.

t. Foreclosure.—Where a mortgage secures notes falling due at different dates, and a bill is filed to foreclose the mortgage after maturity of one, but before that of the other, and the latter note matures before the decree of foreclosure and sale is rendered, the decree may cover the latter as well as the former note, if proper foundation has been laid in the bill, McLane v. Piaggio, 24 Fed. R. 71.

u. Foreclosure—Different owners.—Where two notes are secured by a mortgage, held by different owners, a decree of foreclosure to which the holder of other notes is not made a party will not prevent him from effecting a second foreclosure. Todd v. Creamer, 36 Neb. 430.

v. Foreclosure.—The holder of one of several coupon notes secured by a mortgage, may foreclose on default, and the holders of other coupons are not necessary parties. Boyer v. Chandler, 160 Ill. 394.

w. Waiver of foreclosure.—Right to foreclose collateral is not made by an action to foreclose mortgage securing principal debt. McArthur v. Magee, 45 Pac. 1068.

x. Declaring notes due.—A note and mortgage securing it, made contemporaneously, are to be construed together. Therefore, where a note is payable on or before a date named, and the mortgage contains a provision that in certain contingencies, prior to that date, the mortgagee may elect to declare the whole amount due, held, that such provision in the mortgage authorizes the mortgagee, upon the happening of such contingencies, to proceed not only to enforce the mortgage but also to enforce the personal liability upon the note. Grand Island L. & L. Ass. v. Moore, 40 Neb. 686.

y. Default—Effect of.—A provision in trust deed, that upon default of any of the notes all will become due is valid, and the trustee is authorized to sell for the payment of all notes on default in payment of any one of them. Meier v. Meier, 105 Mo. 411.

z. Note or mortgage, due on default in interest.—A note was made payable in six years from date. In the mortgage securing the note it was stipulated that "if the interest remains unpaid for six months after due, the whole amount shall become due, and payable at once." The interest remained unpaid six months after the same became due. Held, that the principal became due upon such default in payment of interest. Clayton v. Whittaker, 68 Iowa, 412.

aa. Louisiana.—In Louisiana, under the Civil Code, Art. 8170 (3187), the pledgee of a note secured by mortgage has a right, on default of payment, to sue upon the note in his own name, or for the use of the pledgor, subject to the obligation to account to the debtor. Mechanics & Traders Ins. Co. v. Lozano, 89 La. Ann. 821.

bb. Default.—As to when it occurs, see Wolz v. Parker, 85 S. W. (Mo.) 1149.

cc. Suit on note.—A note secured by mortgage, issued by a planter to

the order of his merchant, to make good all advances for the working of a plantation, although received as collateral security, may be sued on directly by the latter, for the exact amount of the advances, as a pledgee could do. Chaffee v. Whitfield, 40 La. Ann. 631.

dd. Same.—Right to give one note secured by mortgage a preference. Morgan v. Kline, 77 Iowa, 681.

ee. Lien.—Lien of mortgage not discharged by giving new notes. Reid v. Abernathy, 77 Iowa, 448; Cook v. Gilchrist, 82 Iowa, 277.

ff. Subrogation.—Subrogation to mortgage security recognized in Bush v. Wadsworth, 60 Mich. 255.

gg. Penalty for failure to enter satisfaction.—Where a negotiable promissory note is secured by a mortgage, and the debt is afterward assigned, but the assignment is not recorded, and the mortgagor has no notice of such assignment, and the debt is afterward fully paid and satisfied, but the mortgagee fails, after demand, and within a reasonable time, to enter, or cause to be entered, satisfaction of record of the mortgage, held, that the mortgagee is liable to the mortgagor for the penalty prescribed by section 8 of the act relating to mortgages. Perkins v. Matteson, 40 Kan. 165.

hh. Vendor's lien—Effect of.—Where a promissory note secured by a vendor's lien is assigned, such assignment will not be effectual to charge a subsequent mortgagee with notice thereof, unless the same is recorded. Patterson v. Tuttle, 278 S. W. Rep. (Tex.) 758.

ii. Payment—Revival of debt.—Where one surety makes a payment on a note after the bar of the statute has arisen, it does not revive the debt against the co-sureties. Long v. Miller, 96 N. C. 227; Green v. Greensboro Female College, 83 N. C. 449.

jj. Future debt.—A mortgage may be consented to to secure an obligation which has not yet risen into existence, but in such case the mortgage can only be enforced in so far as the obligation shall have been created. Morris v. Cain, 39 La. Ann. 712.

kk. Bonds not negotiable without indorsement.—Bonds are not negotiable without indorsement. Thus where a bond was transferred before maturity, without indorsement, it was held to be subject to any defenses between the original parties at the time of the transfer. Spence v. Tapscott, 93 N. C. 246.

§ 184. The assignee’s title to the mortgage security.—In three or four states, notably New York, Pennsylvania and New Jersey, where loans are sought upon the security of real estate as well as upon the individual liability of the borrower, the personal evidences of indebtedness, for which the mortgage is given as collateral security, are bonds, non-negotiable in character. Such obligations are subject to onerous equities in the hands of any assignee, however remote. The equities include those existing between the original parties, and attending the original transaction, and the equitable rights of third persons, cestuis que trust, and others. The bona fide assignee for value of such collaterals is limited in his recovery thereon to the actual amount validly due as between the original parties, subject to set-offs, and the equities stated; and the mortgage, as an incident to the debt, and equally non-negotiable, and subject to the like equities, cannot be enforced by such assignee for any larger sum. Such limited recovery upon enforcing the mortgage security, when given with a non-negotiable bond, is consonant with the approved rule under which the indorsee for value, before due, in good faith, of negotiable promissory notes, secured by mortgage, recovers the face value of the notes, free from antecedent equities, when enforcing the mortgage incident.

<br>

### --- Page 0428 ---

THE TITLE OF THE ASSIGNEE. 339

dent. Under this view, bonds and mortgages constituting a poor security for the loan of money, the use has become general of indorsement of certificates by mortgagors and obligors that they have no defenses, equities or set-offs. Where such certificates are indorsed or attached, the assignee of a bond and mortgage, without notice of equities, and for value advanced on the faith and credit of the representations so made, may invoke the rules of estoppel on pais, or equitable estoppel, as against the mortgagor and obligor, notwithstanding the original transaction, as between the parties was without consideration, or a gross fraud. Under the rules stated, a subassignee, with knowledge, may take a valid title from a donative assignee for value, without notice of equities. The representations contained in such certificates are of as binding effect as if made upon the favored instruments of commerce, and pass upon assignment to successive holders for value, as where negotiable paper is indorsed in blank. Bonds and mortgages, thus freed from antecedent equities, become available collateral securities.

a. Discharge.—A bond and mortgage, taken for the same debt, are so far one that a release or extinguishment of either, without actual payment, is a discharge of the other, unless otherwise intended by the parties; wherefore an acknowledgment upon the record of the satisfaction in full thereof, without any mention of the debt or the bond, prima facie im-

A similar opinion was stated by Justice Sutherland, in a later case and in Corning v. Murray. Even in these early cases, a majority of the court held the more extended view, and the question was finally settled in Bush v. Lathrop, where the rule was established that the assignee of a bond and mortgage takes only such title as his assignor had and no other, and is subject as well to all the equities of third persons as to those of the original mortgagor and mortgagee. In that case the pledgee of a bond and mortgage, holding the same under an assignment of the absolute title thereto as collateral security for a smaller sum than the face of the bond, made a sub-pledge thereof to a third person who advanced its full value in good faith, without notice. The fact that an assignee has no notice of such equities at the time he makes his advance, is immaterial. The rule announced was modified in later cases, but in the leading case of the Trustees of Union College v. Wheeler the Court of Appeals

b. Bonds and mortgages—Indicia of ownership.—If the owner of an unmatured bond, payable to bearer, puts the bond in the possession of a third person, he invests such person with the ordinary and usual evidence of title to that kind of property; and if the person thus held out as owner deals with the bond as the owner, in a transaction with a stranger ignorant of the real facts, and a loss results, the owner and not the stranger, must bear the loss. of New York declared that Bush v. Lathrop, supra, had been overruled only as to the point that an assignor of a chose in action is estopped to set up any equities affecting the title between himself and his assignee in an action brought by a second assignee, and not as qualifying the rule as to the rights of an assignee in enforcing the mortgage, or as to equities growing out of the chose in action itself. The rule is declared well settled that the assignee of a bond and mortgage takes the security subject to equities attending the original transaction, that he takes no greater rights than his assignor, and that the true test is to inquire, what can the mortgagee do by way of enforcement of it as against the property mortgaged. What he can do the assignee can do, and no more. The rule that the assignee of a bond and mortgage takes the security, subject to equities attending the original transaction in favor of the mortgagor and of prior equitable claims of third persons, is followed in several decisions, and is the rule in New York State.

The rule in New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Virginia.—The established rule in New Jersey is that the assignee of a mortgage given to secure a bond (and it would seem a promissory note) receives it subject to all defenses which the mortgagor may have against it, but free from any secret equities existing in favor of third persons, cestuis que trust, and others, of which the assignee has no notice. In Pennsylvania, an assignee for value of a non-negotiable bond and mortgage is subject to all equities, open and secret, of the mortgagor, but not subject to equities of third persons of which he had no notice, express or implied; or subject to the same equities and rules that govern other non-negotiable instruments or claims. The rule applies only where the debtor has an equity for relief, or a ground of defense based on honest transactions between himself and his assignor, and is not intended as a cover for fraud. It was not applied in a case where a married woman, with power to convey her real estate, executed a bond secured by a deed of trust, and the securities passed by assignment to a bona fide purchaser for value, without notice of the fraud. The equities of the assignee were preferred as against a third person, who had actively participated in the fraud, and was seeking to defeat his title.

§ 187. The assignment of bonds and mortgages under estoppel.—The rules of equitable estoppel are invoked for the benefit of the assignee for value without notice, of bonds and mortgages, to relieve him from the onerous defenses and equities to which he is usually subject in enforcing his mortgage security, although advancing a considerable consideration, in good faith, and without notice. The rules of estoppel are applied where one person, either by words or conduct, induces another to believe that he may safely take a certain security, and he, relying upon such representation, acquires such security, the former is never permitted in a court of equity to overthrow the title so acquired. A mortgagor is estopped where,

b. Foreclosure—Title of purchasers.—Where a mortgage securing bonds was pledged for the purpose of carrying on the construction of a canal, by authority of the directors, and the pledge is foreclosed in a strictly legal manner, the fact that at the sale thereunder the bonds brought but little, there being no fraud shown, cannot impeach the purchaser's title. The rules of equitable estoppel are also applied where an owner of a bond and mortgage intrusts the same to an agent, so that he has the full legal and equitable title and the apparent absolute ownership thereof, by whom they are assigned, without notice, to an innocent person who advances his money upon the faith and credit of such title and apparent ownership. The rules are also applied in favor of persons advancing value in good faith, as against cestuis que trust in cases where a trustee holds bonds and mortgages with an apparently absolute power of disposition. It was also enforced in Moore v. Metropolitan Bank, in which a bona fide purchaser for value of a non-negotiable chose in action from one upon whom the owner had by assignment conferred the apparent ownership, making such purchase on the faith thereof, obtained a valid title as against the real owner and the world.

§ 188. Equitable limitations upon the application of estoppel.—In order that the equitable rules of estoppel in pais may be applied, ’t is necessary that the mortgagor shall have done an act or made an admission, the natural effect of which is to influence the conduct of the assignee, and which has induced him to change his position or condition, so that if the mortgagor is afterward permitted to deny the truth of his conduct or his words, the assignee will suffer injury... And where a trustee has made a colorable assignment of bonds and mortgages, for his own benefit, to an assignee for value, chargeable with notice of the misappropriation, no rights, as against the cestuis que trust, can be acquired by such assignee, by reason of his mala fides. § 189. Estoppel in pais, by mortgagor’s certificate of “No defense.” — The rules of estoppel in pais or equitable estoppel, as applied in favor of assignees for value of bonds and mortgages, are most frequently invoked in cases where the mortgagor and obligor, upon the execution of the bond and mortgage, has indorsed a certificate thereon to the effect that he has “no defenses, equities, or set-offs of any kind” against such mortgage, or that the same is a valid security, and that he has received full payment, or other like terms. In such cases, the assignee who has advanced value on the faith of such certificate, in good faith, without notice, is entitled to enforce the security, although there be fraud or want of consideration as between the mortgagor and mortgagee. Where a mortgagor has signed a certificate that he has “no defense” to such security, the fact that an assignment of such bonds and mortgage is an actual misappropriation by an agent intrusted therewith, with full title, is no defense as against an assignee for value, without notice. Even where the money thus obtained has never been accounted for, the mortgage security is not affected by such misappropriation, the purchaser being under no obligation to look to the application of such proceeds, nor responsible for their misappropriation.

Such certificate of “no defense” defeats the equities of third parties arising out of a collateral agreement, the assignee

Nor will the want of a formal acknowledgment by a wife of a mortgagor securing the payment of a bond, in which her husband joined, affect the application of the rules of equitable estoppel arising from such certificates of “no defense.” But, as delivery and assignment of a bond and mortgage for which no value is paid, as between the parties, is essential, a bona fide assignee thereof for value, receiving it at a time subsequent to its execution, is not entitled to priority, in the proceeds of the mortgaged property, as against an intervening lienor, in good faith, who has complied with all statutory requirements as to notice, although the mortgage was executed and recorded prior to the attaching of his lien. Nor is it material, as against the equity of such third person, that at the time of the assignment, the mortgagor made an affidavit falsely reciting that the mortgagee had advanced the whole sum without abatement, and that there were no off-sets, defenses or counter-claims, and although, as against the mortgagor, an estoppel to show the truth arose.

§ 190. The bond and mortgage, under indorsement, quasi-negotiable.—Under the application of the rules of estoppel in pais or equitable estoppel, arising upon the indorsement of certificates of no defense or equities, and like declarations, or acknowledgments of the receipt of the whole sum named, and by other affirmative acts or neglects of the mortgagor, a bona fide sub-assignee for value without notice, acquires a good title as against the owner, or third persons, or creditors, although such bond and mortgage were fraudulently obtained by his assignor. Upon the same rule of estoppel in pais a bona fide grantee for value without notice of a prior unrecorded deed, acquires a valid title, although his grantor is chargeable with full notice of fraud. Certificates of payment and of no defense have been indorsed, in cases where they have acquired the same under assignment from a bona fide holder for value, without notice, although chargeable with notice of fraud or breach of trust in the original transaction. Such representations indorsed upon bonds and mortgages partake, under the operation of the rules of estoppel in pais, of the nature of blank indorsements of negotiable instruments. They pass from hand to hand, and any subsequent assignee thereof, although having notice of equities, may claim protection under a bona fide holder for value, without notice, in the line of assignments. Such rules of estoppel in pais are supported upon the ground that where bonds and mortgages are issued indorsed as stated, for the purpose of obtaining money thereon for the use of the mortgagor, it is a presumption therefrom that the intention of the mortgagor was that the securities should be available as collateral or otherwise, and that the market should not be closed upon the first assignee, except upon his consent to indorse a new certificate. If the rule were otherwise, a bona fide assignee for value, without notice, of a bond and mortgage, so indorsed, would lose one of the chief advantages necessarily belonging to that favored position.

§ 191. Assignment of void, invalid and fraudulent securities.— Where the mortgage security itself is absolutely void, it is not enforced as security for any purpose of reimbursement or indemnity. Where a conveyance, made by a husband through a third party to his wife, is fraudulent as to the creditors of the husband, and the wife is a party to the fraud, no protection for any sum paid or liability incurred will be given her. Otherwise, where an assignee for value is without notice of the fraud. In such case, the assignee is protected to the amount of his advances. § 192. Payments to mortgagee, after assignment.—Payments upon a bond secured by mortgage by the mortgagor to the mortgagee, made after an assignment thereof by the latter, when made in good faith, without notice, actual or constructive, of the assignment, are valid. The sums thus paid in good faith are credited on the bond and mortgage as against any assignee thereof. Nor is a payment made before maturity evidence of bad faith; nor the non-production of the bond and mortgage and indorsement of such payment thereon when made. No presumption that the transaction is not bona fide arises where, upon payment in full of the debt, the securities are not re-delivered and no satisfaction of the mortgage executed, and no inquiries made relative thereto. An assignee of such bond and mortgage is bound by such release as he is by payments of the mortgagor made bona fide. The rule, however, is restricted in its application to persons executing the mortgage directly or indirectly through trustees. A bond and mortgage were assigned by an administrator of a deceased mortgagee, who subsequently by mistake discharged the mortgage without receiving payment. The discharge was duly recorded, and the premises were then sold to a bona fide purchaser for value, without notice. The assignee of the securities brought suit to foreclose. The effect of the recording of the release of the mortgage being to cancel the record thereof, the subsequent purchaser for value, in good faith, without notice, was protected. But the cancellation of a mortgage on the record is only prima facie evidence of its discharge, and the fact that such cancellation was procured or made by fraud or accident, or in mistake, is subject to proof by an assignee or party interested. Nor will such cancellation affect the right to hold other collateral securities, so long as the debt secured by such mortgage remains unpaid.

b. California—Record.—In California, it has been held that the recording of a mortgage is not necessary as between the parties to it: and is only necessary to give notice to third parties. The execution of the mortgage creates the lien, without reference to the recording. Downing v. La Du, 82 Cal. 471.

c. Mortgage securing annuity.—Where a mortgage was executed to secure a note given for an annuity, it was held, upon a petition to enforce the obligation, that the consideration expressed "for value received, and in consideration of love and affection," imported a valuable consideration, and the averments properly raised issues of fact, and that it was error to sustain a demurrer to the petition. Cotton v. Graham, 84 Ky. 672.

d. Presumption from mortgage.—Where a party executes a note and mortgage of even date, and the recitals of the mortgage show it was exe-

cuted to secure an amount equal to the note, the presumption will obtain that the mortgage secures the note. Bailey v. Fanning Orphan School, 14 S. W. Rep. (Ky.) 908.

e. Judgment on notes.—A judgment in personam against the maker of promissory notes secured by a special mortgage, and in which there is a recognition of the mortgage and a decree for its enforcement, merges the notes completely and perfectly, so that hereafter the judgment is the only evidence of the debt, but not so as to the mortgage. It retains its full force, effect and rank after the judgment, as it has before, the judgment only rendering it executory by ordinary fi. fa., but not precluding executory proceedings subsequently. Lalane v. Payne, 42 La. Ann. 152.

f. Maine.—In Maine, where the indorsee of mortgage notes, comprising the entire mortgage debt, puts them into a judgment and execution against the mortgagor, and levies the same upon the mortgaged premises, the mortgage is thereby extinguished. Lord v. Crowell, 75 Me. 399.

g. Usury—Res adjudicata.—Certain notes secured by mortgage were, by the holder, sold and indorsed after maturity, without recourse, and a bill was filed by the purchaser to foreclose, to which the defendant answered, alleging usury in the notes. The indorser was notified by the assignee of the notes, and the indorser's evidence was taken in the case. Upon the trial, the defense of usury was sustained, and since the payments of interest were equal to the face of the notes, the bill was dismissed. The assignee of the notes then brought an action against the assignor on his implied warranty that there was due on the notes what appeared to be due on their face. Held, that inasmuch as the assignor had notice of the bill to foreclose, and participated in the defense, was concluded by the decree in that case as to the fact of usury, and that there was nothing due on the notes. Drennan v. Bunn, 124 Ill. 175.

h. Executor—Application of legacy.—The holder of assigned notes was the executor of an estate which owed the mortgagor and maker of the notes a legacy. Held, that the legacy could not be availed as payment of the notes, until the same was applied as such by the executor. Blair v. White, 61 Vt. 110. In this case the court said: “But, inasmuch as the mortgage security is inadequate, and the orator has in his hands another fund, to which he can legally resort for payment or part payment of his mortgage notes, equity requires that he should resort to that fund before resorting to the mortgage security, to the damage of the defendant; for this course works no injury to either creditor, but does justice to both. But the orator is not bound to resort to that fund, to the detriment of the estate, in respect to the unsecured debts that the debtor owes it.”

i. Sale—Notice.—A trust deed, given to secure the payment of a note, with interest, provided that on default of payment of either principal or interest, the trustee might sell the premises conveyed, on giving twenty days’ notice of the time and place of the sale, in any daily newspaper of the city where the property was situate, and waive any personal notice to the makers of the deed. Before any sale was made, the makers sold and conveyed their equity of redemption to a third person. It was held, the fact that no personal notice of the time and place of a sale subsequently made

was given to the makers of the trust deed, was no ground on which to have the trustee's sale set aside. (Cleaver v. Green, 107 Ill. 67.)

j. Sale with notice.—Where commercial paper is pledged as security for a debt, the pledgee has no right, in the absence of special power to do so, to sell the pledge, but is bound to collect it and apply the proceeds to the payment of the debt for which the pledge was given. And where the pledgee had the special power given him by the pledgor to sell the pledge, at any time before or after the debt became due, at public or private sale, with or without notice, such a sale would invest the purchaser with a good title to the property, and trover will not lie for it. Cole v. Dalziel, 18 Bradw. (Ill.) 23.

k. Execution sale.—A person holding notes and mortgages assigned to him as collateral security may purchase the same at an execution sale under another claim. Clark v. Holland, 72 Iowa, 34.

l. Sale under power.—Speaking of a sale under power in a mortgage given to secure a note, the Supreme Court of Illinois, in Sanford v. Kane, 133 Ill. 199, said: "The power of sale was given by the mortgage to the mortgagee, or to his heirs or assigns. If there was no transfer of the debt so as to pass the legal title thereto, the power could be executed only by the mortgagee, but, if the debt was legally assigned, the assignee was the one authorized to make the sale. In Hamilton v. Lubukee, 51 Ill. 415, the mortgage contained a power of sale given to 'the mortgagee, his heirs or assigns,' in case of default. The notes in that case were never assigned, but were sold and delivered to Eisendrath & Co. The mortgage was assigned by an indorsement made thereon. The court said: 'The mortgage not being an assignable instrument either at common law or under the statute, the power to sell remained with the mortgagee.' And the court referred to Olds v. Cummings, 31 Ill. 188, etc.

The mortgagee or an assignee of a mortgage securing a note upon foreclosure can recover no more than the debt due him as pledgor, and will hold the balance as trustee for the benefit of the mortgagor and his assigns, Handy v. Sibley, 46 Oh. St. 9. Mortgage and notes must be construed together. Schultz v. Plankinton Bank, 141 Ill. 116.

m. Sale by administrator.—An administrator holding notes secured by a mortgage, belonging to his intestate may lawfully sell at private sale and assign to the purchaser such securities, without first demanding payment of the pledgor, whose rights are not affected by such transfer. And such action will not constitute a defense to a foreclosure suit. Drake v. Cloonan, 99 Mich. 121.

n. Renewal note.—Where a renewal note recited the note and mortgage were pledged to secure its payment, the pledge has relation to, and will be given effect as of the date it was first pledged for the payment of the debt evidenced by the renewal note, if the interest of the pledgee requires it. o. Counsel fees.—Not included in a mortgage note. Adler v. Newell, 41 Pac. (Cal.) 799.

p. Onus.—The onus is on makers of negotiable promissory note to show that plaintiff is not a bona fide holder, where fraud is alleged. Halbert v. Elmwood, 1 Kansas App. 95.

CHAPTER XIX.

BONDS AND MORTGAGES AS COLLATERAL SECURITY.

§ 194. The use of bonds and mortgages as collateral security.  
195. The pledge of bonds and mortgages by delivery.  
196. The equities to which the pledgee is not subject.  
197. The pledgee's equities, as against fraudulent releases.  
198. The pledgee's rights, in cases of fraud, misappropriation, etc.  
199. Realization of the securities by pledgee.  
200. Pledgor’s rights upon payment of debt.

§ 194. The use of bonds and mortgages as collateral security.—The use of bonds and mortgages, as collateral security for other obligations, is general in the states where this form of security is adopted. The pledgee, receiving the same in good faith for a valuable consideration, properly assigned, is vested with the legal title to the bond and mortgage, and entitled to enforce the mortgage security in equity with the same rights as a purchaser for value, in good faith, and is also subject to the like equities. Such a non-negotiable bond, as the evidence of a debt or obligation, and the mortgage given as collateral security for its payment, are the subject of pledge. The mortgage security creating a specific lien on the land, the assignment carries the legal estate to the pledgees, and is governed by rules generally applicable to mortgages of a legal or equitable interest in real property.

Campbell v. Parker, 9 Bosw. 322; Manhattan Co., 1 Paige Ch. 48, 50; Clark v. Henry, 2 Cow. 324; Rice v. Dillingham, 73 Me. 59; Carr v. Carr, 52 N.Y. 251; Slee v. …

NOTES.

a. Foreclosure.—A mortgagor gave his note to the mortgagee in payment of a portion of the amount secured by the bond and mortgage. Subsequently the mortgagee discounted the note at a bank which had knowledge of the purpose for which it was given, and thereafter the mortgagee assigned the mortgage to a person ignorant of the partial payment thereon.

A bond and mortgage transferred by an assignment absolute in terms, but in fact as collateral security for a promissory note made by the assignor, by the terms of which the assignor is given authority to sell the collateral securities upon default in payment of the note, is a pledge and not a mortgage or sale of such collateral securities. The pledgor remains the general owner of the collateral where the title has not been passed, the pledgee holding a special property therein as security for the advances made.

§ 195. The pledge of bonds and mortgages by delivery. — A bond as a non-negotiable chose in action, together with

1 Campbell v. Parker, 9 Bosw. 322. 2 Dougherty v. Remington Pager Co., 81 N. Y. 496.

Under the agreement between the mortgagor and mortgagee, the note was to operate as a payment on account of the mortgage only when paid. In an action to foreclose the mortgage brought by the assignee thereof, held that plaintiff could only recover from the proceeds of the mortgaged lands the amount due on the mortgage less the amount of such debt. Fitch v. McDowell, 80 Hun, 207.

b. Foreclosure — Coupon notes. — Foreclosure of a mortgage securing coupon notes may be decreed, although some of the notes secured by such mortgage have not matured. And notes so secured will not lose their negotiable character by reason of foreclosure on failure to pay any installment of interest. Swett v. Stark, 31 Fed. Rep. 858.

c. Corporation bonds. — As to foreclosure of a trust deed securing bonds of a corporation, see Robinson v. Alabama & G. Mfg. Co., 48 Fed. Rep. 12.

d. Attorney's fees. — As to right of trustee to attorney’s fees on foreclosure, see Fowler v. Trust Co., 141 U. S. 384; Alabama & G. Mfg. Co., 51 Fed. Rep. 268.

e. Maturity of notes on default. — The validity of a provision in a mortgage that upon default in the payment of any one bond at maturity, all the bonds shall become due and payable, was sustained by the Supreme Court of North Carolina in Copehart v. Dettrick, 91 N. C. 844; citing, Howell v. Railroad Co., 94 U. S. 463.

f. Release of collaterals. — A principal note for $20,000 was covered by collateral in the shape of two notes for $15,000 each, secured by a deed of trust upon real estate. Upon payment of the principal notes, held that the collateral notes and deed of trust were not released thereby, where it was shown that a contract had been executed, prior to such payment, whereby it was agreed that all notes in the hands of the creditor, including the $15,000 notes, should be held as collateral to other outstanding obligations, some of which remained unpaid when the $20,000 note was paid. Bartalott v. International Bank, 18 Ill. App. 359.

g. Merger. — Not made unless so intended. Hoffman v. Wilhelm, 68 Iowa, 510.
